keeps a cancel: the SQL `SaveRun` never turns a Cancelled row back, the VM file / Community blob store copies the cancel
into a later save of the same run. A cancelled run is no guard trip and no error (run health `skipped`, no fix request).
Entry points: **Operations > Jobs**, "Cancel this run" beside the last run while it is going (Admin, a confirm dialog and a
required reason, audited `job.flowrun.cancel`): in ONE transaction the run is marked Cancelled, its queue request ended and
its lock released -- through the procedure `cfg.FlowRunCancelSet` only (`sql/si-pro-settings.sql`; the web identity
holds EXECUTE on it, granted by `SI-ManagementGrants.ps1`, and no right on `cfg.FlowRun`, `cfg.PipelineLock` or
`cfg.PipelineQueue`: one run, never the table; an existing install gets the procedure and the grant from the update's
schema + grants step; a database without it yet answers Missing) -- then `caj-si-flow` is started once with `SI_FLOW_CANCEL=1`,
`SI_FLOW_CANCEL_RUN`, `SI_FLOW_CANCEL_REASON` and `SI_FLOW_CANCEL_RUNNER` (the lock's holder) to do steps 0 and 2-5.
**Support** starts `caj-si-flow` once with `SI_FLOW_CANCEL=1` and `SI_FLOW_CANCEL_REASON=<why>` (a VM:
`engine\flow\Invoke-SIJobFlowRun.ps1 -HostKind Vm -Cancel -CancelReason '<why>'`); no SQL by people. A cancel without a
reason is refused.

**A run never finishes on the wrong release (#700).** Every new run records the version it STARTED on
(`cfg.FlowRun.Version`; the run record's `Version`). After the update has rolled the jobs to a new version
(`setup/Invoke-SIContainerUpdate.ps1` step 4b, Pro), a run that is going and started on another version -- or on a
version that did not record it -- is cancelled the same way, and one plain line says so ("pipeline run <id> started on
<version> and was cancelled, so it does not finish on the wrong version"); a run of the new version goes on. Only the
update does this, right after it installs (owner: "Updater only") -- the pipeline's own wake-up never cancels a run for
its version; a database that cannot keep versions (its schema not applied again) is left alone. Existing installs gain `Version` and `CancelledBy` (nullable) when the update applies the Pro schema,
before any roll.

**A job stopped from outside is not a platform error (#700).** An execution that ends `Stopped` (in Azure, by a person,
by a release tool) gets class `stopped`: it is never started again as a container that never started the engine (working
rule 4 retries only `job-failed`), never restarted on a new install's first collection either (owner: "Stop is final"
-- a failed step there is still restarted), and the run stops there (`Get-SIJobFlowBlocked`:
the steps after it are Skipped `flow-stopped`, the run ends Stopped with "... was stopped from outside the pipeline -- the
run does not go on by itself"). A run whose runner died is still resumed (a platform failure) -- ONCE: its stopped
execution then ends it Stopped, a finished state that is never resumed again. A job stopped at its OWN run limit is still
self-healed (that is judged by the time it ran).

### 7c. Steps side by side, and the classifier's unchanged skip (#528)

> Measured internal 2026-10-09: the 12 steps strictly one after the other took ~1 h 30 (ptc 15, identity 12, azure 22,
> endpoint 1, publicip 2, correlation 1, RA 10, RA detailed 12, CMDB SQL 2, vulnerabilities 4, data sync 5, mails 1 min).
> Rule: only what the code proves independent runs together.

**What reads what (verified in the code 2026-10-10).** A *need* skips its dependents on a failure; a *read* (the map's
`reads`) is a same-day read the job does without -- it then uses the previous run's output -- so it orders the steps but
skips nothing.

| Job | Needs (same day, hard) | Reads (same day, soft) | Reads only the previous run (a cycle, by design) |
|---|---|---|---|
| identity | ptc (catalog) | -- | endpoint's device tiers (`Get-SIEndpointTierMap`) |
| azure | ptc | **identity** (`Get-SIIdentityTierMap` -> `XENG_AccessedByT0/T1Count`, the `CrossEngine_AccessedByTieredIdentity` proof, the AI-classify input) | endpoint's VM correlation (`EndpointAzureCorrelationCache.ps1`, 8 days, latest per VM) |
| endpoint | ptc | **identity** (`Get-SIBulkDeviceUserCorrelation` MostFrequentUser tier, `AssetProfileByLogonUser`) | -- |
| publicip | endpoint, azure | -- | -- |
| RA / RA detailed | the profiles + correlation | each other's AI-summary snapshot (leader / follower) | -- |

**The default layout (level 2):** `ptc -> identity -> [azure ‖ endpoint] -> publicip -> correlation -> RA -> RA detailed
-> Deliver` (stage `withPrevious` in `config/job-flow.locked.json`, `JobFlow.DefaultTogether`). A `withPrevious` step
starts together with the step SHIPPED above it only when that step is installed (`Test-SIJobFlowTogetherWithShippedAbove`
/ `JobFlow.TogetherWithShippedAbove`): without azure, endpoint starts on its own instead of joining identity. Not grouped:
identity ‖ azure (azure reads identity's tiers of the same day -- an operator decision, it would save ~11 min internal at
the price of a one-day-late `XENG_AccessedBy*`), RA ‖ RA detailed (the shared AI summary), anything in Correlate /
Deliver (not proven independent; Deliver's steps are short).

**The runner** (`Invoke-SIJobFlow`, unchanged): a group's steps are started one after the other in one pass (each saved
`Starting`, then `Running` with its execution), then polled together until all ended; the next group waits for the
slowest. A failed step never stops its partner (it is followed to its end); `stop` stops what had not started;
`skip-dependents` skips the steps that NEED the failed one; the stage fails when any of its steps failed (rule 4). A
runner that stops mid-group resumes the record: each `Running` step is polled, a `Starting` one is reported Interrupted --
nothing is started twice.

**CONVERGE-DEFAULTS (framework §12.16).** A stored pipeline carries `defaults` (its layout level; absent = 1). Read below
the current level (`Update-SIJobFlowDefaultLayout`; the web app `JobFlow.ConvergeDefaultLayout`, same rule): when it still
has the OLD default -- no group anywhere and each stage exactly the shipped steps in the shipped order -- each
`withPrevious` step is set to start together with the step above it, every other step setting is kept, one migration note
says so; any other pipeline is left as it is. Either way it is marked the current level, so once saved the decision is
never made again: a person who then runs azure and endpoint one after the other keeps that. Read-time, like the other
stored-pipeline migrations (the updater step, a moved Risk Analysis): the runner reads the definition on every wake-up,
so no updater step is needed; the next save stores it.

**The classifier's unchanged skip.** The privilege tier classifier's inputs cost seconds (2 Graph lists, 14
service-principal lookups, 2 ARM lists); its AI pass is the minutes. Each run collects the inputs and fingerprints them
(`Get-PTCInputFingerprint`: every role / permission / action, sorted, plus the built-in AD group names, the engine file's
hash -- its prompts and lists change with a release --, the AI switch and the AI deployment). The catalog's `Metadata`
records `InputFingerprint`, `GeneratedAtUtc` and `Complete` (every item tiered: nothing at Tier 99, nothing kept from an
older catalog, every input section collected). `Get-PTCUnchangedDecision` skips the AI pass only when the fingerprint
equals the last catalog's, that catalog is complete, and younger than `SI_PrivilegeTierClassifier_RefreshDays` (default
7; 0 = every run) -- the run then ends successfully with `skipped: unchanged since <date>` in its log and run-health row,
the catalog (local and in storage) untouched. A dry run always rebuilds (beside the catalog). The older `<24 h` age skip
before the collection is kept.

### 8. How to **scale up** under load

KEDA scales workers based on queue depth. Adjust the cap:

```powershell
az containerapp job update --name caj-si-endpoint-worker --resource-group rg-<suffix> --max-executions 60
```

Or globally on next bootstrap:

```powershell
$global:SI_Bootstrap_KedaMaxReplicas = 60
.\Bootstrap-ContainerAppJob.ps1
```

### 9a. No PowerShell modules: the module-free runtime

<a id="9a-how-powershell-modules-are-pre-staged-in-the-image"></a>

**Design rule (operator decision 2026-10-05, REQUIREMENTS #305):** SecurityInsight v3 uses **no PowerShell modules** -- no `Az.*`, no `Microsoft.Graph*`, no `AzLogDcrIngestPS`, `MicrosoftGraphPS`, `ImportExcel` or `powershell-yaml`. Every call is native: REST against the Microsoft endpoints, and .NET for everything local. Nothing is installed from the PowerShell Gallery at build time or at run time, so there is no module version to pin, no drift between a VM and a container, and no Gallery outage that can stop a run.

**The image** therefore has no `Install-Module` layer:

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/powershell:lts-ubuntu-22.04
COPY . /app/
ENTRYPOINT ["pwsh","-NoProfile","-File","/app/container/Start-SIInContainer.ps1"]
```

A smaller image, a faster `az acr build`, and a faster job start (no module import at the top of every execution). Updating the image is now only about SecurityInsight's own code (§9b).

**The runtime layers** -- what replaced each module:

| Concern | Native implementation | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Tokens** | One function per audience: `Get-SIAzureToken -Audience Arm \| LaQuery \| Storage \| KeyVault \| Graph \| Monitor`. A **managed identity** asks its endpoint (Container Apps `IDENTITY_ENDPOINT`, Azure Arc, Azure VM IMDS); a **service principal certificate** signs a JWT client assertion with the private key read from the X509 certificate store by thumbprint (no `Cert:` drive, so it works in a Linux container). Cached per identity + audience until 5 minutes before expiry. | `engine/_shared/SI-AzRest.ps1`, `engine/_shared/SI-LogIngest.ps1` (`Get-SILogIngestToken`), `auth/SI-ManagedIdentity.ps1`, `auth/Find-SICertificate.ps1` |
| **Azure Resource Manager** | `Invoke-SIArm` -- GET / PUT / PATCH / DELETE, list with `nextLink` paging | `SI-AzRest.ps1` |
| **Resource Graph** | `Search-SIResourceGraph` -- every page, following `$skipToken` | `SI-AzRest.ps1` |
| **Log Analytics queries** | `Invoke-SILaQuery` -- the data plane (`api.loganalytics.io`), which returns the service's own semantic error instead of a generic one; cells come back as text, as the callers expect | `SI-AzRest.ps1` |
| **Key Vault** | `Get-SIKeyVaultSecretValue`, `Set-SIAzKeyVaultSecretRest` | `SI-AzRest.ps1` |
| **Storage** (blob, queue, table) | OAuth with `x-ms-version`; never a storage key | `SI-AzRest.ps1` |
| **Ingestion** | The Azure Monitor **Log Ingestion API**: rows are posted (compressed, batched under the size limit) to the data collection endpoint with the rule's immutable id. Custom tables and data collection rules are created and extended by SecurityInsight itself over ARM. | `engine/_shared/SI-LogIngest.ps1` |
| **Microsoft Graph and Defender** | REST with the same tokens, paging and throttling handled in one place | `engine/_shared/SI-GraphRest.ps1` |
| **Excel reports** | Written as Open XML with .NET (zip + XML) | `engine/risk-analysis/_shared/RA-XlsxWriter.ps1` |
| **YAML rule packs** | Parsed by SecurityInsight's own reader | `engine/_shared/SI-Yaml.ps1` |

**Storage access is identity-only.** SecurityInsight's own storage account (the `sistaging` blobs, the
fingerprint / CMDB / Shodan tables, the shard queues, run logs and the identity ledger) is reached only
with the run's signed-in identity, over OAuth. There is no storage-key option: no setting, no job secret,
no key fetch. The identity needs three data roles on the account -- **Storage Blob Data Contributor**,
**Storage Queue Data Contributor** and **Storage Table Data Contributor** -- and setup grants them for
every host type:

| Host | Identity | Who grants the three storage roles |
|---|---|---|
| Container Apps Jobs, managed identity | the jobs' user-assigned identity | `Bootstrap-ContainerAppJob.ps1` (`-GrantIdentityRoles`), from the identity grant plan |
| Container Apps Jobs, certificate or client secret | the SecurityInsight app identity | setup (`Initialize-SIInfra`) |
| Windows VM, app identity (certificate or secret) | the SecurityInsight app identity | setup (`Initialize-SIInfra`; `setup\Grant-SIIdentity.ps1 -AppId <client id>` grants it again) |
| Windows VM / Arc server, managed identity | the machine's identity | `setup\Grant-SIIdentity.ps1` (the same grant plan as the container identity) |

A storage key left in an older configuration (or a key-mode switch) is ignored without a message, and the
next container setup removes a storage-key secret an older setup put on a job.

**Shared-key access is OFF on a new account.** Every install path that creates the storage account
goes through ONE create gate, `New-SIAzStorageAccount` → `New-SIAzStorageAccountRest`
(`engine/_shared/SI-AzRest.ps1`), whose body is `Get-SIStorageAccountCreateProperties`:
`allowSharedKeyAccess = false`, `defaultToOAuthAuthentication = true`, `minimumTlsVersion = TLS1_2`,
`allowBlobPublicAccess = false`, HTTPS only -- whatever the caller passes. The callers are
`Bootstrap-Storage.ps1`, `setup/ConfigWizard/backend/Initialize-SIInfra.ps1` (the guided install, free and Pro,
and the unattended setup run it) -- setup scripts only: a collection run
creates no storage account (see "A collection run assigns no role and creates no resource"). (The retired SI Analyzer's
own account path is deleted with it.) With shared-key access off, an account key and a key-signed SAS stop working; a user-delegation
SAS (signed in with Entra ID) keeps working.

**A collection run assigns no role and creates no resource.** An identity, endpoint, Azure or public-IP collection
(and, collected in parts, its producer and every worker) makes no role assignment and creates no resource group,
workspace, data collection endpoint or storage account. Setup does: `setup/ConfigWizard/backend/Initialize-SIInfra.ps1`
(the guided install and the unattended setup run it) creates the resources and
grants the app identity; `setup/Grant-SIIdentity.ps1 -AllowSchemaCreate -Apply` and the container setup grant a managed
identity. The roles are the narrow ones, never plain Contributor:

| Role | Where | What the run does with it |
|---|---|---|
| Monitoring Metrics Publisher | the rules' resource group | sends rows through the data collection rules |
| Monitoring Contributor | the rules' resource group (and the endpoint's, when it is another one) | creates its rules and adds a new column to one |
| Log Analytics Contributor | the workspace | creates its tables and adds a new column to one |
| Storage Blob / Queue / Table Data Contributor | the storage account | its own run state |

What the run does instead is LOOK (`engine/asset-profiling/shared/SI-RunAccessCheck.ps1`), read-only and once per
process -- a worker does not repeat what its producer checked:

1. Do the workspace, the rules' resource group and the endpoint exist (and the storage account, when its resource
   group is configured)? Only a clear "not found" counts; the endpoint is looked for by name in the whole subscription
   before it is called missing, because the send finds it there too.
2. May the identity send? One read of its role assignments in the subscription. A role counts when it is held at the
   scope or above it and its definition allows the action, so Contributor, Owner or a custom role is never reported
   as missing; a role that looks missing is looked for once more with group memberships included before anything is
   said.
3. Only a run that had something to create (a new table, a new rule or a new column) is also checked for the two
   create roles, after the create step, from the role assignments already read.

Something missing is ONE line in the run log -- `access check: ...` -- naming it and the setup command that fixes it,
said once per process. The run then goes on exactly as before and the send (or the create) fails with its own error.
An identity that may not read its role assignments, a role definition that cannot be read or a lookup that is
refused gives no line: what cannot be read is never guessed. The setting `SI_PrestageInfra` is retired with the
behaviour it switched; a value left in a configuration is ignored.

**An existing account is not changed automatically.** `setup/Set-SIStorageSharedKey.ps1` reports the
account's settings and what would break; `-Disable` switches shared-key access off (and Entra ID on as the
default) only when nothing still needs a key, otherwise it changes nothing and lists what to fix
(`setup/_shared/SI-StorageSharedKey.ps1`, pure):

| Check | Source | Blocks when |
|---|---|---|
| Key traffic | the account's `Transactions` metric split by `Authentication`, last `-Days` (default 7) | any `AccountKey` or `SAS` request (a VM, a script or a tool outside SecurityInsight shows up here too); metrics that cannot be read also block -- unknown is not "unused" |
| Queue scaler | every Container Apps job in the subscription that uses the account (`SI_StorageAccount`, or a scaler on its queues) | an `azure-queue` rule with a connection secret, or with no managed identity |
| Older release | the same jobs | a retired storage-key secret or setting still on the job |
| Data roles | role assignments at the account and above (`atScope()`) | the identity the job signs in as (`SI_SPN_OBJECTID`) lacks Storage Blob / Queue / Table Data Contributor |

`-Enable` is the way back. Reading needs Reader + Monitoring Reader on the account; switching needs
Storage Account Contributor.

**The KEDA queue scaler signs in with the jobs' managed identity.** A worker job
(`caj-si-<engine>-worker`) gets its `azure-queue` scale rule from `Get-SIKedaQueueScaleArgs`
(`container/_shared/SI-ContainerConfig.ps1`): queue `si-<engine>-shards`, the account, `queueLength=1`, and
`--scale-rule-identity <the jobs' user-assigned identity>` -- on create and on every update, so an older
worker (whose scaler had no sign-in at all) gets the identity on the next run of setup. In ManagedIdentity
mode the identity already holds Storage Queue Data Contributor; in Certificate mode the grant plan adds
**Storage Queue Data Reader** on the account for the scaler (`-KedaQueueScaler`). The Secret sign-in has no
identity, so `-UseKEDA` with it is refused before anything is created.

**One HTTP seam, one retry rule.** Every Azure call goes through `Invoke-SIAzRestHttp` (`HttpWebRequest`: a 4xx body and headers read the same way on PowerShell 5.1 and 7). 429 / 408 / 5xx / no response: wait (`Retry-After` when sent) and retry in the run; 401 once: refresh the token and repeat once; any other 4xx: fail fast with the service's own response. Tests mock the seam, so the whole layer is proven offline.

**Sign-in at setup and in the tools.** Nothing borrows a `Connect-AzAccount` / `Connect-MgGraph` session any more. Setup, the updater and the diagnostics request their tokens through the same functions, as a managed identity or a service principal with a certificate (the private key stays in the certificate store). The diagnostics scripts share `diagnostics/_DiagnosticsAzure.ps1`, which takes the identity from parameters, from `SI_DIAGNOSTICS_APPID` / `SI_DIAGNOSTICS_TENANTID` / `SI_DIAGNOSTICS_CERTTHUMBPRINT` (or `SI_DIAGNOSTICS_MANAGEDIDENTITY`), or from the install's own config.

**PowerShell 5.1 and 7.** The layer avoids `?.` / `??` and `RSA.ImportFromPem`, so the same files run on a Windows VM under Windows PowerShell 5.1 and in the Linux container under PowerShell 7.

**Upgrading from 2.2:** the modules 2.2 installed on a VM can stay or be removed -- v3 never loads them (see RELEASENOTES).

**Guarded:** `tests/pester/SIv3-NoPsModules.Tests.ps1` fails the build if a runtime script (engine, launcher, container, auth) loads, installs or calls a module, or a Dockerfile installs one. (Token requests with a client secret go through `Invoke-SILogIngestHttp`, the same `HttpWebRequest` shape.)

### 9b. How to update the image (after engine code change)

Two equivalent paths — both server-side via `az acr build`, both zero-downtime:

```powershell
# Path A: full bootstrap (also reconciles cron, env vars, KEDA caps)
cd C:\SCRIPTS\AutomateIT\SOLUTIONS\SecurityInsight
.\Bootstrap-ContainerAppJob.ps1

# Path B: image-only roll (faster — skips KEDA/cron reconcile): build the image server-side, then point the jobs at it
az acr build --registry acr<suffix> --image si-orchestrator:<tag> --file container/Dockerfile .
az containerapp job update --name caj-si-<engine> --resource-group rg-<suffix> --image acr<suffix>.azurecr.io/si-orchestrator:<tag>
```

Path B is the right one when only engine code changed (no Dockerfile change; there are no modules to bump since §9a). Path A is the right one when the change also touches cron, env vars, KEDA caps, or any param exposed via `$global:SI_Bootstrap_*`.

### 9c. How the entrypoint dispatcher works (SI_ROLE)

Every job in the fleet uses the **same** Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT (`pwsh -NoProfile -File /app/container/Start-SIInContainer.ps1`). The script branches on `$env:SI_ROLE` at the very top:

| `SI_ROLE` | What runs | Set by Bootstrap on |
|---|---|---|
| `worker` | `Start-SIInContainer.ps1` continues to collection path | `caj-si-<engine>-worker` and legacy `caj-si-<engine>` |
| `producer` | dispatches to `Invoke-ShardProducer.ps1` | `caj-si-<engine>-producer` |
| `ra` | dispatches to `Start-RiskAnalysisInContainer.ps1` | `caj-si-risk-analysis` |

**Why not `--command`/`--args`?** The az CLI uses argparse `nargs='+'` for both, which stops consuming tokens at any leading-dash arg. PowerShell flags all lead with `-` (`-NoProfile`, `-File`), so `--args -NoProfile -File /app/...` gets parsed as `--args` (empty) plus unknown globals `-NoProfile -File`. The SI_ROLE env-var dispatch sidesteps this entirely — same ENTRYPOINT for every job, different code path inside.

### 10. Common issues

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| `Key Vault '<name>' not found` | Pre-create KV before running Setup. See § 1. |
| `New-Guid : The term 'New-Guid' is not recognized` | Az SDK's autorest path calls it in a constrained child runspace. Define the shim before any Az cmdlet — see § 3. |
| `az login (interactive) failed` | Container phase requires az CLI signed in. Pre-`az login` or pass SPN secret env vars. |
| `az acr build` fails with `denied: requested access to the resource is denied` | ACR admin user is disabled. Caller's SPN needs `AcrPush` on the registry. |
| Worker scale stuck at 0 | Queue isn't getting messages — check producer execution log for crash. |
| Engine throws `AuthorizationPermissionMismatch` on Storage | SPN missing `Storage Blob Data Contributor` on `st<suffix>` (Phase 2 should have granted it). |
| `Required global $global:OpenAI_apiKey is empty in ...custom.ps1` | Community `Write-SICustomConfig` only emits the KV-pull line, not the 4 OpenAI globals. Workaround: set `$global:OpenAI_endpoint/_deployment/_apiVersion/_apiKey` inline before invoking bootstrap (same shape as `platform-defaults.ps1` OpenAI globals block). Long-term fix: bootstrap should treat OpenAI as optional when `$global:SI_EnableAI` is false. |
| Container App Job execution `Failed` with `-NoProfile -File` not recognised | Old bootstrap put `--command pwsh --args "-NoProfile ..."` per-job. argparse can't pass leading-dash strings as values. Fix: pull new image (SI_ROLE dispatcher landed in v2.3) AND re-run `Bootstrap-ContainerAppJob.ps1` so UPDATE clears stale `command/args`. |
| `caj-si-schema-discovery-*` jobs fail with no orchestrator | schema-discovery is a stage inside asset-profiling, not a standalone engine. Remove from `$Engines` (bootstrap default does this since the fix) and delete dangling jobs: `az containerapp job delete --name caj-si-schema-discovery-{producer,worker} --resource-group <rg> --yes`. |

### 11. Teardown

```powershell
# Stop all auto-runs, keep data
foreach ($e in 'endpoint','identity','azure','schema-discovery','risk-analysis','privilege-tier-classifier','asset-tagging','publicip') {
    az containerapp job update --name "caj-si-$e-producer" --resource-group rg-<suffix> --cron-expression "" 2>$null
    az containerapp job update --name "caj-si-$e"          --resource-group rg-<suffix> --cron-expression "" 2>$null
}

# Full delete
Remove-AzResourceGroup -Name rg-<suffix> -Force
```

## Architecture and security (3.0)

One place that says how SecurityInsight 3.0 is put together and secured, read from the code. The sections after
this chapter hold the detail; this chapter is the summary they agree with. Where a part is a design that is still
being built, it says so.

### A1. Components

| Component | Edition | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Collection engines -- endpoint, identity, Azure, public IP -- and the privilege-tier classifier | Community + Pro | PowerShell engines that read Defender XDR, Entra ID, Azure Resource Graph / Resource Manager and Log Analytics, profile every asset and give it a tier. The public-IP engine can also ask Shodan about your own public IPs (optional, paid key). |
| Risk Analysis and trend | Community + Pro | Turns the profiles into ranked findings (Identity, Endpoint, Azure, Public IP and cross-engine), writes them to Log Analytics, Excel, JSON and mail (optional AI summary), and keeps the daily trend. |
| Pro engines | Pro | Cross-engine correlation (one CI across sources), asset properties, the data sync into SQL, the vulnerability close-loop and its connectors (SQL, ServiceNow, REST), the ServiceNow CMDB feed, the close-loop / exemption mail job, asset tagging, the template release job. |
| Pro web app | Pro | ASP.NET Core in a Container App: findings, fifteen collection views, tier board, exemptions, management views, wall board, chat, settings, access, template releases, deviations, jobs. |
| MCP server | Pro | A separate Container App with its own managed identity and read-only database access, offering the same curated read-only tools as the chat to MCP clients that present an Entra token. |
| Updater job | Pro, containers | Pulls signed releases and template packs, requests and renews the licence, builds the image in your registry, rolls the jobs, verifies and rolls back. |
| Azure SQL database | Pro | Settings and their history, templates and your overrides, exemptions, access mappings, the identity ledger, vulnerability state, and the copies of findings the web app reads. |
| Log Analytics workspace | both | The SecurityInsight tables (profiles, Risk Analysis, trend, run health, tag activity). |
| Key Vault | both | Licence, install key, connector secrets, optional keys (Azure OpenAI, Shodan, SMTP), magic-link key. |
| Storage account and container registry | both (registry: containers) | Run logs and outputs, staging shards, shared customisation files; the container image. |

Engines run on a Windows server (Task Scheduler; an Azure VM or an Azure Arc-enabled server) or as Azure Container
Apps jobs. Pro runs in containers. Everything is installed in the customer's own tenant and subscription.

**The SQL database size (#507).** SecurityInsight's databases (`sqldb-si-pro`, `sqldb-si-identity`) are never on the
Basic tier: measured on a tenant of about 23,000 users (97,000 records a run), Basic's 5 DTU averaged 14 % with log-write
peaks up to 98 % while the records were written, and its 2 GB cap cannot hold a large tenant. One rule
(`setup\_shared\SI-SqlTier.ps1`, `Get-SISqlDatabaseTier`) gives the size: **Standard S3 (100 DTU) for every Pro install,
whatever the tenant's size** (#584, owner 2026-10-11, approved: the CIs page was slow on S2 -- reliability over cost; S2
from #509, operator 2026-10-09: *"it is very little money"*; until then S1 below 5,000 directory objects); max size 250 GB, the Standard tier's default. That rule sizes the Pro database (`sqldb-si-pro`: the records, the CIs and the findings -- the writes Basic
could not take). The identity ledger (`sqldb-si-identity`, or the configured `SI_LedgerDatabase`) holds only the object
identifiers and is **S1 at any tenant size**. A size the customer sets wins (`SI_Bootstrap_SqlServiceObjective` in the
install's config, or `SI_UPDATER_SQL_SERVICE_OBJECTIVE` on the updater job: a DTU size, Basic, S0-S12 or P1-P15).
- **New installs:** the guided install creates both databases at their size (`az sql db create --service-objective`).
- **Raise by default:** both automatic update paths (the updater job and the VM sync hook) run the script with `-Apply`,
  so the change is made on every install's next update. Only a person running the script by hand without `-Apply` (or
  with `-DetectOnly`) gets the plan alone.
- **Existing installs:** every update (`setup\Invoke-SIContainerUpdate.ps1 -Apply` step 7, which the updater job and the
  VM sync hook both run from the release) raises a smaller SecurityInsight database to the rule's size by one ARM PATCH of
  its sku (`{"sku":{"name":"S3","tier":"Standard"},"properties":{"maxSizeBytes":268435456000}}`; an existing S2 gets the sku alone) -- an online change: no
  data loss, open connections reconnect once when Azure switches over. It **never lowers** a database and never touches
  one above S3, on Premium, on vCore or in an elastic pool; it touches only SecurityInsight's own databases on the
  install's servers (the resource group's, and the configured `SI_ProSqlServer` / `SI_LedgerSqlServer` /
  `SI_Pro_DataSqlServer`). One plain line per database goes to the run log; the updater keeps the summary in the Pro
  database (`cfg.InstallState` `SqlTier`). It never fails the update: a database that cannot be changed is a line, and
  the next update tries again.
- **The right it needs:** `Microsoft.Sql/servers/databases/write` on the database. The updater's identity has it through
  Contributor on the install's resource group (`Install-SIUpdaterJob -GrantSpnRoles`), where the guided install puts the
  server. For a server elsewhere the run reads the identity's permissions first and, when the right is missing, says so
  ("give it the role *SQL DB Contributor* on server ...") -- it grants nothing itself.
- **The tenant's size during an update:** since #509 it no longer decides the database size; it is still read and logged
  (Graph `$count` as the updater's identity, else the collection jobs' size).
- **Cost** (list prices, pay-as-you-go, West Europe, USD per database per month, 730 hours): Basic 4.90, S1 29.43,
  S2 73.61. A Pro install (two databases) since #509: S2 (Pro) + S1 (ledger) 103.04 at any tenant size (was S1 + S1
  58.87 for a small tenant).

**The container job size, at install and on every update (#509).** Operator 2026-10-09: *"include these guidance rules
for si and pim so you automatically adjust during installation. both si and pim are allowed to go to 4 cpu/8 gb if
needed"*. ONE rule, `Get-SITenantSizedJobResources` (`container\_shared\SI-ContainerConfig.ps1`): below 5,000 objects the
job kind's default (2 CPU / 4 GiB); from 5,000 **4 CPU / 8 GiB**. This rule sizes CPU and memory only -- the run limit
does not depend on the tenant's size (below). Objects: identity = users +
groups + service principals, endpoint = devices, the CI build (`asset-correlation`) and every Risk Analysis job
(`risk-analysis`, `risk-analysis-detailed`, `ra-<name>`) = all of them. Setup applies it at install from Graph `$count`
(Bootstrap); **every update** applies it again (`setup\Invoke-SIContainerUpdate.ps1` step 8, `setup\_shared\SI-JobSizing.ps1`,
`Invoke-SIJobSizing`), so an install made before the rule, or a tenant that grew, is brought up on its next update.
- **The counts on update**, the first that can be read, and the log says which: Graph `$count` as the updater's identity;
  else the records the last collection wrote in the Pro database (`sidata.CiRecord` per provider: Entra users / groups /
  service principals, the largest device count of any provider); else the asset counts the engines recorded in
  `SI_RunHealth_CL` (the largest run of the last 7 days). None: only a failure raises a job.
- **Learn from failures:** when a job's LAST execution ended out of memory (Container Apps system log `OOMKilled` / exit
  137, a run-health END that says OutOfMemory, or a run that started, recorded no end and stopped well before its
  timeout) or at its replica timeout (it ran for the whole timeout), the job goes up **one band** even when the counts do
  not ask for it: 2 CPU / 4 GiB, then 4 CPU / 8 GiB. A job already at 4 CPU / 8 GiB that ran out of memory is left and
  the line says the work needs splitting (queue scaling), not a bigger job. The run limit is not part of this.
- **SecurityInsight chooses no run limit** (owner 2026-10-13: *"we are not to judge that and it breaks the whole
  solution"*, *"why have a limit, if the environment has 100000000000 objects"*). Azure makes every Container Apps job
  carry a run limit (`replicaTimeout`), so **every engine job gets the longest one Azure takes**: ONE named value,
  `Get-SIJobRunLimit` (`container\_shared\SI-ContainerConfig.ps1`) = **604,800 s (7 days)**. It is the default of every
  job setup creates (a new install, at any tenant size) and the floor every update raises every existing `caj-si-*` job
  to (`Invoke-SIJobFloor`, the update's step 8c -- not the updater, which keeps its own limit; the pipeline job has its
  own 7-day rule below). The floor needs no run history and no count, so a job that never finished a run is raised like
  any other. One line per job: *"job size: caj-si-asset-correlation raised 4.0 CPU / 8.0Gi, 2 h -> 4.0 CPU / 8.0Gi,
  7 days -- a step gets the longest run limit Azure takes (7 days); SecurityInsight sets no shorter one"*, or *"... runs
  4.0 CPU / 8.0Gi, 7 days -- nothing to raise"*.
  **Why 7 days:** Microsoft documents no maximum for `replicaTimeout` (the resource reference says only *"Maximum number
  of seconds a replica is allowed to run"*, an integer, no upper bound). 604,800 s is the longest value Azure is proven
  to take -- the pipeline job has run with it on live installs since 2026-10-12 -- and 7 days is also the longest lease
  a storage queue gives a collection worker's part. No larger value is established; when one is, it is changed in that
  one function.
  **What went before and is gone:** the tenant-size run-time bands (2 h / 24 h / 72 h), the rule "3 x the longest
  finished run of the last 14 days, 4 h to 72 h" and "a run stopped at its limit gets at least double". They gave a job
  more time only after it had FINISHED a run or had been recognised as stopped at its limit -- a customer's CI build was
  stopped at 2 hours three runs in a row and four updates left it at 2 hours.
  **The only thing that watches a running step** is the pipeline's report of a step with no sign of progress (no log
  line and no run-health record for 2 hours): it reports once and the step keeps running.
- **The pipeline job itself** waits for every step inside its own execution, so it gets **7 days** -- it never ends
  before a step does. (A runner that does end early loses nothing: the next wake-up resumes the run and follows the
  running step.)
- **Raise only, capped, the customer wins:** never lowers CPU, memory or run time; never above 4 CPU / 8 GiB (the largest
  consumption size); `SI_Bootstrap_Cpu_<Engine>` / `_Memory_<Engine>` keep the job's CPU and memory.
  **`SI_Bootstrap_ReplicaTimeout_<Engine>` now means a SHORTER run limit set on purpose** (300 s to 604,800 s; it cannot
  be longer than what every job gets). It is honoured as before: setup writes it, and an update leaves the run limit of
  a job that has the setting alone (the line says *"its run limit is the customer's own, <setting> -- kept"*).
- **The change:** ONE read-modify-write ARM PATCH per job (the job's whole template back with the new size, its trigger
  with the new run time when that changes; secrets are never sent back), with `SI_QUEUE_LEASE_SECONDS` = timeout + 300
  on a KEDA worker whose timeout grows (never above 7 days, the longest lease a storage queue takes). The write never
  sends a shorter run limit than the job has at that moment. One plain line per job; detect-only plans; never fails the
  update.
- **Running setup again never lowers a job.** On a job that exists setup writes the LARGER of its own value and what
  the job has now -- the run limit on its own, CPU and memory as a pair -- so a size raised after an out-of-memory run
  survives a re-run of setup. A value the customer set still wins, also downwards.
- **A run limit above 24 hours that Azure does not take.** Azure has taken 7 days on every install so far; should it
  refuse a run limit above 24 hours somewhere, nothing fails. Wherever a longer one is sent -- the job create and update at install, the update's job sizing, the
  pipeline job -- a refusal of that request (a 400, or an error that names the replica timeout) is answered by sending
  the SAME request once more with 24 hours: the CPU / memory change in it is never lost, a KEDA worker's queue lease
  follows, and neither an install nor an update fails for it. When the second request is accepted the log says
  *"Azure did not accept a run limit of N hours for <job>; it keeps 24 hours."* and the rest of that run asks for 24
  hours at once. When the second request is refused too, the run limit was not the cause and the original error stands.
  The pipeline's own step limit follows whatever the job really has, so nothing else changes.
- **No give-up on elapsed time (owner 2026-10-13: "Report on no progress, keep running").** The pipeline stops no step
  for the time it takes, and it abandons no collection for the time its parts take.
  *The step timeout* (the stored `timeoutMinutes` of a pipeline step, default 240) no longer stops anything: when a step
  has run longer, the pipeline says so ONCE -- in its log and on the step's record: *"<job> has run for N minutes,
  longer than its step timeout of M minutes. It keeps running: ..."* -- and the step runs on. The state "timed out" is
  no longer given to a step by the pipeline (older run records keep it). The stored value is kept and is still edited
  in the pipeline editor; its label there still says "timeout" (web app text, to be changed separately).
  *The parts of a collection* are waited for until every part has its DONE or FAILED marker and the run's records are
  published; the former wait of 180 minutes plus the worker's run limit, after which the collection was called
  INCOMPLETE, is gone. That wait ends by itself: a worker that dies gives its part back within one short lease (below),
  and a part handed out more than 5 times is parked with a FAILED marker, which ends the step as failed with the part
  named.
  What ends a step: its own end -- the job finished or failed, or Azure stopped it at the job's own run limit. What
  watches a step that stands still: the no-progress report.
- **A collection worker holds its part with a short lease that it renews.** A queue worker takes its part for
  **10 minutes** and a heartbeat on its own thread renews that every **2 minutes** for as long as the worker process
  lives (`engine\asset-profiling\storage\WorkerQueue.ps1`: `Start-SIWorkItemLeaseBeat`, a second runspace, so one long
  call on the worker's own thread does not let the hold lapse; the same pattern as the CI build's watch). Before, the
  lease was as long as the worker job's run limit and never renewed -- with a run limit of days, a worker killed
  mid-part (out of memory, a platform restart) locked its part for days.
  A worker that dies stops renewing: its part is visible again within 10 minutes and the next worker takes it.
  A renewal the queue REFUSES -- another worker holds the part now (`PopReceiptMismatch`), or the part is gone (404) --
  means this worker has LOST the part: it says *"part N of M: this worker no longer holds the part (...) -- it stops
  here, so the part is not written twice"* and its process ends (exit 4) from the heartbeat's thread; it never deletes
  the message and never writes the DONE marker. A renewal that merely fails (network, sign-in) is said once and tried
  again on every beat; the worker goes on. At the end the heartbeat is stopped and the message is deleted with the
  NEWEST receipt (every renewal gives a new one); a part that failed keeps its message, which is visible again when
  the lease ends. The rule "a part handed out more than 5 times is parked" is unchanged. **The heartbeat's thread starts empty and signs in by itself.** A second runspace has nothing the worker's entry
  point loaded, so it loads what it needs (`Get-SIWorkItemLeaseBeatLibraries`): the queue code (with `SI-AzRest.ps1`)
  AND the sign-in file the worker's entry point hands it (`-SignInLibraries`) -- a container that signs in with its
  managed identity hands over `auth\SI-ManagedIdentity.ps1`, which its entry point loads for the worker's own thread
  only (the engine code never names that file: a VM never has it). On the first live collection (2026-10-13) the thread loaded the queue code alone, its
  first renewal failed with *"the managed-identity sign-in helper is not loaded in this run"*, and no heartbeat
  started in any container; the tests had used the in-memory queue, which needs no sign-in. The tests now run the real
  path (a storage context that is not the mock, the renewal over REST, a managed identity's token) in the thread
  itself, with the thread loading only what the product gives it.
  **When the heartbeat cannot be started** the worker says WHY in its line (*"... could not be started -- its first
  renewal failed: <reason>. The part is held with one lease of 125 minutes instead; a worker that dies keeps it that
  long."*) and holds the part with ONE lease of **2 hours 5 minutes** (`Get-SIWorkItemFallbackLeaseSeconds`; what a
  worker held its part with before the heartbeat existed) -- never the job's run limit, which is 7 days: that fallback
  locked a dead worker's part for a week. A part that takes longer than that lease may be handed to a second worker.
  What then keeps the run right: a part's records are stored under the part's own number and merged by record id, and
  a part has one DONE marker -- the second worker's work is spent twice, the run's records are not doubled; a part
  handed out more than 5 times is parked. (Rows a part sends straight to Log Analytics are not protected this way.)
- **Self-healing in the same run.** A job stopped at its own run limit -- one that no update has yet given the longest
  limit -- is not left for the next update and the next scheduled run. When a step's job (or, for a collection in
  parts, its producer or one of its workers) ended
  at its own run limit, the pipeline (1) gives that job the SAME run limit by the same write as the update's floor
  step -- the longest Azure takes (7 days), 24 hours when Azure takes
  no more, a queue worker's lease in step; (2) starts the step again, ONCE, in the same run; (3) carries on with the
  steps after it when it succeeds. This is the same for every kind of step: a collection, the CI build, a delivery.
  The log has one plain line and the run health one row per action: *"<job> was stopped at its run limit of N h; the
  limit is now M h and the step is started again"*. There is never a second retry of the same step in one run: stopped
  at its limit again, the step fails with that reason. Nothing is raised and nothing is started again when the customer
  set that job's run limit themselves, when the job has the longest limit already, when Azure takes no longer limit, or when the
  pipeline's identity may not change the job (the reason names the right) -- the step then fails as before, in plain
  words. A run that was killed for memory, or that failed by itself, did not reach its limit and is not started again:
  a longer limit does not help it. The pipeline changes a job with the right it already has to start it (Container Apps
  Jobs Contributor on the jobs' resource group); no new right is needed.
- **The run goes on without one source.** A source is one collection step: identity, azure, endpoint or the public IP
  scan (a collection in parts is the same step). When one of them has failed for good (after the one retry above, or
  for any other reason) while at least one other collection of the same run succeeded, the run does NOT stop: the CI
  build, Risk Analysis, the data steps and delivery run, and that source's records stay exactly as its last good
  collection left them. Nothing of that source is shown as gone, retired or fixed -- absence is never remediation:
  - *The step stays failed.* It is shown and recorded as failed, the run as a whole is recorded as failed, and the
    usual failure notification goes out. The run's record, its log and its run-health record say in one sentence which
    source it went on without and from when that source's data is: *"this run went on without endpoint: its data is
    from 2026-10-10 14:05 UTC, because its last collection did not complete"*.
  - *A half-written collection never counts as a complete one.* The records of a collection are written in batches. In
    every batch the first record of each feed (source system + record type) is written "not complete", and all of them
    are set complete in one statement only when every batch of the collection is in the database (the feed close,
    `Complete-SIRecordFeeds`), which also registers the collection (`sidata.RecordCollection`: which step wrote it and
    how many records). A collection that stopped half-way therefore leaves its feed "not complete": the CI build reads
    absence only from a complete newer collection, so every record the failed collection did not reach is *frozen*
    (it keeps its CI active) instead of turning *not seen*. When a collection step fails after one of its processes
    had already closed its part, the pipeline holds that collection the same way (one record marked "not complete",
    the collection's row marked held).
  - *The database does not depend on Log Analytics.* A collection has two outputs: its profile rows go to Log
    Analytics (Risk Analysis, the data sync and correlation read them there), and its records go to the database (the
    CI build reads them there). Neither waits for the other. The rows are built once and handed to both; the post to
    Log Analytics and the write to the database each run on their own and each report on their own line of the run's
    result (`LA` and `SQL`). A post that fails, is skipped (no sign-in for it) or was never asked for (outputs without
    Log Analytics) leaves the records going to the database, and their collection is closed there -- the feed close
    means "every record of this collection is in the database" and reads nothing from Log Analytics. A database that
    cannot be written leaves the post as it was, and the collection is NOT closed. The optional copy of the records to
    Log Analytics (`SI_LaExport`) is the same: it comes after the database write of each batch, and a copy that fails
    is said and counted, never a reason to stop writing or closing. A run collected in parts follows the same rule: a
    part hands its records over whatever its own post did, and the last step counts a bucket as failed only when it did
    not reach the database. What a run then is:

    | Log Analytics | Database | The run | What follows |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | written | written, closed | `success` | -- |
    | failed / skipped | written, closed | `success-partial`, naming Log Analytics | the step ends well; the CI build has this collection; what reads the profile tables is on the previous snapshot, and Risk Analysis says it is built on incomplete profile data |
    | written | failed / not closed | `error`: "The records could not be written to the database" | the step FAILS and the source is a dropout: the run goes on with that source on its last good collection, and nothing of this collection is closed as complete. The same in one process and in a run collected in parts (there the run's last step writes the records, and a bucket that did not reach the database fails it) |
    | failed | failed | `error`, the database's | as the row above |

    The database wins. A collection whose records did not reach it -- a batch could not be written, the collection
    could not be closed, or the audit below held the rows -- is a failed collection whatever else was written: Log
    Analytics having the rows does not change that, and neither do JSON or Excel files written next to it.
    A failed post alone does NOT fail the step. A failed step is a dropout, and a dropout holds every collection that
    step closed -- so "the step failed" and "its records are complete in the database" cannot both be true; a failed
    post therefore makes the run partial and leaves the database complete.

    One thing holds BOTH outputs: the audit before the post. Rows whose key columns are all empty are a verdict on the
    rows, not on Log Analytics -- they could not give the records their profile part either -- so neither is written.
    A dry run and a mock run write no records.
  - *The state of each source is kept* (`sidata.SourceState`: its last good collection, how its newest attempt ended,
    since when it has been on its last good collection). The next collection of that source that completes ends the
    dropout by itself.
  - *A CI is frozen only when all its sources are down.* While a source is on its last good collection, a finding or
    a vulnerability record that goes missing is frozen -- never counted absent, never closed -- only when EVERY source
    that describes its CI is down. A CI that at least one healthy source still describes closes its findings as usual.
    The unit is the CI, because that is what can be told with certainty: which feeds each collection step writes is
    registered when a collection closes, and every record says which CI it belongs to. Frozen: every CI that only
    dropped sources describe, every finding owner that is not a CI, and every CI no record points to. As usual: every
    other CI -- for example a device with a Defender and an Azure record closes as usual while only Defender is down,
    and is frozen while both are. A finding that IS seen in the run is never frozen (it is updated). When the feeds of
    a dropped source are not known, or the database cannot be read, nothing is closed in that run. When the source is
    back and the finding is still absent, it closes normally after the usual number of complete runs.
    *The known consequence:* a finding that only the dropped source could see, on a CI another source still describes,
    can be counted absent and closed after the usual complete runs although nothing shows a fix. It opens again, as
    reopened, when that source is back.
  - *Labelled everywhere.* While a source is on its last good collection, every page of the web app carries one
    line per such source at the top (the shared layout): *"Endpoint data is from 10 Oct 2026 14:05 -- the last
    collection from that source did not complete."*, the time in the viewer's regional format. The data sync marks
    each loaded collection that was calculated meanwhile (`sidata.CollectionSource`: which source, from when), so a
    collection opened later still says what it was calculated on. Every Excel export carries the same sentence as a
    note on its info sheet (UTC), and every mail that carries data carries it above its footer. The words are the same
    in all three places.
  - *The age of a source is known and said.* Every run that rests on an older collection of a source says how old it
    is, in the log and in the run's run-health record: *"endpoint has had no good collection for 3 day(s) -- its data
    is from 2026-10-09 14:05 UTC"*. Data quality stores it as a number of the run (days since the last good collection,
    per source; 0 while the newest collection completed) -- a number only, never a warning by itself.
  - *After 7 days delivery waits.* When a source has had no good collection for `SI_Pro_SourceDropout_HoldDeliveryDays`
    days or more (default 7; 0 = never), the Deliver stage does not run: nothing is mailed and no ticket is changed
    until that source collects again. The calculation (the CI build, Risk Analysis) goes on. The steps of Deliver are
    recorded as skipped with the reason, the log and the run's record say it in one line, and it is not a safety-check
    event (it would mail on every run). A single step a person starts by hand is not held.
  - *Risk Analysis produced nothing new.* When Risk Analysis failed or did not run, every delivery step that needs it is
    skipped and Deliver does not start (see below): no mail is sent again as new and no ticket is touched; the operator
    gets the run's failure notification, and the views keep the last good results.
  - *A collection that completes with far fewer assets: the customer decides.* Findings and vulnerabilities go up and
    down and are never judged by count. Assets are: when a source's collection completes but one of its feeds (source
    system + record type -- devices, users, Azure resources ...) holds fewer records than its last good collection by
    `SI_Pro_DataQuality_AssetDropPercent` (30 %) or more, the safety check *Collection: far fewer assets from one
    source* decides, at the moment the collection closes -- before the CI build reads it. A feed whose last good
    collection had fewer than 20 records is not judged (a small source moves by whole assets). The choice is
    `SI_Pro_SourceDropout_AssetDropAction`:
    - `confirm` (default) -- the smaller collection is not taken as the truth: everything it no longer lists is kept
      as the last good collection left it (frozen, exactly as when a collection fails), the run goes on, and one
      event says so. When the next complete collection of that source shows the same level, the drop is accepted by
      itself and the records follow -- a real clean-up (many Azure resources removed) needs no person and takes
      effect one run later. When the next collection is back to normal, the drop never took effect.
    - `accept` -- the collection is taken as it comes; the check only reports it, once.
    One event per drop, never one per run; the check never stops or delays a run. Turning the check off takes every
    collection as it comes. A collection published by several processes at once is not judged.
  - *What still holds a run back.* Every collection of the run failed (there is nothing new to calculate); the tier
    classifier failed (it is a prerequisite of every collection, not a source -- it writes no records); or any other
    step of Collect failed. Then the Correlate stage does not start and Deliver never starts, as before.
  - *The customer's saved choices keep working.* A collection step set to "stop" still stops the pipeline at that step.
    "Carry on" and the default ("skip the steps that need it") now behave the same for a collection step: the run goes
    on. Nothing changes for any other step.
- **A failed CI build lets no data out of that run.** When the CI build has failed for good, Risk Analysis and every
  delivery step that needs it are skipped and Deliver does not start -- also in a run that went on without a source.
  The data of the last good run stays in place and visible; nothing is deleted or shown as fixed. The run's
  record says it in one sentence: *"this run was held back: <step> did not succeed, so N step(s) after it did not run
  and nothing was delivered from this run -- the data of the last good run stays in place"*. Two saved choices remain
  the customer's own: a stage set to "run anyway" (Deliver then starts after a failed CI build, but its steps that need
  the CI build are still skipped; it never starts after a Collect in which nothing was collected), and the CI build
  step itself set to "carry on", which lets Risk Analysis run on the previous CI build inside Correlate while Deliver
  still does not start.
- **One failed step does not cost the rest of the run.** The pipeline's map says per step which kind of need it has:
  a step either needs the result of *this* run, or it works on what is stored and holds back by itself whatever is not
  complete. Two steps are of the second kind: the data sync (it loads only whole collections whose run is shown
  complete, keys every asset by its durable id and closes no finding on a collection that is not complete) and the
  verification service (it only reads). After the CI build or Risk Analysis did not succeed -- with a Collect that is
  good -- those two still run, so the web app has what the completed collections brought. Everything else stays held
  exactly as above: Risk Analysis after a failed CI build, every connector that writes to a CMDB or to ServiceNow, the
  vulnerability tickets and the daily mail; the data sync itself sends nothing to an output in such a run. The run
  stays failed in its record, its own health record is a warning, and the log, the run's note and the report say which
  step failed, which steps ran all the same, which were held, and who must act: *"this run is not complete: <step> did
  not succeed; from the last good run, not from this one: <what is missing>; ..."*. Nothing is closed, no ticket is
  changed and no mail is sent because a step failed.
  *The connectors need the findings, not the summary.* Risk Analysis Summary is the overview for management; the
  integrations work from the findings (Risk Analysis Detailed) and the merged assets. The map marks the summary as
  nice-to-have, and the CMDB connectors, the vulnerability connector, its ServiceNow form and the data sync as steps
  that run without it. So when the summary is the only step that failed after a good Collect, those steps run in
  full, on this run's own result -- the data sync sends to its outputs as in a complete run -- and each step's record
  says why. They are held when Risk Analysis Detailed or the asset correlation did not succeed, when a step they need
  failed, on a new install's first collection, when delivery waits for a source that is too old, and when the summary
  is saved as "on failure: stop". The daily mail always waits for a complete run.
  *The report is a warning that opens a fix request.* A run that went on after a failed step reports itself through
  the same record as every run: outcome warning (not a failure that stops, never a success), the step it went on after
  named as the failed step, with that step's own error class and who fixes it. A warning that names a failed step is
  handled as a fix request by the vendor; when the cause is a permission, licence or setting of the install, it says
  that the customer acts. The run's own record starts the sentence with "warning, to be fixed". A run that was stopped,
  or in which a step that ran all the same failed too, stays a failure.
- **The first run of a new install is its own flow.** An install is on its *first collection* while its database
  holds no complete collection; the pipeline asks that once, at the start of every whole run. Three things are
  different until the first collection is complete, and nothing else:
  *Wait for merged assets.* Nothing is shown before the asset build has finished whole -- no single collection, no
  half-built asset list. The moment the asset build has finished, the data sync runs at once, on what is stored, so
  the merged assets are the first data view while Risk Analysis still runs; the findings follow when the data sync
  runs again at its own place. The run's note says where the first collection is: *"first collection running: nothing
  is shown before the asset build has finished whole ..."*, then *"... the merged assets are in the web app now ..."*,
  then *"first collection complete"*. A delivery at once that does not succeed is said and never fails the run.
  *Two restarts.* A step that fails (never one whose execution was stopped on purpose -- "Stop is final", #700) is started again at once -- the step carries on from what it
  finished -- up to two times (`SI_Pro_Pipeline_FirstRunRestarts`, 0 = never). Each restart is kept in the step's own
  record. After that the step stays failed, and the run ends as every run that went on after a failed step: with the
  warning that names the step, what is missing and who must act, reported as a warning that opens a fix request. Only
  the steps that collect, correlate and load the web app are started again; a step that Microsoft only throttled is
  not.
  *Whole collections only.* What reaches the web app is a whole collection, marked with what is still missing.
  **What the first run never compromises** -- the rules towards a CMDB and ServiceNow hold on the first run and on
  every run after it: the delivery at once tells the data sync that it runs on what is stored, so nothing goes to an
  output from a run that is not complete; no step that writes to a CMDB, to ServiceNow or to a ticket, and no mail, is
  ever started early or started again, and on a first collection that is not complete none of them is started at all
  (also not when only the summary failed); CMDB first, then the tickets. The connectors' own guards are not read or
  changed by the pipeline: an incomplete run and an empty result are refused, the closure ceilings and the scope rule
  hold, the close reason is carried, a match-only asset is never created, nothing is created by default, and a CI is
  never keyed or created from a provisional id. A first run has nothing asserted before it, so it can close, resolve
  and retire nothing.
  *A new install's first collection* has no last good run. Its sentence is *"first collection, not complete yet: <step>
  did not succeed; missing: <what is missing>"*, and it never shows a half-built asset list: while the asset build has
  not finished whole the data sync waits too; once the assets are built whole, a failed Risk Analysis no longer keeps
  them from the web app. A saved "on failure: stop", a Collect in which nothing was collected and a source that is too
  old hold the run as before. Off for the whole install: `SI_Pro_Pipeline_GoOnAfterFailedStep = $false`.
- **One CI build at a time.** Two CI builds side by side would write the same CIs, links, identity records and
  `SI_CI_CL` rows at once. Every way a build can start -- the pipeline, a job run by hand, a release check, Risk
  Analysis building the CIs in its own run -- shares one place, the database, so that is where it is decided:
  - *The lock.* The job that builds the CIs takes an exclusive application lock in the install's database before its
    first write (the identity records of the object map) and holds it to its end; the CI build itself takes the same
    lock when it runs on its own. The lock belongs to a database connection that is opened for it alone and stays open
    for the whole build. The database frees it the moment that connection ends -- so a build that is stopped or killed
    frees it by itself, and there is no stored flag that could go stale and block the next build.
  - *A second build waits.* A build that finds the lock held builds nothing beside the first. It waits -- one line
    when it starts to wait (*"CIs: another CI build is running (since <time>, <which run>) -- this one waits for it and
    then builds what is left"*), one line every five minutes -- and then runs as an ordinary build, which is
    incremental and quick when the first one just finished. The wait has no limit of its own: the job's run limit is
    the limit, and a build stopped there is the ordinary "stopped at its run limit" case.
  - *Running now is not "stopped".* A build that never finished leaves its state as "running", and the next build
    carries on from it. A waiting build reads that state only after it holds the lock, so a build that is running now
    is never taken for a stopped one.
  - *A dropped connection.* The build checks its lock before every batch it writes and before it writes its own
    state. When the lock's connection was lost, the build takes the lock again at once; it goes on only when its own
    note of who holds the lock is still in place, which proves no other build ran in between. In every other case --
    another build holds the lock now, or held it meanwhile, or the check cannot be made -- the build stops before it
    writes anything more and leaves the build's state alone; the next build builds what is left.
  - *The safety check* **CI build started while another was running** is the report, not the lock: one event for a
    build that had to wait, naming both runs. It never stops, delays or fails a run and sends no mail. Switched off,
    no event is made -- the second build still waits.
  - An install without a database has no CI build in SQL, so there is nothing to lock.
- **A job that is already running is not started a second time.** The lock above is what keeps two CI builds apart;
  the starters also avoid asking for a second run in the first place:
  - *The pipeline.* Before it starts a step, the pipeline asks Azure whether an execution of that step's job is running
    now (somebody ran the job by hand, a release check started it). If so it starts nothing: it FOLLOWS that execution
    as the step's own run -- *"step N <job>: already running (<execution>, started <time>) -- the pipeline follows it
    instead of starting another"*, also kept in the run's note -- waits for it like for any step, and judges the step
    by its result, so the steps after it run on fresh data. A collection in parts follows its producer the same way;
    the queue workers are never asked about, because several of them at once is how a collection in parts works.
    Nothing went wrong, so no safety check reports it. When the question cannot be answered, the log says so and the
    step is started as before.
  - *A second pipeline run.* The install has one pipeline lock and one queue. A scheduled start, "Run the pipeline now"
    and "run this stage / step now" all go through them: while a run holds the install, a new request waits in the
    queue (kept once) and runs when that run has ended -- a forced start never runs a second pipeline beside it.
  - *Run now in the web app.* A job that is a step of the pipeline runs through the pipeline's queue. Any other job is
    started at once -- unless an execution of it is running now: then nothing is started and the page says which
    execution is running and since when.
  - *The release check.* The live smoke of a release starts each job it wants to see run only when that job is not
    running in the environment already; a job that is running is said and left alone (and not judged by that release).
  - *The job itself.* As before, a container job that finds an earlier execution of itself still running does nothing
    and ends ("skipped: previous still running"); that check needs the job to be able to read its own executions.

### A2. Identities and secrets

- **Managed identity first.** One setting, `SI_AuthMethod`, decides how every engine signs in: `ManagedIdentity`
  (default -- a container job's, an Azure VM's or an Azure Arc server's identity, system- or user-assigned),
  `Certificate` (a service principal with a certificate, the recommended choice when a service principal is
  needed) or `Secret` (a service principal with a client secret -- kept so community and existing installs keep
  working). See *How SecurityInsight signs in* below.
- **Separate identities.** The collection jobs share one identity that holds read permissions on your tenant
  (Defender `Machine.Read.All`, never a write permission) plus write access only to SecurityInsight's own
  workspace, rules and storage. Asset tagging has its **own** identity with exactly three tenant writes (Defender
  machine tags, Tag Contributor at the tagging scope, Entra custom security attribute assignment), granted only
  when you opt in. The web app and the MCP server each have their own user-assigned managed identity; the web app
  uses its identity to read the database and to start, stop and read the Container Apps jobs.
- **The updater job is the exception:** it signs in as a service principal with a certificate, held as a Key Vault
  reference, with rights on the registry and the install's resource group.
- **No secret in settings or environment.** Containers receive non-secret settings as environment variables;
  anything that looks like a secret is skipped and reaches a job only as a job secret backed by Key Vault.
  Connectors and settings store only Key Vault secret *names*. The web app and the MCP server hold no secret at all.
- **Entra-only SQL.** The Pro database server is created with Entra-only authentication; its Entra admin is a
  role-assignable security group (setup refuses a group that is not role-assignable, because anyone who could manage
  a normal group's membership could take over the database). Job and app identities are contained database users
  with only the rights they need (the MCP server reads only).
- **Least privilege at install.** The guided install asks where the collection identity may read (one
  subscription by default, or a management group, or the tenant root). The person installing needs Contributor and
  Role Based Access Control Administrator on the install's resource group; subscription rights only to create the
  resource group or register providers. Grants the installer cannot make are printed as exact commands for someone
  who can. `diagnostics/Test-SIInstall.ps1` checks that the install's identity holds no write role outside its
  resource group beyond the documented grants.

### A3. Network -- what is private and what is public

- **The web app: you choose.** It runs in your own Container Apps environment and is reached either **from the
  internet behind Entra sign-in** -- the guided install's default (`webAppAccess = external`, worded *"From the
  internet, behind Entra sign-in (add Conditional Access)"*) -- or **from your network only** (`internal`).
  `Deploy-SIManagement.ps1` run on its own defaults to `Internal`. Either way every page except a health probe
  requires an Entra sign-in and an app role, and Conditional Access applies to the sign-in.
- **No virtual network by default; private networking is an option setup builds.** By default the Container Apps
  environment is created without a virtual network, and the Pro database's firewall admits Azure services; access to
  the database is by Entra identity only. With the install option *Private network* setup puts SecurityInsight into
  your virtual network itself -- see [A3b](#a3b-private-networking----an-option-setup-builds).
- **Storage** is reached with the job's own identity (OAuth and RBAC); there is no storage-key option.
- **Outbound only.** Nothing connects in to your environment. The engines call Microsoft's APIs (Graph, Defender,
  Azure Resource Manager, Log Analytics), optionally your Azure OpenAI resource and Shodan, and -- Pro updater only --
  Invardia's update and licence endpoints. The web app talks only to Entra sign-in, Azure Resource Manager, Microsoft
  Graph, your SQL database, your Key Vault, Log Analytics and your Azure OpenAI resource.
- **Browser hardening.** A strict Content Security Policy (scripts, styles and connections from the app itself only;
  framing refused), HSTS, `nosniff`, no referrer, and anti-forgery tokens on every change.

### A3b. Private networking -- an option setup builds

Off by default: the default install is unchanged. With **`privateNetwork`** (the guided install, page *Where to
install*) setup builds the private variant itself (`setup\_shared\SI-PrivateNetwork.ps1`):

| Part | What setup does |
|---|---|
| Created private | The Key Vault (public access *Disabled*, its firewall *Deny*, trusted Microsoft services allowed), the storage account and the Pro database server are **created** with public access *Disabled* -- never public first, so a policy that refuses a public resource never sees one, and no firewall rule or exception is ever made for them (neither for Azure services nor for the machine that runs setup). Right after the storage account and the vault are made (step `private-network-data`), and right after the database server is made (in `pro-sql`), their private endpoints and zones are made, and **before anything reads or writes them** the machine that runs setup must resolve their names to the private addresses. It is in your network but asks your DNS resolver: until your network team has added the records, the install **stops** with one action -- the exact A records (name -> private address) -- and the install command continues from there, making nothing twice. |
| Its own network (optional) | Give no `vnetId` but an address range (**`vnetAddressPrefix`**, at least a /25, e.g. a /24) and setup makes SecurityInsight's own spoke network `vnet-si` (`vnetName`) in its resource group, in the install's region, read back. Its subnets are then the first /26 (the environment) and the second /26 (the private endpoints) unless you give them. An existing network is never changed: its address space is left as it is, and a subnet range outside it or overlapping one of its subnets is refused with the reason. Your network team peers it with your hub (the hand-off below). |
| Subnets | In your virtual network (`vnetId`): `snet-si-apps` for the Container Apps environment (at least /27, delegated to `Microsoft.App/environments`) and `snet-si-endpoints` for the private endpoints (a /28 is enough). Created when they are not there (`appsSubnetPrefix`, `endpointsSubnetPrefix`); an existing **empty** subnet is delegated; a subnet in use or delegated to something else is never changed -- the install stops with the reason. A subnet is written back with everything it had (network security group, route table, NAT gateway, service endpoints). |
| Container Apps environment | Created **in** the apps subnet, **internal**: it has no public address. The web app's ingress is "external" to the environment, which in an internal environment means *reachable from your virtual network only*. |
| Private endpoints | `pe-si-sql` (the Pro database server), `pe-si-vault`, `pe-si-blob`, `pe-si-queue`, `pe-si-table`, `pe-si-registry`, each in the endpoints subnet and read back until it is provisioned and approved. The registry is changed to **Premium** first (a private endpoint needs it). An endpoint of the same name that points elsewhere is never replaced. |
| Private DNS | The `privatelink.*` zones (database, vault, blob, queue, table, registry), each linked to SecurityInsight's network; each endpoint keeps its address in its zone (a zone group). In SecurityInsight's resource group -- or, with `privateDnsZonesResourceGroupId`, the zones in the resource group your hub keeps its central zones in are **used, never created**: a zone missing there is on the hand-off list. Azure links a network to only one zone of a name, so a zone of that name your network is already linked to (anywhere setup can read) is used instead of making a second one. The environment's own zone (its default domain; `@`, `*` and `*.internal` to its internal address) is always in SecurityInsight's resource group, linked to its network. A link name that another network already holds is never repointed (a hash suffix instead). |
| Your hub network | SecurityInsight writes **nothing** on your hub by default -- no peering, no record in your zones, no link of its zones to your hub. `hubVnetId` (optional, may be in another subscription) only makes the hand-off exact. Two answers, both off, let setup do part of it with your approval: **`linkZonesToHub`** (the environment's zone linked to the hub) and **`peerToHub`** (the peering in both directions, PIM4EntraPS's settings, both read back *Connected*; never half a peering -- when the second side cannot be made the first is removed). Either one reads the installing identity's rights on the hub first (Network Contributor on the hub virtual network) and, without them, changes nothing and stays on the hand-off list. |
| The network hand-off | At the end of the install (and of every run of the cut-over below) one exact list for your network team, with the real names, ids and addresses: the peering of SecurityInsight's network with your hub in both directions (network access on; forwarded traffic, gateway transit and remote gateways off -- both sides must read *Connected*), the environment's zone and its records (link it to your hub, or add the zone on your DNS / resolver), each private endpoint's A record by zone (to add in your zones of those names), the DNS servers SecurityInsight's network asks, the rights setup would need to do it itself, and the `Resolve-DnsName` / `Test-NetConnection` checks with the expected private address. Written as `network-hand-off.txt` next to the install's state, with **`prepare-hub-securityinsight.ps1`**: one self-contained script your hub's owner can read or run (PowerShell 7 or 5.1, a browser sign-in, Azure REST only, no module; it shows its plan first and makes the changes only with `-Apply`; it never deletes anything and never makes a zone). |
| Public endpoints | The data resources are created private (above); one that is still open (an existing install moving, below) is closed at the **end**, after every step that still reaches the database, the vault or the storage from the machine that runs setup, only once every private endpoint reads back, and only once the names (the web app, the database server, the Key Vault, the storage endpoints) **resolve to private addresses from inside**: from the machine that runs setup when it is in your network, else from a one-time job in SecurityInsight's own environment (`caj-si-insidecheck`, always removed), else on the operator's word (`-ConfirmedFromInside`). Until then they stay **open** -- a closed resource nothing can reach is never left -- and the install ends with one action: do the hand-off, then run the install again from inside (a resource your policy keeps closed already is named as reachable from inside only). Then: the database server, the storage account and the Key Vault `publicNetworkAccess = Disabled` (the Key Vault's firewall *Deny* as well, trusted Microsoft services allowed) -- no firewall-only state. The registry's public endpoint stays open until image builds run inside your network (below). **Once closed, they stay closed**: no setup run, update or support step opens them again -- not even for a few minutes. |
| The in-network SQL identity | `id-si-sql`, a user-assigned identity made a member of the database server's admin group before the database closes. No standing job carries it; only the one-time support job below does, while it runs. |
| Support access to a private database | The vendor support identity's own database user is made **before** the database closes (the move of an existing install refuses to close it otherwise). Afterwards support reaches the database **only from inside**: `setup\Invoke-SISupportSqlAccessJob.ps1` creates a one-time job in SecurityInsight's own private environment, signed in as `id-si-sql`, that makes (or confirms) that user, reads it back, and is removed -- no firewall rule, no public access, no jump host. It gives no role, membership or permission to anything. |
| Image builds inside the network | An agent pool of the registry (`si-vnet-pool`, one agent) in the endpoints subnet, made by the steps `registry-agent-pool` and then `registry-public-off` of `setup\Set-SIPrivateNetworking.ps1` (also on a new private install).
