Setup and the updater use the pool by themselves once the registry is closed; closing it is refused until the pool runs and the registry's private endpoint is approved. |

The steps are `private-network-subnets` (before the container setup) and `private-network` (after mail, before the first
run); they are in the plan only when the option is chosen. Both are safe to run again. After the install, run setup
commands from a machine in that network (for example Azure Cloud Shell in your virtual network).

**An existing install** moves with `setup\Set-SIPrivateNetworking.ps1`, run by Invardia support through the Support app,
one environment at a time. It shows the plan first (nothing changes); `-Apply -Steps <list>` makes exactly those steps,
each idempotent and read back: `subnets` (with `-VnetAddressPrefix`: its own network first), `peer-to-hub` (only when you name it -- that is your approval -- with `-HubVnetId`), `registry-premium`, `private-endpoints`, `private-dns`, `private-environment`,
`move-jobs`, `move-apps`, `sql-identity`, `support-sql`, `public-access-off`, `registry-agent-pool` and
`registry-public-off` -- so a moved install ends in the same state as a new private one. Azure cannot move a Container Apps environment into a virtual network, so the cut-over makes a
second, private environment (`cae-si-private`) and moves every job and app into it: each is removed and created again
under the same name with the same identities, settings and schedule, and the role assignments made on it are made
again. A job that is running, or that holds a secret that is not a Key Vault reference, is not touched (it is said). The
web app's new address is **added** to its sign-in registration (the old one stays). The old environment is left in place,
empty. One rollback record per run (a file and a short copy in the install) puts it back with `-Rollback <record>
-Apply`: the jobs and apps moved back, and what the run created removed. A record that closed a public endpoint is
rolled back only on your own decision to leave private networking (`-ReopenPublicAccess`); without it nothing is
changed. The vendor support identity's database access is never removed.
Every later setup run finds `cae-si-private` and keeps using it.

**Outbound: the Microsoft Security Update Guide (#772).** Risk Analysis reads the release date of each Microsoft update by its KB from
`https://api.msrc.microsoft.com/cvrf/v3.0` (public, no sign-in, HTTPS 443; `/updates` once, then only the monthly / out-of-band
release documents of the last 24 months that are new or revised), at most once a day, and keeps the dates in the install
(Pro `sidata.KbReleaseDate`, Community `OUTPUT\msrc-kb-release-dates.json`) -- never per finding. A network that does not allow
`api.msrc.microsoft.com` outbound (a private network's firewall, a proxy) is said in ONE line per run and the patch cycle uses the
cached dates and, for the rest, the month the update's name says (its Patch Tuesday); `SI_PatchCycle_MsrcDates = off` makes no
call at all. Add the host to the egress allow list where outbound traffic is restricted (#570).

### A3c. Customer-managed keys -- an option, and how the key is rotated

Microsoft-managed keys stay the default. With **`customerManagedKeys`** (page *Data and scope*) your data is encrypted
with a key in **your** Key Vault (`setup\_shared\SI-CustomerKeys.ps1`):

| Part | What setup does |
|---|---|
| The vault | Soft delete and **purge protection** on -- Azure requires both for a customer-managed key. Purge protection is one-way: Azure never turns it off, and a deleted vault keeps its name for its retention days. |
| The key | `cmkKeyName` (default `si-data`) in `cmkKeyVaultId` (default: SecurityInsight's own vault). Used as it is when it is there (it must be RSA); created when it is not: RSA 3072, wrap / unwrap only, with a **rotation policy** -- a new version every year, expiry after two years, a notice 30 days before. SecurityInsight never removes a key. |
| The identity | A managed identity `id-si-keys`, with *Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User* on the **key only** (not the vault). A new right takes minutes to be honoured: setup waits for it. |
| The Pro database | The server's Transparent Data Encryption protector = your key (the server signs in to the vault as `id-si-keys`), **automatic rotation on**. It covers every database on the server. |
| Storage | The storage account encrypted with your key, **versionless** -- Azure uses a new key version by itself. Blobs and files use it; queues and tables keep the service's keys unless the account was created with account-scoped keys for them (they hold work items and run state). |
| Log Analytics | Only through a dedicated Log Analytics cluster (`cmkLogAnalytics`): `cluster-existing` links the workspace to your cluster (`logAnalyticsClusterId`, which must already hold a customer-managed key); `cluster-new` makes `log-si-cluster` with your key (a commitment of 100 GB a day; Azure takes up to two hours -- the step says so and links the workspace when it is run again). Data the workspace received before the link keeps Microsoft's keys. `off` (the default within the option) leaves Log Analytics on Microsoft's keys. |

The step is `customer-managed-keys` (after the updater, before support access), in the plan only when the option is
chosen; a part that fails is a warning, and what was not switched stays on Microsoft-managed keys -- nothing is ever
switched to a key the identity cannot use. **An existing install** moves with `setup\Set-SICustomerManagedKeys.ps1`
through the Support app: plan first, then `-Apply -Steps vault-protection,key,identity,key-access,storage,sql` and, when
chosen, `log-analytics`; `-Rollback <record> -Apply` goes back to Microsoft-managed keys (the key itself is kept, purge
protection stays on).

**Key rotation.**
- *Automatic (the default).* The key's rotation policy makes a new version every year. The database server (automatic
  rotation on the protector), the storage account (versionless key) and the Log Analytics cluster (no key version set)
  each take up the new version by themselves, normally within a day. Nothing in SecurityInsight changes.
- *Now.* Key Vault > the key > *Rotate now* (or a new version by your own process): the same as above.
- *Another key.* Run the cut-over again with `-KeyName <new key>` (or `-KeyVaultId` for another vault): the identity
  gets access to the new key, then storage, the database server and the cluster are switched to it, each read back.
- *Never delete or disable a key version that data or backups may still be encrypted with* -- the database's
  point-in-time and long-term backups keep the version they were made with. Expired versions stay usable for unwrap.
- *Revoking access is a kill switch:* removing `id-si-keys`' right on the key (or disabling the key) makes the database
  inaccessible within minutes and the storage unreadable until access is given back.

### A4. Sign-in and access layers

1. **Entra sign-in.** Every user signs in with Entra ID (single sign-on, your MFA and Conditional Access). The app
   registration requires assignment, so only people or groups given one of its app roles can sign in at all.
   **Session: at most 8 hours, fixed.** The web app signs users in through the sign-in front SecurityInsight and PIM
   Manager share: the authorization-code flow with PKCE, the code redeemed with the web app's managed identity as a
   federated credential (no secret, no certificate), a session that ends 8 hours after the sign-in whatever the activity,
   and the ID token renewed with Entra about every hour -- so your Conditional Access sign-in frequency, and a disabled
   account, take effect on top of the 8 hours. An install from before the front is moved behind it by its product update
   once the federated credential and the organisation-wide consent to `openid profile offline_access User.Read` are in
   place; the update only reads Entra -- when either is missing it names `setup\Set-SISigninFront.ps1 -Apply` in the update
   result and changes nothing. `Set-SISigninFront.ps1 -Off` is the way back and a choice the update keeps
   (`SI_Web_SigninFront=false`). The web app's own sign-in (the way back) keeps the same fixed 8-hour session.
   **The front's store (#852, front 1.3.0 on).** The front keeps its sessions, its token cache and its Data Protection
   keys in the install's own Pro database (schema `signin`, two tables the front creates on first use) and wraps the keys
   with an RSA key in the install's own Key Vault (`signin-front-dp`, wrap / unwrap only); it refuses to start without
   `SIGNIN_SQL_SERVER`, `SIGNIN_SQL_DATABASE` and `SIGNIN_KEYVAULT_KEY_ID` (`SIGNIN_STATE_MI_CLIENT_ID` names its identity:
   the web app's managed identity). Its identity gets exactly: "Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User" on that ONE key,
   a contained database user (by its client id), the schema `signin` as its own and `CREATE TABLE` -- never `db_owner`,
   never a vault-wide role. A sign-in that may not name another schema owner creates the schema itself and gives the
   identity CONTROL on that one schema (the same rights). Who makes it (`pro-management\deploy\SI-SigninFrontStore.ps1`,
   one library): a new install with the database users (`Deploy-SIManagement.ps1 -SigninStoreKeyVaultName`, the
   installer's rights); `setup\Set-SISigninFront.ps1 -Apply` (step 2b); every update (`Invoke-SIContainerUpdate.ps1` step
   9g). Each piece only when missing, one line each, read back; the record `cfg.InstallState 'SigninFrontStore'`. The front
   gets the four settings -- beside every other setting it has -- ONLY when every piece reads back: a front 1.3.0 is never
   rolled in without them, so a piece the update may not make (one customer action naming `Set-SISigninFront.ps1 -Apply`)
   leaves the running front as it is. A front before 1.3.0 ignores the settings and the unused schema. SecurityInsight's
   own Data Protection keeps its own application name ("SecurityInsight Pro"); the front's is "signin-front".
   **The web app's own API for the front (#852 step 9h; #905).** From front 1.4.2 the front can hand the web app an ACCESS
   token for its own API (`SIGNIN_UPSTREAM_SCOPE = api://<client id>/user_impersonation`) instead of the ID token. It needs
   the identifier URI, the delegated scope `user_impersonation` and the app's organisation-wide consent to it
   (`pro-management\deploy\SI-SigninFrontApi.ps1`); the scope is handed to the front ONLY when all three read back. Every
   update checks them in step 9h, and `Get-SISigninFrontApiUpdateOutcome` keeps three outcomes apart, because only one is
   anybody's action: **cannot read** (a 403 on the READ of the app registration, its service principal or its grants --
   the updater's identity has no directory read) = an Info line only, saying the front stays on the ID token (it signs in
   as before); never a customer action -- on 2026-10-27 the 1957 update raised `config-missing` on every install that took
   it while all three were in place on each. **Read, in place (or added)** = the update hands out the scope itself.
   **Read, missing, and the WRITE refused** = the ONE customer action (`config-missing`), naming
   `setup\Set-SISigninFront.ps1 -Apply` and what else that script does (a new web app revision, Easy Auth off, the client
   secrets deleted unless `-KeepClientSecrets`) and telling to run it first without `-Apply`. The read the update needs is
   one it may already hold: `Directory.Read.All`, which `Install-SIUpdaterJob.ps1` gives the updater's identity when the
   installer may (for the tenant size) -- covering the application, its service principal and its oauth2PermissionGrants.
   No new or wider grant (not `Application.Read.All`, not ownership of the app). `Set-SISigninFront.ps1` is on the
   package list of `release\Build-SISupportScripts.ps1` (it builds the front's image from the release's source, so it is
   not a standalone download) with its documentation page; `SIv3-SigninScopeRead` fails when any customer action names a
   `setup\<Script>.ps1` that is on neither list.
2. **Four roles**, checked on the server for every page and every action (section 6a):
   **Reader** -- every view, export and the chat, no changes; **Delegated** -- exemptions, overrides, tier moves and
   reviews only inside the scopes assigned (security domain, optionally narrowed to asset kinds and tiers),
   read-only elsewhere, no admin pages; **Admin** -- everything in the install except roles, the licence, updates and
   template releases, and support access; **SuperAdmin** -- all of it. A kiosk *Wallboard* role sees the wall board
   only. Whoever runs setup becomes SuperAdmin. A bulk action outside the scope is refused as a whole, and a staged
   change is checked again when it is committed.
3. **The chat follows the role.** It can only call the fixed, read-only tools; only an Admin's or SuperAdmin's chat
   can read the settings history. The MCP server accepts Reader, Admin and SuperAdmin tokens; its settings tool is
   for Admin and SuperAdmin.
4. **Magic links** (off by default): a mail link may carry a signed (HMAC-SHA256, key in Key Vault), single-use token
   that opens one read-only page for up to 60 minutes (setting) without signing in. Conditional Access does not see
   such a link, which is why it is off by default.
5. **How someone signed in is recorded** on every session (Entra, magic link, magic link confirmed with a one-time
   code), and a role can require the stronger forms for an action such as approving.

**Departments and external advisors (#254 departments: built in v3, phase 1; #258 advisors: the v3 design).** Departments own assets and
recommendations: an asset's department comes from a policy (platform tags first, then SecurityInsight rules,
configurable), an override per asset, or an override per recommendation -- the recommendation override wins over
the asset override, which wins over the policy; anything left is in an *Unassigned* queue. A department has
technical and business owners, technical and business approvers, delegates and advisors, and is a Delegated scope type
that restricts what its members **see** to their own assets and findings. **Technical approvers** approve planning a fix
into the department's maintenance window: once a department lists any, only one of them (or someone the role framework
lets approve, such as an Admin) applies *Auto in the maintenance window*. **Business approvers** decide the exemption
requests raised from the department's own findings (*accept the risk*), in addition to the security domain and category
owners, and are asked by mail. On the admin pages the people are ONE table -- a row per person and role, the person
picked from a searchable list (the directory's users and groups when the directory lookup is on, and people already on
a department) or typed as an e-mail address (someone not found is an outside person with a name and company) -- created
with the department and saved in one transaction with one change-history row per change. A refused or failed change is
shown on the page in a notice that stays, never only in a passing message. External advisors (a consultant or a company) are linked to a
department. With a magic link they can view, comment and recommend; to **approve** they need a second check -- a
one-time code sent to the same mailbox, or an Entra sign-in as a B2B guest with their own company account, so the
customer controls and revokes access in Entra and Conditional Access applies. Links are per person, short-lived,
revocable, scoped to the department and audited; department owners may sign in either way.

### A5. Change control and approvals

- **Review & commit.** Tier moves, documents (exclusions, weights, rules) and settings are staged and written only on
  *Review & commit*, each in one transaction with an audit row. Nothing is deleted; an exemption is ended.
- **Governed exemptions** (section 4d): owners and approvers per security domain, request -> approve / reject with a
  comment, standard periods (3 / 6 / 12 months or a date), monthly owner review, mail. Only an approved exemption
  applies. Today the approvers are the domain's listed approvers or an Admin -- and, for a request raised from a
  department's own findings or made on a department's own page, that department's business approvers.
- **Settings history.** Every setting change, access change, exemption step and template release is a row in the
  change history (`cfg.ChangeLog`) with who, when and why.
- **The audit trail cannot be changed, enforced by the database** (framework AUDIT-1.3). `cfg.AuditEvent` (the trail)
  and `cfg.ChangeLog` (the change history it is built from, which also holds the used sign-in-link nonces) refuse
  UPDATE and DELETE to every database user except the owner: `DENY UPDATE, DELETE ... TO public` in
  `sql\si-pro-settings.sql`. **Why a DENY, not a trigger:** SecurityInsight's runtime identities are ordinary
  users. The jobs and engines hold the least-privilege role `si_engine` (#672; db_datareader + db_datawriter on an install
  not yet moved -- see "The engine identity's database rights" below). The web app holds db_datareader, named grants and
  `si_audit_writer` (INSERT + SELECT). The MCP server and support hold db_datareader. None holds db_ddladmin or
  ownership, so a DENY binds every one of them, including an identity added later under any name. PIM uses an
  INSTEAD OF trigger because its runtime identities hold db_ddladmin and could undo a DENY. The ONE way rows leave
  the trail is the retention procedure `cfg.AuditRetentionApply`. It is owned by the schema owner, so its own DELETE
  passes the DENY (ownership chaining; static SQL only). It refuses anything below 13 months and never uses a cutoff
  younger than that many months before the server's clock. It removes at most one batch per call, and only for a
  caller in db_datawriter (the data sync job) or the owner. A refusal is a THROW and removes nothing. **Honest
  limit:** the database owner (the server's Entra admin group, which runs setup) is not bound by a DENY.
- **A change a job carries out names the person who asked for it** (framework AUDIT-1.1). Much of what is decided in
  the web app is put in force by a job: a committed change (settings, documents, rules, asset tags, schema overlays,
  the report designer, CMDB links, connector setup) at each job's next run, an approved exemption request, a released
  held close set, a template release, *Run now* and *Run flow now*. For these rows the trail's **Actor is the person
  who initiated the change** (who staged it, or who requested it). The row's After also carries `approvedBy` (the
  approver, when an approval applied, such as the domain owner who approved an exemption request), `appliedBy` (the
  job) and `jobRun` (its run). Its **CorrelationId is the commit or request id**, so the web request, its change rows
  and every job row that carries the change out share one id.
  - **Recorded at commit.** The web app writes `cfg.ChangeAttribution` in the same request: the request's correlation
    id, the changed target (`doc:rule/<key>`, `setting:<name>@<scope>`, `connector:<name>`,
    `exemption-request/<id>`, `release/<run>`, `job/<job>`, `jobflow/daily`, ...), who initiated it and who approved
    it. The table is additive, append-only (the same `DENY UPDATE, DELETE ... TO public`), and the web identity may
    only INSERT into it.
  - **Keyed by the target, not by the live row.** A removal (a reset document, a revoked or ended exemption, an
    unlinked asset, a removed connector) is therefore still attributed after its row is gone.
  - **How the jobs read it.** Every job the web app starts for a person carries the request id and the person in its
    environment (`SI_AUDIT_CID`, `SI_AUDIT_STARTED_BY`). The jobs' audit writer looks the id up and names that
    person on every row the run writes. The settings layer of every Pro job records, at run start, one
    `settings.change.apply` event per committed change that is new to that job. The vulnerability connector looks a
    released set up by its run.
  - **No person asked.** A scheduled run, an expiry, the retention and the close-loop's own closes keep the job as
    the actor, and the row says so (`initiatedBy: no person`). A scheduled flow run also names who last set the flow
    (`flowSetBy`).
  - **Honest limit:** the steps a manual flow run starts are separate job executions; their own rows name the job,
    and the flow's `job.flow.run` row names the person.
- **Template releases by ring** (section 9b): template packs reach an install through its update ring, are checked
  against their SHA-256, and are released per detection method by a SuperAdmin through Review & commit; your
  overrides are never changed and any method can be rolled back.
- **One deviation report** (section 14) lists every override, exemption, exclusion, disabled detection, tier move
  and changed setting with its owner, reason and expiry.
- **Guarded connectors**: plan (*whatif*) before *apply*, only items the connector created are changed, and a large
  or sudden drop is held for a person.

### A6. Licensing and integrity

- **Signed licence.** A JSON licence signed with RSA and SHA-256, stored as a Key Vault secret and verified offline:
  signature, dates (with the licence's grace period, 30 days by default), product and tenant. The
  verifier trusts two signers -- the AutomateIT licensing key and the Invardia licensing key -- so licences from
  either verify. A licence that names no tenant is valid in no tenant.
- **The edition decides, not a feature list** (framework section 12.6a LICENCE-FEATURES, #510). The signed licence names
  its EDITION in `sku`; SecurityInsight maps edition to features in its own catalog (`engine/SI-FeatureCatalog.ps1`). A
  Pro edition (sku Pro, Pro-Business, Pro Enterprise, Pro-DesignPartner, pro-single-tenant, Trial) runs EVERY Pro
  feature, including features released after the licence was signed -- no licence is re-signed for a new feature. An
  MSP edition (sku naming MSP) adds the multi-tenant features (none today). Pro Business and Pro Enterprise differ only
  by the signed `limits`. The licence's `features[]` list is informational and counts only for an explicit paid
  add-on, which must be listed by name (`*` does not cover an add-on); SecurityInsight has no add-ons today. A
  Community sku, an invalid licence, one past its grace period or one for another tenant gives Community.
- **Bound to the real tenant.** With a managed identity, the tenant is read from the identity's own token (a
  setting cannot change it) and an unproven tenant fails closed; with a service principal, it is the tenant it signs
  in to. A licence copied to another tenant does not unlock Pro. Without a valid licence the Pro components say so
  in one line and do nothing; every Community component keeps running.
- **Signed updates** (section 12c): the updater accepts a manifest only when its RS256 signature verifies against
  Invardia's update-signing **public** keys embedded in SecurityInsight (a key list fetched over the network is never
  trusted on its own), the product and kind match, its sequence is not lower than the one applied, and the
  download's size and SHA-256 match. A manual step holds the update until you accept it. The update-signing private
  key is held by Invardia and is exportable by the owner's decision; SecurityInsight relies only on the embedded
  public key list, which is also how keys are rotated.

### A7. Touch points with Invardia

| What | When | What is sent |
|---|---|---|
| **Licence request** (section 12b) | Pro: when there is no valid licence for the tenant, or it ends within 30 days | product, version, the tenant from the identity's token, an install id, optionally edition and a contact e-mail and the current licence's id / end date. The answer is verified offline before it is installed. |
| **Update pull** (section 12c) | Pro updater, nightly | the licence and the install key (header); the install key is claimed automatically with the licence when the install has none. Nothing else about the estate. |
| **Support app** | only when you create it | Invardia Support is an app registration the customer creates in their own tenant with Invardia's script, at a *troubleshoot* level (Key Vault metadata without secret values) or a *setup* level (Key Vault Secrets Officer); at both levels it becomes an owner of SecurityInsight's own app registrations and a member of the database admin group. That group is its one way in to the Pro databases: the database server's administrator is the group (recorded by the server as a group), the Support app is a member, and it has no database user of its own. The install adds the membership and never removes it; the end of the install reads the administrator back, and an install run as the Support app proves the sign-in. An install made earlier reaches the same state with `setup/Grant-SISupportAppDatabase.ps1` and with every update: a database user an earlier version made for the Support app is removed, but only in a run that has itself read back the group as administrator and the membership -- otherwise the user stays and the run says so. SecurityInsight's `setup/Grant-SISupportAccess.ps1` adds the SecurityInsight part and `-Remove` takes it back. It is never the engine's identity. |
| **Status reports (telemetry)** | daily, and once per engine run; on by default, `SI_Telemetry_Enabled = $false` turns it off | Community: anonymous -- a random install id, the product, edition, version, hosting type, the kind of sign-in identity, licence state, and per run the job, outcome, duration, failed stage, an error class and counts as ranges; no tenant, host name or error text. Pro: the same, identified by the install key, with the tenant, the host and the error text (shortened, secrets removed). See "Status reports to Invardia (telemetry)" under Operations. |

Apart from the status reports (which can be turned off), the Community edition never contacts Invardia.

### A8. Data retention

| Data | Kept for | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| Log Analytics workspace (every SecurityInsight table) | 90 days when setup **creates** the workspace; an existing workspace keeps its own retention | setup (create only) / you |
| Individual SecurityInsight tables | the workspace's retention -- SecurityInsight never sets table retention | you |
| Trend table | recommended 365 days; the trend engine prints the exact command and does not apply it | you |
| Pro database: copied collections (findings, daily aggregates, facets, services) and assets no longer seen | 90 days (`SI_Pro_DataRetentionDays`), pruned by the daily data sync | setting |
| Pro database: the finding rows of a collection (findings, recommendations, prepared issue rows; Summary rows) | per kind the newest complete collection and the one before it; older ones, and collections a stopped run left loading once a newer one is complete, lose their rows at the next data sync -- the collection's aggregates stay until the 90 days above | -- |
| Pro database: vulnerability state and events, the identity ledger, settings and their history, exemptions (ended, never deleted), template revisions, connector runs and items | kept until you delete them | -- |
| Pro database: the audit trail (`cfg.AuditEvent`) | kept forever by default; with `SI_Pro_AuditRetentionMonths` (at least 13), older rows are removed by the data sync's audited retention step, which records itself -- through `cfg.AuditRetentionApply` only, because the database refuses any other UPDATE or DELETE (section A5) | setting |
| Run logs (local and in blob storage) | 30 days (`SI_LogRetentionDays`) | setting |
| Configuration snapshot logs | 7 days | fixed |
| Staging shards in blob storage | 7 days, when the storage lifecycle rule is applied (`Bootstrap-Storage.ps1`) | setup / you |
| Risk Analysis exports (Excel / JSON) and their timestamped `.bak` copies, collection-engine JSON / Excel outputs, the fingerprint table, shared customisation files | no automatic pruning | you |
| Azure SQL backups | Azure SQL's defaults; SecurityInsight changes none | you |

### A9. The scripts you run -- documented, dry-run first, logged, signed

Every script a person runs follows the same rules, so a security reviewer can approve each one before it runs: the
configuration scripts SecurityInsight hands you as standalone downloads (`https://invardia.com/support/si/<Script>.ps1`)
and the scripts that ship in the release package and run inside an install (the guided install, the updater job, the
container update, the Pro settings and template imports, the flow task, the deviation report, ...):

- **A documentation page per script** at `https://invardia.com/docs/si/scripts/<Script>/`. The page is rendered from the
  script's manifest, `<Script>.doc.json`, which is built with the script and handed over next to it: its purpose, when
  to run it, the roles it needs to run (`runAs`: Entra role, Azure role, Exchange role, with the scope and why), every
  change it makes (`changes`: create / update / grant / remove, the object, the permission and scope, why, how to undo
  it), its parameters (read from the script itself), what it only reads, every host it calls (`network`, read from the
  code it carries), what `-WhatIf` shows, how to undo the whole script, its version and its SHA-256.
  The page shows the manifest only while it matches the published script exactly (the same version and SHA-256);
  otherwise it says the documentation is pending or out of date.
- **The documentation link comes first.** `Get-Help .\<Script>.ps1` shows it (`.LINK`), and the first line every run
  prints is `Documentation: <that page>`.
- **"What does this script do?" wherever a script is named.** Every page of the web app that names one of these
  scripts (a setup step, a notice, an error that says what to run) shows the link to that script's page next to it --
  added once, to every rendered page, after the sentence that names the script. A mail that tells its reader to run a
  script carries the same link.
- **`-WhatIf` changes nothing.** Every script supports `-WhatIf` (and `-Confirm`). Under `-WhatIf` it signs in, reads
  and prints what it WOULD change -- and writes nothing, even when a switch that normally applies a change (`-Apply`,
  `-Disable`, ...) is passed too. The product's test suite runs every script this way with every outside call replaced
  (Azure Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Log Analytics, mail, SQL, `az`, the browser sign-in) and fails on any write.
- **A transcript of every run** is kept on the machine it ran on, in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SecurityInsight\script-logs`
  (`SI_SCRIPT_LOG_DIR` moves it), named `<Script>-<yyyyMMdd-HHmmss>.log`; the last line a run prints is its path. A
  secret is never printed or written to it: secret parameters are `SecureString`s or Key Vault secret NAMES.
- **No second download.** A script carries everything it runs: the standalone file embeds its helpers, each checked
  against its SHA-256 before it runs. Nothing is fetched and executed at run time.
- **Save, then run** -- never pipe a download into PowerShell. Every command block SecurityInsight shows (web app, mail,
  setup output, docs) is line 1 the download, line 2 (more only when really needed) the command with every value it
  knows filled in -- nothing else inside the block: no checksum, signature or comment lines. The documentation link
  sits next to the block. Add `-WhatIf` to see what a script would change first. For example:

  ```powershell
  Invoke-WebRequest https://invardia.com/support/si/Grant-SIIdentity.ps1 -OutFile Grant-SIIdentity.ps1
  ./Grant-SIIdentity.ps1 -WhatIf
  ```

  To verify a download, compare `Get-FileHash <Script>.ps1 -Algorithm SHA256` with `SHA256SUMS.txt` (published next
  to the scripts).
  `tests\pester\SIv3-CommandBlocks.Tests.ps1` (and the web app's `CommandBlockTests`) fail on a block that breaks this.
## Editions, configuration and updates (3.0)

### 1. Two editions, one tree

SecurityInsight ships as the **Community** edition (the public repository) and a licensed **Pro** edition.
Which component belongs to which edition is declared in ONE place, `engine/SI-FeatureCatalog.ps1`:

| Component | Edition |
|---|---|
| asset profiling (endpoint / identity / azure / publicip), privilege-tier classifier, cross-engine correlation and the full asset properties, Risk Analysis, Risk Score, trend, CMDB from a CSV, AI classification and the AI summary, Shodan, asset tagging, verification and data health, the database, the web app (its free pages), the in-cloud updater on the signed Community channel | Community |
| the ServiceNow and SQL CMDB connectors with the vulnerability close-loop, governance (departments, exemptions, follow-up tasks, security owners) and its mails, mail alerts and management summary mails, roles and scopes, the audit trail, template releases, the AI chat and the MCP server, the signed licence and updates through Invardia, support | Pro |

Since 2026-10-27 (owner decisions on the Community edition): correlation, the full asset properties, asset tagging,
verification and data health are Community. The web app and the MCP server ship as one file set in both editions; their
paid pages, actions and services are switched off by the licence (the list of record is
`pro-management/src/SI.Management.Web/Licensing/ProFeatures.cs`; the MCP server answers only while the installation's recorded
licence names a Pro edition). The paid ENGINES stay out of the public copy as files.

- A Pro component asks the catalog before it does any work. Without a valid licence it prints **one line**
  saying so and publishes nothing; the run still succeeds and every Community component runs as before.
- The licence is a signed file. `setup/Set-SILicense.ps1` (shipped with Pro) verifies it — signature, expiry,
  tenant — **before** storing it as the Key Vault secret `SI-License`; unattended setup does the same from
  `Licence.Path`. The engines read it from the vault the config names (also the 2.2-style vault setting).
- The Community edition never contacts a licence server and needs no licence. The public repository
  contains no Pro code: the publish step excludes every Pro path, and a test asserts it.

### 2. Configuration layers — your file wins

Every launcher loads configuration in this order; a later layer overrides an earlier one:

| # | Layer | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | built-in engine defaults | shipped |
| 2 | platform settings (managed installs only) | platform |
| 3 | `launcher/<engine>/LauncherConfig.defaults.ps1` | shipped |
| 4 | `config/SecurityInsight.custom.ps1` | **you** |
| 5 | `launcher/<engine>/LauncherConfig.custom.ps1` | **you** — per-engine override |

Until 3.0, layers 3 and 4 were the other way round, so a shipped per-engine default silently replaced
the value you set (about 60 settings were affected). The shipped defaults files now assign a value only
when nothing earlier set it.

`config/SecurityInsight.custom.reference.ps1` lists every setting the engines read, with its default; a
test pins the settings added in 3.0 and fails the build if a setting nothing reads comes back.

**Setup upgrades the file instead of replacing it.** The wizard, unattended setup and the command line
parse your existing `SecurityInsight.custom.ps1`, keep every value in it, and append only the settings
it lacks in one marked block — after writing a backup of the previous file.

### 2b. Changing settings

Community: edit the custom files (`config\SecurityInsight.custom.ps1` and the engines' `LauncherConfig.custom.ps1`); the shipped defaults stay untouched and your file wins. SecurityInsight Pro keeps every setting in its database and changes them in its web app, with a review before saving and a change history.

**Every setting explains itself.** Each of the roughly 300 settings has:

- a **plain name** ("Azure asset limit"), with its internal name (`SI_AssetLimit_Azure`) shown small underneath for support and scripts;
- what it is **for**, in one sentence;
- its **default** -- what really happens when you leave it alone ("No limit (every discovered resource)", "Off", "Read from your Key Vault at run start"), never a bare "(none)";
- **what changes if you change it**, including run time, cost, data completeness and risk;
- **when to change it** -- most installs never should;
- its **unit** where it has one (days, hours, minutes, rows, attempts), shown beside every value.

Settings are grouped by what you want to do, in this order: **Mail & notifications**, **Schedules & what runs**, **Collection scope & limits**, **Risk Analysis reports**, **AI**, **Connectors & CMDB**, **Data & retention**, **Sign-in & Azure resources** (set at install, rarely changed) and **Advanced / diagnostics** (diagnostic switches, older names kept for existing configuration files, internal plumbing). Each area has a one-line description and a count. Within an area the common settings come first; tuning knobs are marked *advanced* and folded away until you open them. A setting that belongs to one collection engine carries the engine as a small tag.

**The Pro Settings page** (Configuration > Settings) works like PIM Manager's settings page. A bar at the top picks a **category** (one is shown at a time; the browser remembers the last one, and a link from another page opens the right one). Each category holds **cards**, one per topic -- *Mail server*, *Risk Analysis report mails*, *Daily vulnerability mail*, *Mails to departments*, ... -- with one sentence saying what the card is for and **one Save**. Inside a card every setting is a field you change in place: a **switch** for on/off, a **number** with its limits and unit, a **dropdown** with plain words, a **text box**, and for a list of mail addresses **address chips** (type an address and press Enter, a comma or a semicolon; x removes it; an entry that is not an address is refused before anything is saved). A secret is the **name** of its Key Vault secret, never the secret. An empty field shows its default in grey; a small dot marks a value changed from the default, with *Reset to default* beside it. A field that only works with another setting says so -- *Needs Send the daily vulnerability mail on -- it is off now* -- with a link to it. Everything else (what it is for, what changing it does, when to change it, the default in full, the internal name for support, the comment from the configuration file, the change history) sits behind a small **(i)**, closed until you open it. Each category's tuning knobs are folded under *Show advanced*.

Save writes only the fields that changed, each one validated against the settings catalog first (if one is refused, nothing is written and the card says why in red next to the field) and then stored with the version check and a change-history row (reason *changed in Settings*). A value someone else changed since you opened the page is not overwritten -- reload and save again. The licence settings are changed by a SuperAdmin only. A value a field cannot show (for example a list stored on a text setting) and the CMDB source (changed on its own page, which explains the switch first) link to their page instead. You can search by the plain name, the internal name or any of the explaining text; the box also filters as you type.

**The Licence card** (category *Licence & updates*) shows the **installed** licence first: the customer, the edition, the date it is valid until and its state -- *Valid*, *Ends soon* (within 30 days), *Not valid yet*, *In grace*, *Expired*, *Wrong tenant*, *Does not verify* or *Missing* -- coloured, with one sentence on what happens next. The updater job verifies the installed licence every night with the same offline checks the engines use (signature, dates, tenant) and records the result in the Pro database; the web app shows that record and never reads the licence itself. The renewal request (requested / waiting / installed / rejected) is the line under it.

Community installs get the same words at the end of `config\SecurityInsight.custom.reference.ps1`, in a generated **settings glossary** grouped the same way. Both come from one source in the product, so the web app and the reference never disagree.

**Templates are ours, configuration is yours.** SecurityInsight Pro separates two things. *Templates* are the content we develop and improve: the detection rules, the Risk Analysis reports, the risk weights index, the tagging rules and the service model -- just like the `.locked` files of a Community install. *Configuration* describes your environment and is yours alone: every setting, including the names of your tables, DCRs, DCE and workspace (the default in the settings list is the only default), and the **CMDB ownership map** -- per asset type, which import connector already owns it in your CMDB. The ownership map is one document on the Settings side (*Exclusions, weights, rules* -> *CMDB ownership*): setup fills it from the shipped map once, you change it there, and every change is staged and saved through Review & commit. A template release never changes a setting or the ownership map. An install that had names or ownership entries as template overrides keeps every one of them: setup carries each name over as a setting and the ownership entries into the ownership document, unchanged, and keeps the old rows as history.

### 2c. How SecurityInsight signs in — managed identity first

One setting chooses the identity the engines use, on every host:

| `SI_AuthMethod` | Signs in as |
|---|---|
| `ManagedIdentity` (**default**) | the host's managed identity — an Azure VM's, an Azure Arc-enabled server's, or a container job's. `SI_ManagedIdentityClientId` selects a user-assigned identity; empty = the system-assigned one. |
| `Certificate` | a service principal with a certificate (recommended when a service principal is needed) |
| `Secret` | a service principal with a client secret |

- **Existing installs keep what they have.** When `SI_AuthMethod` is not set, a configured service principal
  stays in use and a managed install keeps its platform identity; only an install with no service principal
  falls to the managed identity.
- **The decision is made once**, after the last configuration layer, and every token request in the run
  follows it — Microsoft Graph, Defender, Azure, Log Analytics ingestion, storage, Key Vault and SQL.
- **The host decides the endpoint.** A container job uses its identity endpoint; an Azure VM uses the
  instance metadata endpoint; an Azure Arc-enabled server uses the Arc agent's endpoint, whose key file
  can be read only by a local administrator or a member of *Hybrid agent extension applications* — run the
  scheduled task as one of those.
- The identity needs the same permissions as a service principal would (Graph application permissions,
  Azure roles, SQL user). Container setup grants them to the job identity; for a VM or Arc server, grant
  them to that machine's identity.
- The asset-tagging engine follows the same decision: as the managed identity it takes its Microsoft Graph,
  Defender and Azure tokens from the identity endpoint; as a service principal it signs in by certificate or
  by client secret, as before. Because it is the one engine that writes, give it its **own** identity
  (`setup/Grant-SIIdentity.ps1 -Tagging`) — never the read-only collection identity. See *Asset tagging*.
- A support account signing in to an install to help is never the engine's identity.

### 2d. Default names

A new SecurityInsight install names what it creates after its purpose: `<type>-si-<ring>-<edition>-<hosting>`, for example `rg-si-prod-community-ca`, `log-si-prod-community-ca`, `stsiprodcommunityca01`. The ring is `prod` for a single production install; the edition is `pro` when you install with a licence and `community` otherwise; the hosting is `ca` for Container Apps and `vm` for a server. Each resource group setup creates is tagged product, ring, edition, hosting, tenant, owner and purpose. Entra objects read `SecurityInsight (prod-community-ca)`, and the Pro database is administered by one role-assignable group, `grp-si-sql-admins`. These are only defaults: you may choose your own names, and an existing install keeps the names it already has.

### 3. Container jobs read your settings through the environment

A container never sees `config/SecurityInsight.custom.ps1`. `Bootstrap-ContainerAppJob.ps1` loads it,
and passes **every non-secret setting** to each job as an environment variable `SI_CFG_<name>`
(type-preserving: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays). The container entrypoint turns them back into
the same `$global:` settings before the engine starts — so a setting means the same thing on a VM and in
a container, without a per-setting mapping.

Secrets never travel that way: a name that looks like a secret (key, secret, password, token,
connection string) is skipped, and the bootstrap passes the secrets an engine needs as **job secrets**
(Azure OpenAI key, Shodan key, Pro licence). Storage needs no secret: every job reaches it with its own
identity. Azure OpenAI is optional: without it the job runs without AI classification. The bootstrap creates one job per engine, including trend (and the Pro engines when
their code is present), each on its own schedule after the engines it reads.

Setup records where the containers live (`SI_Bootstrap_ResourceGroupName`, `SI_Bootstrap_AcrName`,
`SI_Bootstrap_SubscriptionId`) so later updates find them; an install made before 3.0 records them once
with `setup/Invoke-SIContainerUpdate.ps1 ... -Save`.

### 3a. Container parity — a container job runs like the VM launcher

Every feature of the VM launchers works when the engines run as Container Apps jobs. The settings are layered the same
way, in the same order:

1. **The engine's shipped defaults** (`launcher/<engine>/LauncherConfig.defaults.ps1`) — the container loads them first,
   exactly as the VM launcher does. They hold no tenant value and nothing the container decides itself (sign-in,
   storage, targets).
2. **Your config** (`config/SecurityInsight.custom.ps1`) — passed to every job as `SI_CFG_<name>`.
3. **The engine's own launcher config** (`launcher/<engine>/LauncherConfig.custom.ps1`) — setup reads it separately for
   each engine and passes it to that engine's jobs only, winning over your config name by name, as on a VM. Every Risk
   Analysis job shares the `risk-analysis` one.
4. **The Pro settings database**, when you have one.
5. **The job's own environment variables** (`SI_RA_*`, `SI_ASSET_LIMIT`, `SI_SINKS`, `SI_FORCE_FULL_RUN`) — these win only
   when they are **present**. An absent one never overwrites a setting from the layers above.

Secret-looking names never travel as settings. A few settings whose names only look like secrets are let through by
exact name: the AI token limits (`AI_MaxTokens`, `AI_MaxTokensPerRequest`, `OpenAI_MaxTokensPerRequest`) and
`SI_IdentityTokenTenantId`.

| VM launcher switch / setting | In a container job |
|---|---|
| `-InstallPath`, `-LauncherConfigPath` | the image root; the engine's launcher defaults and custom file reach the job as described above |
| `-WhatIfMode` | the `WhatIfMode` setting -- a dry run: profiling and Risk Analysis keep their results in local files (nothing to Log Analytics, mail, the export location, the fingerprint / CMDB caches or the run-health table), the tier classifier writes `<catalog>.dryrun.json` beside the catalog, asset tagging reports what it would change |
| `-AssetLimit`, `-Sinks`, `-ForceFullRun` (endpoint, identity, azure, publicip) | `SI_ASSET_LIMIT` / `SI_SINKS` / `SI_FORCE_FULL_RUN` on the job when set, else your `SI_AssetLimit_<Engine>` / `SI_Sinks_<Engine>` / `SI_ForceFullRun_<Engine>` (a full run also when the solution-wide `SI_ForceFullRun` is on, as on a VM), else all assets, JSON + Excel + Log Analytics, incremental |
| `-StorageAccountName` | the job's storage account, reached with the job's own identity |
| trend `-Grain`, `-DryRun`, `-Weeks` | the `SI_Trend_Grain`, `SI_Trend_DryRun`, `SI_Trend_Weeks` settings |
| Risk Analysis `-ReportTemplate`, `-Summary`, `-Detailed` | one job per report: Summary and Detailed with your `RiskAnalysis_ReportTemplate_Default_Summary` / `_Detailed` (else the shipped templates), plus any extra report jobs you list |
| Risk Analysis copy of the report rows to Log Analytics | **off** (an optional output, #830), as on a VM, unless you switch it on (`SendToLogAnalytics = $true`, or `SI_RiskAnalysis_SendToLogAnalytics` / `-RiskAnalysisSendToLogAnalytics` at setup) |
| Risk Analysis `-BuildSummaryByAI`, mail | your `BuildSummaryByAI` and mail settings; an AI summary without Azure OpenAI on the job runs without it and says so |
| Risk Analysis `-AutoBucketCount`, `-AutoBucketCache`, `-AutoBucketMax`, `-ResetCache` | your settings, else the VM defaults (bucketing and cache on, cap 131072); the bucket cache is kept in your storage account between runs |
| Risk Analysis `-ShowConfig`, `-DebugQueryHash` | the `ShowConfig`, `DebugQueryHash` settings |
| Your customisation files (CMDB.csv, custom Risk Analysis queries, exclusion and weight files, enrichment rules, schema overlays, decision files) | shared to the `sioverlay` container of your storage account by setup and after every update, and restored by each job to the same place a VM reads them |
| Console-only switches (`-SuppressErrors`, `-SuppressWarnings`, trend `-ShowWeeklyRate`) | not needed: a job keeps its whole run log in your storage account, and the weekly rate is written on every run |
| Developer tools (`-Mock`, `-RunAssetSimulation`, `-AssetSimulationAmount`) | VM only, by design — never on a scheduled job |

**Schedules.** Each job has its own schedule. The privilege-tier classifier runs first (default 01:00 UTC), because the
profilers read the tier catalog it builds; publicip runs after the endpoint and Azure profilers (05:15 UTC), because it
reads their results. Set them with `SI_Bootstrap_ScheduleClassifier` / `SI_Bootstrap_SchedulePublicIp`. Without Azure
OpenAI the classifier job is not created — it would classify every role as Tier 99 (manual review) and replace the
shipped catalog — and setup says so in one line. In a container the classifier reads the catalog it shared last time,
so it skips a rebuild within 24 hours exactly as on a VM.

**Job sizes.** Replica timeout, CPU and memory are settings per engine: `SI_Bootstrap_ReplicaTimeout_<Engine>` (seconds,
300–604800, that is up to 7 days), `SI_Bootstrap_Cpu_<Engine>` (0.25–4) and `SI_Bootstrap_Memory_<Engine>` (for example `4Gi`), where `<Engine>`
is the engine name as in the other per-engine settings (`Endpoint`, `PublicIp`, `RiskAnalysis`, `RiskAnalysisDetailed`,
`PrivilegeTierClassifier`). Unset, a job gets 2 CPU / 4 GiB (more for a tenant of 5,000 objects or more) and the longest
run limit Azure takes, 604800 s -- SecurityInsight chooses no run limit, so the timeout setting can only make a job's
run limit SHORTER, on purpose. A value that is not valid is ignored with a warning; setup carries on.

**Extra report jobs.** List them in your config; each becomes its own job `caj-si-ra-<name>`:

```powershell
$global:SI_Bootstrap_RiskAnalysisJobs = @(
    @{ Name = 'identity-weekly'; Template = 'RiskAnalysis_Detailed_IdentityOnly'; Cron = '0 12 * * 0' }
    @{ Name = 'board';           Mode = 'Summary'; Template = 'Board_Report';     Cron = '0 7 1 * *' }
)
```

`Name` is 1–22 lower-case letters, digits or `-`; `Mode` (Summary or Detailed) may be left out when the template's name
says it; `Cron` is in UTC. A job that is not valid is not created, and setup says why.

**Customisation files and Pro.** An install with the Pro settings database keeps its configuration there, so its jobs
do not use the shared files. A Community install needs no licence for them. The container image never carries them, so
the first image and every updated image behave the same.

### 4. Updating

| Install | How it updates |
|---|---|
| **Community, VM** | `Update-SecurityInsight.ps1` takes the release its **update ring** approves from the signed release channel on GitHub, checks it, and applies it with a backup and an automatic restore (see "The Community update channel" below). No git needed. |
| **Community, containers** | The same command; after the files it runs the NEW release's container update hook (below), and puts the files back too if the containers are rolled back. |
| **Pro / managed** | The managed sync delivers the release the customer's ring is on; after a sync that changed SecurityInsight it runs the same container hook (`solution.deploy.json`). Rings are a platform mechanism, not SecurityInsight's own. |
| **Pro, containers** | An updater job in the customer's subscription takes the release its ring has from **Invardia** -- a signed manifest, checked before anything changes (see 12c) -- and rolls the jobs. The vendor's own read-only feed (a revocable URL held as a job secret, decided from the ring map) remains as an internal test path. |

Both editions run the same containers; they differ only in the licence (which features run) and in how an
install is updated. The updater code ships in both editions — what Pro adds is the Invardia client and its updates (the
release SecurityInsight gave the install's ring; SI's own update feed is retired). A container install switches to the
updater with `setup/Upgrade-SIToPro.ps1`, run from the Pro package. It reuses the container hosting setup saved and the
engine identity; the customer adds the update ring (and, without `-UseManagedIdentity`, the SPN certificate's secret name).
It records the job as the owner of the rollout, and from then on the container hook leaves those containers to the
job (`-Force` rolls by hand anyway). A re-run of container setup keeps that record.

**The Community update channel.** A Community install updates from Invardia's signed Community channel, never simply to
"whatever is newest" (the same path PIM's Community edition uses, 2026-10-28):

- **Rings.** Ring 3 (broad) is the default; ring 2 is early release -- set `{ "ring": 2 }` in
  `config\update.custom.json`. A release reaches ring 2 only after SecurityInsight's own internal ring has run it, and
  ring 3 only after ring 2 had it. The public `main` branch moves to a new major version only once ring 3 has it, so an
  install that still runs a plain `git pull` gets it last.
- **The channel** is `GET https://invardia.com/api/updates/securityinsight/community/<ring>`, anonymous (no install key, no
  code, no licence): 200 = the signed answer, in the same shape as the manifests SecurityInsight Pro receives from
  Invardia, so both editions are checked by the same code; 204 = nothing released to the ring yet; 404 = no such ring. The
  archive it names is the public GitHub release zip. (The `channel.json` file on an `update-channel` branch is retired.)
- **Checked before anything is downloaded:** the RS256 signature over the manifest bytes against the update-signing keys
  this version ships with (`engine/_shared/InvardiaUpdate.verify.ps1` -- a key fetched over the network is never
  trusted); the product, the kind, a ring the manifest names IS the install's ring, the same MAJOR version as installed; a
  sequence never lower than the one already applied (a rollback is a new, higher sequence that names an older version);
  the download link is https. A release that asks for a **manual step** waits until it is accepted with
  `-AcceptManualStep <sequence>`; one that needs a newer **starting version** waits with the reason.
- **Download:** the release zip, which must have exactly the signed size and SHA-256, hold `VERSION` = the signed version,
  and still carry the update client (a release without it would end updates for the install).
- **Apply on a VM:** this install's scheduled tasks are paused (a running engine means the update waits for the next run;
  the task that runs the update itself -- or the job flow -- is never paused); every file the release replaces or removes
  is backed up (`.si-update\b\<previous version>`); the release is written; the install is checked (the version, every
  file's hash, every PowerShell file parses, the client is present); then, on a container install, the new release's
  container hook runs. **Any failure restores the backup and verifies it.** The tasks are resumed in every case.
  `*.custom.*` files, `logs`, `output`, `data`, `staging`, `.git` and `config\asset-tagging.config.json` are never
  touched. Files a previous update installed that the new release no longer has are removed; on the first update by the
  channel, files it did not install are left in place.
- **Not here:** a folder that is part of an AutomateIT tree (updated by the managed sync) or that holds SecurityInsight Pro
  (updated by its updater job) is never updated from the community channel.
- **Running it updates** -- there is no report-only mode (`-Apply` is accepted and changes nothing). Schedule it as its
  own daily task: it is never a step of the job pipeline, and it waits while an engine runs.
- A folder that is also a git clone keeps working; a scheduled `git pull` there stops once the channel moves the folder
  past the public `main` (git reports local changes), which is harmless, and the update says so.

**Releasing to a ring (the vendor, framework UPDATE-1.7).** SecurityInsight decides which version goes to which ring;
Invardia only signs the entry -- the zip stays on GitHub. `setup/Publish-SICommunityRelease.ps1 -Version <v> -Ring <2|3>`
signs in as SI's own publisher identity (`Invardia.Publisher.securityinsight`, certificate only), REGISTERS the version
(`POST /api/releases/securityinsight/community {version, tag, engineChanged}` -- tag is always `''` = the stable
`v<version>` zip, as PIM's community-register; a ring name never belongs in it) and RELEASES it
(`POST /api/releases/securityinsight/community/rings/<ring> {version}`), then reads the signed entry back
(`GET /api/updates/securityinsight/community/<ring>`, anonymous) and checks it with the client's own code. Rings 2 and 3
are customers: `-OperatorApproval` carries the operator's words. Plan by default; `-Apply` sends. This replaces the old
step "the owner registers and releases in Invardia's back office". `-SignedEntryOut` saves the served entry for the record.
(The tool that wrote ring entries into a `channel.json` on an `update-channel` branch, `setup/Publish-SIUpdateChannel.ps1`,
is retired, 2026-10-28: installs read Invardia's answer directly.)

**No 2.2 hand-over (retired 2026-10-28, owner).** SecurityInsight 2.2 is no longer updated: its public `main` branch stays at
2.2.460, and SecurityInsight 3 is published to its own branch (`v3`) and installed beside 2.2. The planned 2.2.461
hand-over release (a 2.2 update that moved a 2.2 install onto this channel) and its channel plan are retired; a 2.2 install
that pulls `main` keeps 2.2.460. The Community client refuses a release of another major version than the one installed.
**The container update hook** (`setup/Invoke-SIContainerUpdate.ps1`) is detect → build → roll → verify →
roll back:

1. **Detect** — is this a container install, and which jobs run an image other than the one built from
   *this* tree? The image tag is `v<VERSION>-<content hash>`, so two trees with the same version but
   different code never share a tag.
2. **Build** — the registry builds the image from the solution folder (packed here with `.dockerignore` applied,
   uploaded, built by ARM `scheduleRun`, followed to its end -- `setup/_shared/SI-AcrBuild.ps1`, #521), only when that
   tag is not already in the registry.
3. **Roll** — point each job at the new image, recording its previous image first.
4. **Verify** — read every job back; each must now carry the new image.
5. **Roll back** — on any failure after a job changed, every changed job returns to its previous image and
   the hook exits 1 so the caller reports the update as failed.

It runs detect-only unless given `-Apply`. It talks to Azure over REST only (#521, no az CLI, no PowerShell module):
signed in ONCE with SecurityInsight's own token client -- the updater job's identity (`SI_UPDATER_*`), else the run's own
sign-in from the config (`SI_SPN_*` app or managed identity) -- and says so in one line, instead of failing on a registry
call, when that identity cannot reach the registry.
**Release integrity.** A Pro release comes only from Invardia's update platform (SecurityInsight's own update feed is retired, 2026-10-06): its size and SHA-256 are in the signed manifest, which must verify against the keys built into SecurityInsight and name the install's ring; the updater computes the SHA-256 of the archive it downloaded and compares it before anything is extracted or rolled -- a mismatch stops the update. The publisher (`Publish-SIRelease.ps1`) checks that Invardia stored the same SHA-256.

**Software bill of materials.** Every release archive carries a CycloneDX 1.5 SBOM, `SOLUTIONS/SecurityInsight/sbom.cdx.json`,
built by the release tooling from the archive itself after everything the edition does not ship was removed: the container
base images of every Dockerfile (the final image of each `required`, a build stage `excluded`), the .NET packages each
project references directly (the web app, the MCP server, their core library, the shared sign-in front, the PDF helper;
`pkg:nuget` purls, per project in `dependencies`), and every file of the release with its SHA-256. It does not list itself,
and the same archive always gives the same SBOM. Because it is inside the archive, the archive's SHA-256 in the signed manifest
covers it; a copy (`securityinsight-<version>.cdx.json`) is published with the release notes. `setup\Test-SIReleaseSbom.ps1`
checks an archive (with `-ExpectedSha256` = the signed value first) or an installed SecurityInsight folder against it. The
packages those packages bring in are resolved when the install builds its images and are not listed.

**Guided install as a command.** `setup/Install-SecurityInsight.psd1` exports `Install-SecurityInsight`, which forwards every parameter unchanged to `setup/Install-SecurityInsight.ps1` and leaves its exit code in `$LASTEXITCODE` (0 installed, 1 a step failed, 2 a check failed, 3 config.json not valid). Every event's action carries both a text and a command; a note without a command is part of the message, and a failure without a command of its own gets the resume command. Paths are built for Linux (Azure Cloud Shell) as well as Windows.

**Install diagnostics.** `diagnostics/Test-SIInstall.ps1` reads the install's config (without running it) and reports, read-only: rows and the last time per SecurityInsight table, the latest start and end per engine with how it ended, the data collection rules, and isolation -- the install's identity holds no write role outside its resource group beyond the documented grants, and its data collection rule names are unique in the subscription. Exit 1 when anything is wrong. `diagnostics/Invoke-SIJobsOnce.ps1` runs every Container Apps job once in schedule order (jobs that start at the same time run together, groups run one after the other), reports each outcome and duration, and exits 1 on any failure; `-PlanOnly` shows the order. Both use plain REST (no Az modules) and sign in as the Az session, or as the install's own identity.

### 4a. Log Analytics ingestion — SecurityInsight's own REST client

Every upload goes through one set of SecurityInsight functions, and they do the work over plain REST -- there is no
module and no switch:
- **Sign-in** follows the run's decision (managed identity, certificate or secret), with tokens cached per audience.
- **Lookup** of the data collection endpoint and rules is by name, but only within the configured subscription and
  resource group, so two installs with the same names in different places never mix.
- **Schema changes are additive.** A missing table is created; new columns are added to an existing table and its
  rule; nothing is deleted or rebuilt, and an existing rule keeps its endpoint and transformation.
- **Upload** batches are sized from their measured size (under the 1 MB limit, measured after compression when
  compressing). Throttling and server errors are retried as the service asks; any other refusal stops with the
  service's own message. The rows accepted are counted against the rows given.
- One collection time is stamped per run, identical across every batch.

### 4b. Excel without a module

Risk Analysis writes its .xlsx with SecurityInsight's own writer: the Open XML parts zipped with .NET, one sheet per
call added to the workbook on disk (a same-named sheet is replaced), with a de-duplicated shared-string table. The
per-cell work runs in a small helper compiled at run start; if compilation is blocked, a PowerShell copy writes the
same bytes, only slower. No Excel module is needed on a VM or in the container, and a 120,000-row × 30-column
export takes about 20 seconds on Windows PowerShell 5.1.

### 4b-1. A Risk Analysis result that did not reach Log Analytics is a failed run

The web app, the data sync and the connectors read a Risk Analysis run from its own result table in Log Analytics
(Summary or Detailed). When that table did not receive the run's rows in full -- whatever the cause: the run ran out of
memory while preparing the rows, a post failed part way, the rule could not be updated -- the run is a **failed** run:

- The workbook and the JSON file are written first and stay on disk; the mail and the guards run as usual.
- Run health records `error` with the reason (not `success-partial`), and the engine then ends with an error, so the job
  ends failed.
- The pipeline reads a step's exit, never run health: a failed Risk Analysis step means the steps that need its result
  (the vulnerability connectors, the data sync, the close-loop mail) do not start on it, and Deliver does not start
  after a Correlate that did not succeed.
- When a run is started on its own instead: the data sync holds a collection whose run ended `error` (only a
  `success-partial` run is loaded, marked partial), and the close-loop closes nothing unless the newest snapshot is at
  most 26 hours old and every run covering it ended `success`. The same snapshot read twice never counts as a second
  run in which a finding was absent.
- The last lines of the log say it: the result was not delivered, the web app keeps showing the earlier run, nothing
  downstream was given a partial result.

A post that was refused (key columns empty on every row, or a rule that does not declare a column) ends the same way.
What stays `success-partial`: a report or bucket that could not be read, new columns Azure was not storing yet, a
profile under the run whose own run was partial -- the rows of the run are in the table in those cases.

A failed upload of the workbook to storage is reported as a warning and does not fail the run: the blob is a copy for
people; the data sync and the web app read Log Analytics and the database, never that blob.

### 4b-2. Delivery never needs the whole result in memory several times

A Detailed result of a large install (tens of thousands of rows × ~320 columns) is one large set of objects. Delivery
holds it ONCE: nothing of a part outlives its post. Summary and Detailed run through the same delivery.

- **The trend row and the findings read the result's own rows** (`$global:final`), recorded as "published" only once
  every part was posted and counted -- not a kept copy of the posted parts. A posted row differs from its source only by
  the host columns (Computer, ComputerFqdn, UserLoggedOn), legal column names, the empty columns of its part and values
  its column's type converted (rounded into a whole-number column, text moved to `_Text`, a number to `_Number`). The trend
  rolls up severity, tier, asset and score and reads text as the Log Analytics job path does; the findings read the
  finding's key, asset, title, severity, scores and its text fields. None of those is changed by the preparation, so the
  values they read are the posted values -- except a score the table rounds, which they now see exact.

- **Log Analytics in parts** (`RA-Delivery.ps1`). The rows are prepared and posted part by part: each part is copied
  (the type alignment rounds in place, and the mail and the AI summary must not see a rounded value), stamped, given the
  host columns, legal names, every column of the part, every value in its column's type -- and posted before the next part
  is built. A part is sized by measured bytes, never a row count: the first from the rows' own JSON size, every later one
  from the bytes the ingest client reports it posted per row; each part is still split into posts under the 1 MB limit.
  The rows posted are counted against the rows given, and a shortfall fails the run. The key columns are checked on the
  whole result before the first part goes out (as before) and on every prepared part; a key column the preparation left
  empty on every row fails the run after the posts.
- **The JSON file** is written row by row, never as one string.
- **The 'Risk factors' sheet**: adding a sheet to the workbook reads the workbook's existing shared-string table as a
  stream (once to count it, once to copy it), never whole.
- **The storage upload** goes from the file one 4 MB block at a time, and the backup of the previous workbook is copied
  range by range (read against its ETag), never downloaded whole. The block is a transfer buffer, not a limit.
- What only built the result (the export pool, the last report's query result and working sets) is let go before the
  workbook is written.

The rows and columns delivered are the same as before. What only a real large run shows is the peak memory of a run of
that size; the offline tests show that delivery memory does not grow with the number of parts.

### 4c. Pro configuration in SQL — templates and your overrides

In Pro, everything that is a file in Community lives in the Pro database. The content we develop — rules, Risk
Analysis reports, the risk index, the service model, asset tagging — is held as **templates** (our version of each
item) plus **your overrides** per item: inherit (use the template), override (your version), or disable. Exclusions,
weights, the CMDB ownership map and every setting (names included) are your own configuration, not templates. A new
template version never touches your overrides or your configuration; an override whose template changed underneath it
is flagged. At run start the two are merged per item and handed to the engines
in the same form they read from files, so the engines run the same code in both editions. Anything invalid stops
the run before it starts, with one run-health record. **Exemptions** (one finding, one issue everywhere, or one
asset) have a reason and an end date, and are ended, never deleted -- see *Exemptions* below for how they are
requested, approved and reviewed. `setup\Import-SIProSettings.ps1` brings an existing installation's files in,
storing only what differs from the templates.

### 4d. Exemptions (Pro) -- requested, approved, reviewed every month

An exemption says "we accept this finding for now, and here is why". It is a decision someone is accountable for,
so it follows one flow:

1. **Security owners at two levels.** On *Configuration > Security owners* an Admin names, by sign-in name / e-mail:
   **Security Domain Owners** (level 1) for a security domain -- Endpoint, Identity, Azure, PublicIP and any other
   domain in your data -- and **Security Category Owners** (level 2) for one category inside a domain: the finding's
   *Category* exactly as the Risk Analysis reports carry it (the column between *SecurityDomain* and *Subcategory*,
   e.g. Identity / Authentication, Identity / Sign-in Behaviour, Endpoint / Vulnerabilities). Owners at both levels
   **decide** the exemption requests of their scope and **receive the monthly review** of it. The page shows a
   two-level tree (each domain, then the categories the latest collection carries plus any typed in), the people on
   each node, who in effect decides it, and flags every node nobody owns; it sorts and filters like every small table.
   People named for "every domain" own all domains; exemptions made before domains existed belong to "every domain".
   The older per-domain **approver** role still decides requests (existing set-ups keep working), but owners do not
   need it.
2. **Request.** Anyone with access (Viewer or Admin) selects findings -- ticked rows, or every row matching the
   current filter, in Findings or any collection view of findings -- and requests ONE exemption for all of them:
   the same reason, period and (optionally) approver. A selection becomes one request per security domain -- and per
   category where that category has its own owners -- so each part is decided by its own owners. **Who is asked is the
   most specific owner:** the category's owners when the category has any, else the domain's owners (else, for an
   existing set-up, the domain's approvers). The request page shows, per request, exactly who is asked and who else
   may decide; the request mail goes to the people asked, with one link to decide. Each finding's category comes from
   its Risk Analysis row; a finding without one is decided at domain level.
3. **Period.** A dropdown: 3 months, 6 months, 1 year or a custom end date, pre-selected from the default period
   setting (6 months). An exemption without an end date is possible only when the setting allows it (off by default);
   the end date must be after today and at most about three years ahead.
4. **Approve or reject.** The request's owners -- its category's owners, or its domain's owners; a Domain Owner may
   always decide a request in their domain too, and so may the domain's approvers -- or an Admin approve or reject,
   with a comment (required to reject). **One approval is enough.** Anyone else is refused (the page answers *403*,
   names who the request is asked of, and the refusal is in the audit trail). Approving writes the exemptions at
   once, with the approver's name and each finding's category -- the approval IS the review; there is no separate
   *Review & commit* step. The requester gets the decision by mail. **Only an approved exemption applies**: Risk
   Analysis and the views read the approved exemptions only, from the next run. Someone who may decide a request may
   approve their own in the same step. The Admin staging path (*Review & commit*) still works and is recorded as
   approved by the Admin who commits it; an exemption staged without an end date gets the default period.
5. **Monthly review.** On the review day (the 1st by default) **every owner gets ONE mail** for everything they own:
   a Category Owner the exemptions of their category, a Domain Owner those of the whole domain, someone owning several
   domains / categories one combined mail -- never one per node, and each exemption listed once. It shows exemptions
   ending soon, expired, and all active (each with its domain / category), with one link to the *Review* page (narrowed
   to their domain / category when they own just one). There they **extend** (a new period from today), **keep**
   (unchanged, but reviewed) or **end** each exemption, one at a time or many at once -- each exemption by the owners of
   its category or domain (or an Admin). Owners are also warned once before an exemption ends (30 days by default),
   again in one mail per person. An active exemption nobody has reviewed for 45 days (setting) is flagged **review
   overdue** on the Exemptions page and on *Operations > Deviations*; it still applies.
6. **States.** A request is *requested*, *approved* or *rejected*; an exemption is *active*, *expired* (its end
   date passed) or *ended* (an owner or Admin ended it). Every step -- request, decision, extend, keep, end, and every
   owner / approver change -- is in the change history with who and when.

**Mail.** The web app never talks to a mail server: it queues the request and decision mails in the Pro database,
and the close-loop mail job sends them -- together with the expiry warnings and the monthly review -- through the
same SMTP settings as the Risk Analysis mail. Right after it queues a mail, the web app starts that job once so the
mail goes within minutes; if it cannot, the mail goes with the job's daily run. Mails can be switched off with one
setting; the flow works the same without them.

**Settings** (Configuration > Settings > E-mail + links, the web app's own): default period (6 months), allow exemptions without an
end date (off), review overdue after (45 days), exemption mails (on), monthly review day (1), expiry warning
(30 days before).

**How the owners are stored.** Domain-level people stay in the domain roster table (`cfg.DomainRole`, roles
*owner* / *approver*); Category Owners live in their own table (`cfg.CategoryRole`: domain + category + person),
because the domain roster's key cannot take a category without being rebuilt and the schema only ever adds. A
request carries the category whose owners decide it (empty = the domain decides); each request item and each
approved exemption carries the finding's own category, which is what scopes a category owner's review. One
resolution decides everything: *asked* = the category's owners, else the domain's owners, else the domain's
approvers; *may decide* = the category's owners + the domain's owners (and "every domain" owners) + the domain's
approvers, plus an Admin through the role framework (a Delegated user scoped to the domain too); *reviews* = the
category's owners + the domain's owners. Every add and remove is one transaction with its change-history row and an
audit event (*domainrole.member.add / remove*).

**Exempted findings stay in the data; the views decide what to show.** An exemption never removes or skips a
finding anywhere in the pipeline:

- **Risk Analysis marks, it does not drop.** Every approved exemption -- one finding, one issue on every asset, or every
  issue of one asset -- reaches the run, and Risk Analysis keeps every row and marks the ones it covers with three
  columns: `SI_ExemptionId`, `SI_ExemptedUntil` (yyyy-MM-dd, empty = no end date) and `SI_ExemptionRequestId`. Log
  Analytics receives every row, marked. An exemption is no longer turned into an exclusion: the exclusion lists are
  the customer's own "never report this" rules (a different concept, unchanged), an exemption is an accepted risk that
  stays visible to whoever asks for it. Because a marked finding is still reported, the vulnerability close-loop never
  reads an exempted vulnerability as fixed.
- **The Pro database keeps the mark.** The data sync loads every finding of a collection into `sidata.Finding` with its
  mark (`ExemptionId`, `ExemptedUntil`, `ExemptionRequestId`) -- the mark is resolved per collection: what was exempted
  when the collection was taken. An exemption approved later applies from the next run; one that ends later stays
  visible as exempted in the collections it covered.
- **One predicate, everywhere.** Whether a finding counts is one rule: it carries no mark (`ExemptionId IS NULL`). The
  web app applies it to every read of a page at once (its query layer rewrites every finding source to the counted
  rows), the PowerShell reports and mails use the same text, Log Analytics reads use `SI_ExemptionId` the same way, and
  the view `sidata.vExemptedFinding` lists the marked findings.
- **Both variants pre-computed.** Every pre-computed aggregate (the daily trend, the per-collection breakdowns, the
