  per-department totals, the per-service risk) has a "counted" twin over the unmarked findings, filled by the data sync
  for each collection right after its base; the trend rollup in Log Analytics writes counted dimensions beside the plain
  ones. A page answers either way from a pre-computed table, never by grouping finding rows per view. Measured on SQL
  Server Express, 30 daily collections of 20,000 findings (2 % exempted): the twin adds about 0.2 s (daily) and 1.6 s
  (breakdowns) per collection to the sync; a 30-day trend reads in 3-70 ms from the twin against 2.7-3.0 s for a live
  group-by over the 600,000 finding rows. (Subtracting at read time was not an option: distinct asset counts and the
  highest scores cannot be subtracted.) A collection loaded before the twins existed is read from its base table --
  it holds no exempted finding, because Risk Analysis left them out then.
- **Settings and the per-view tick.** Three settings give the default; every view has a tick that overrides it for that
  view only (in its URL, carried through its links, drill-downs and exports; never saved):

  | Setting | Default | Applies to |
  |---|---|---|
  | `SIWeb_Exempted_ShowInViews` | off: hidden | the findings browser, the collection views, the asset page, the CMDB pages. "Show exempted" shows them, each marked *Exempted until &lt;date&gt;* |
  | `SI_Exempted_CountInManagement` | off: not counted | Risk Analysis's workbook, JSON, summary and mail (Log Analytics always keeps every row); the management dashboards, KPIs, trends, closure (*Open now*), the Services view and the wall board (no tick: a kiosk). "Include exempted" recomputes the figures with them, labelled *Including exempted: simulated* |
  | `SI_Exempted_InDepartmentReports` | off: not counted | the department pages, the business owners' monthly report, the technical owners' digest and review |

  Every surface that leaves exempted findings out says so: *N exempted not counted · show*; a mail says how many it left
  out. An export follows its view, with an *Exempted* column when exempted findings are included. The close-loop's own
  history (new / closed / reopened) is per vulnerability item and is not split by exemption.
- **No exempt-everything button.** "Request exemption for all N matching" is offered only when the view's filter
  narrows the collection (a severity, domain, report, asset, column filter or search) and N is at most
  `SIWeb_Exemption_BulkMax` (500); otherwise the button is replaced by a hint saying how to narrow. The request page
  checks both again when it opens and when it is submitted, and refuses a crafted request with the reason.

### 4e. Configuration in 3.0: where each 2.2 file went

**Community: nothing moves.** A 3.0 Community install reads every 2.2 configuration file from the same folder,
under the same name, with the same "your custom file wins over the shipped one" rule. Your `*.custom.*` files and
your `LauncherConfig.custom.ps1` files are yours and are never overwritten by an update. The only behaviour changes
are listed under *What changed or went away* below.

**Pro: the files become database items, edited in the web app.** `setup\Import-SIProSettings.ps1` (run by the guided
Pro install) reads your 2.2 files and stores only what differs from the shipped defaults. It prints every item it
imports and every item it does not import, with the reason. A Pro run reads its configuration from the database
only, so **a file the importer does not carry over is not used by Pro**.

| 2.2 file (shipped default / your file) | What it controls | 3.0 Community | 3.0 Pro: stored as | 3.0 Pro: where you edit it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `RiskAnalysis_Queries_Locked.yaml` / `RiskAnalysis_Queries_Custom.yaml` | Risk Analysis reports, their severity and tier scope, report templates | same files | shipped reports = default templates; your reports = your overrides and own reports | Template conformance and Template releases (accept / keep); *Reports & outputs*: report catalog (scope, on / off), report templates, custom reports, output scope per destination (6e). |
| `riskscore.index.custom.csv` (2.2: shipped, edited in place) | the risk score index | 3.0 ships `riskscore.index.locked.csv`; an unchanged 2.2 copy is removed, an edited one is kept as your own rows, read first (2.2 form converted on load, no score changes) | default template rows + your changed / added rows | **Risk index** page |
| `riskscore_weighted.schema.custom.json` | business weighting of the risk score, and the risk-model mappers | same file | the weighting section as a document; the other sections as a configuration item | weighting: *Reports & outputs > Weights* (a grid; 6e). Other sections: shown read-only there (Risk Analysis 3.0 does not read them). |
| `<Report>.weighted.custom.json` | weighting for one report | same file | a configuration item per report | *Reports & outputs > Weights* (per report; 6e) |
| `RiskAnalysisGlobalExclusions.custom.json`, `<Report>.exclude.custom.json` | findings left out of the reports | same files | exclusion documents (global, per report) | *Reports & outputs > Exclusions* (lists; a v2.2 file can be imported); exemptions per finding on the findings pages |
| `<Report>.exclude.json` (made from the shipped `.exclude.json.sample`) | the same, under the older name | same file | **not imported yet** -- rename it to `<Report>.exclude.custom.json` before importing | -- |
| `asset-profiling-enrichment\**\*.locked.yaml` | the shipped detection and tier rules | same files | default templates | **Profiling rules** (change, turn off, reset), Tier board (move a rule to a tier, turn it off), Template conformance |
| `asset-profiling-enrichment\**\*.custom.yaml`, and the rules folder set by `SI_EnrichmentDataRoot` | your own rules and your changes to shipped rules | same files | your rule documents (turning a shipped rule off = a switch on its template) | **Profiling rules** (form or YAML); Tier board pins |
| `AssetTagging.locked.yaml` / `AssetTagging.custom.yaml` | the asset tags written to Defender | same files | default templates + your overrides and own tags | **Asset tagging** |
| `config\asset-tagging.config.json` | which automatic exclusion tags are on | same file | a configuration item | **Asset tagging** (gates and device-name patterns) |
| `asset-profiling-schema\<engine>.schema.custom.json` | your extra or changed profile columns | same files | a configuration item per engine | **Schema overlays** |
| `asset-profiling-schema\*.schema.locked.json`, `risk-analysis.schema.locked.json` | the table contracts | same files | shipped with the code, not configuration | -- |
| `privilege-tier-catalog.locked.json` / `privilege-tier-catalog.custom.json` | the tier of each directory and cloud role | same files | the catalog the classifier writes, shared with the jobs through your storage account | regenerated by the classifier; change a tier with a rule on the Tier board |
| `asset-profiling-providers\generic-cmdb\CMDB.csv` | services, owners and criticality per asset | same file | SecurityInsight's own CMDB, or a CSV / ServiceNow CMDB | **CMDB** and **Service map** pages (upload or migrate the CSV) -- see the note below |
| `config\SecurityInsight.custom.ps1` | every setting | same file | settings (solution scope) | **Settings** |
| `launcher\<engine>\LauncherConfig.custom.ps1` | per-engine settings | same files | settings (engine scope) | **Settings** (choose the engine scope) |
| the vulnerability close-loop settings (`SI_VulnSync_*`) | where fixed vulnerabilities are closed | same settings | a connector | **Connectors** |
| mail settings | who receives the reports | same settings | settings | **Configuration > Settings > E-mail + links** |

**The two decision files, and when a missing one is said.** `asset-decisions.custom.yaml` (tier overrides, exceptions,
exemptions) and `correlation-decisions.custom.yaml` (never-merge, force-merge, pin-id) are looked for in three places:
the file a person named (`SI_AssetDecisionsPath` / `SI_CorrelationDecisionsPath`; then only that file is read), the
root of the rules folder (`SI_EnrichmentDataRoot`) and `config\`. Only the NAMED file is reported when it does not
exist -- its decisions are not in force, and the run says so. The other two places simply hold a file or not: a
SecurityInsight Pro run points the rules folder at its own run folder and writes a decision file there only when the
database holds a decision, so an install with none reads none and is told nothing (one line at verbose level). No
empty file is written to make a message go away.

**The profiling and tagging editors (Pro web app, Configuration).** Three pages edit what the 2.2 YAML / JSON files
held, with the same meaning, so a change made in the web app behaves exactly as the same change in the file:

- **Profiling rules** -- every asset-profiling rule the next run applies (vendor, changed, turned off, yours), with
  its engines, purpose, category, the tiers it sets and the condition kinds it uses. A rule is edited as a **form**
  (its fields; per detection: *any* or *all* conditions, each a kind and the values it looks for, the assets it skips,
  the tier and the rest it sets) or as **YAML**; both show the same rule, and every shipped rule fits the form. Values
  keep their type (a quoted number stays text). A rule with a structure the form cannot hold opens as YAML. Turn a
  vendor rule off, reset it to the vendor's, or add your own rule. A rule moved to another tier on the tier board keeps
  that move on top of your text (so it must keep setting a tier).
- **Asset tagging** -- the tag rules written to Defender (name and what it sets -- a tier or *excluded* --, mode,
  query engine, the gate that switches it on, device-name scoping, description, queries) and the **gates**: the four
  automatic exclusions, every switch a tag names, and the device-name patterns. A tag's name part is its identity: a tag
  of yours with the vendor's name part replaces the vendor's (change only its tier, for example).
- **Schema overlays** -- per profiling engine, the profile columns you add or replace (name, type, purpose, the stage
  that writes it, a default of the column's type, description), aggregator contributors (an id and its settings) and
  the raw-payload paths to keep. The run merges it over the shipped layout as before (same name / id replaces, a new
  one adds, include paths are added).

On every page readers see everything and an Admin edits. **Check** validates with exactly the rules the run applies at
start (a stored item the run would refuse would stop the run, so the web app refuses it first) and shows the exact text
that will be stored; **Stage** puts the change on **Review & commit**, where it is written in the editor's name with a
change-history entry and refused if someone changed the same item meanwhile. Everything the forms do not show (notes,
extra keys) is kept as it was. The run materialises the items into exactly the files the engines already read --
`*.custom.yaml` beside the shipped rules, `AssetTagging.locked.yaml` + `asset-tagging.config.json`,
`<engine>.schema.custom.json` -- so no engine reads anything new. A rule that was imported from a 2.2 custom file is
changed where it is kept; it never gets a second copy.

**What changed or went away in 3.0**

- **Power BI refresh is retired.** `SendToPowerBI` and the `PowerBI_*` settings are no longer read; while a
  configuration still turns the refresh on (`SendToPowerBI` true or any `PowerBI_*` value), every VM launcher run
  says so in one line. The results are still in Log Analytics: read them with the shipped Azure Monitor workbook
  (`preview\AzureWorkbook`), a Power BI report connected to the workspace, your own queries, or the Pro web app.
- **Exclusion files are read from `risk-analysis-detection\` only.** Older README versions placed
  `<Report>.exclude.custom.json` and `RiskAnalysisGlobalExclusions.custom.json` in `config\`, where they were never
  read (in 2.2 either); moving them turns them on.
- **`asset-profiling-enrichment\identity\PrivilegeTierClassifier.json`** has not been read since 2.2.25; tenant groups
  are tiered with a group-membership rule (see *Privilege-tier catalog*).
- A few settings that did nothing, or did something else, were removed or corrected; an old config that still sets
  one is harmless. `SI_Shodan_DcrName` / `SI_Shodan_TableName` are no longer used (public IPs go to
  `SI_PublicIP_Profile_CL`); while either is set, the public-IP run says so in one line.
- The endpoint-class override file `asset-profiling-enrichment\endpoint\endpoint-tiering.json` was never used by the
  tier calculation; it is no longer read.
- **The risk index has a shipped name and a name of yours (3.0).** 2.2 shipped the index as `riskscore.index.custom.csv`;
  3.0 ships it as `riskscore.index.locked.csv`, which every update replaces, and `riskscore.index.custom.csv` is only
  ever yours (never shipped, gitignored). On the first Risk Analysis run after the update -- whichever way the update
  arrived -- a `riskscore.index.custom.csv` that is byte for byte an index SecurityInsight shipped (line endings and a
  BOM aside) is removed and the shipped index takes over; an edited one is kept as your own rows, checked before the
  shipped rows (a 2.2-form file is converted on load with exactly the scores it gave), and the run log says so once.
  Only a `git pull` install with an edited file has to step around it once: 2.2's `git pull --ff-only` stops on a
  tracked file with local changes. Exact steps: RELEASENOTES v3.0.0 *Upgrading from 2.2.x*.

**Before moving a 2.2 installation to Pro, check these** -- the importer does not carry them over yet:

- `<Report>.exclude.json` files (rename them to `<Report>.exclude.custom.json` first);
- asset-tagging rules kept anywhere other than `asset-profiling-enrichment\endpoint\AssetTagging.custom.yaml`, or
  under another file name;
- `asset-profiling-enrichment\endpoint\server-applications.json` (your own server-application tiers);
- `launcher\<engine>\launcher.override.ps1` files -- move what they set into the settings;
- `CMDB.csv` is moved for you: the guided Pro install (step *Your v2.2 CMDB in the Pro database*) and the settings
  import (`setup\Import-SIProSettings.ps1 -Apply`) import it once into SecurityInsight's own CMDB, from where the
  profilers and Risk Analysis read it (section 6c, *In Pro the runs read this CMDB*). A file with a wrong line is not
  imported: the install report lists the lines -- fix them and import it on the **CMDB** page.

### 5. Pro data backend (SQL)

SecurityInsight Pro keeps its findings in its own database as well as in Log Analytics, so its web app can browse,
filter and trend them quickly.

- **What is copied.** A daily job (after the vulnerability close-loop) copies every Risk Analysis Detailed collection
  whose run finished successfully, once per collection. Findings are stored as a few indexed columns plus the full
  row as JSON.
- **All or nothing.** A collection becomes visible only when the database holds every row Log Analytics held. A
  load that stops part way stays invisible and is redone on the next run; an incomplete run is held, not loaded.
- **Scale follows measurement.** Reads are split into parts sized from the measured data size (a part that is
  still too large is re-read in more parts); writes are chunked, with chunk size following measured time.
- **Assets (CIs).** Keyed by the identity ledger's correlation id, else the asset id — never a provisional id — with
  every identifier kept beside it.
- **Daily aggregates.** After each load the day's finding totals and the vulnerability lifecycle (opened, closed,
  reopened, open at end of day) are rebuilt; dashboards and trends read only these, and drill-down reads one
  collection's indexed findings.
- **The Summary report rows (#583).** The same job copies every Risk Analysis **Summary** collection
  (`SI_RiskAnalysis_Summary_CL`, the rows the RiskAnalysis_Summary workbook is built from) whose run is shown complete,
  once, whole, into `sidata.SummaryLoad` / `SummaryRow` / `SummaryAsset` (`engine/_shared/data-sql/SI-DataSummary.ps1`).
  Every column is a real typed column (tier, a rating rank, the scores), so the *Summary* page filters and orders on
  indexes and never parses JSON per row; each impacted asset is a row of its own (name and id, in the row's order).
  Kept apart from `sidata.Collection`: a Summary run has its own collection time. Every column is read the si_ name
  first, else the old name (the output rename). Collections past `SI_Pro_DataRetentionDays` are removed. The step never
  fails the data sync: a failed collection is said and loaded on the next run; a database without the tables is told
  once (the updater adds them).
- **Data for the collection views.** After each load, the job also fills in, for every collection, the columns the
  web app's collection views show (weighted risk score, risk rating, MITRE tactics and techniques, compliance tags,
  CVSS, known exploit) from the stored row, and pre-computes per collection how many findings, CIs and how much risk
  sit under each tactic, tag, rating, CVSS band and score. Collections loaded before an update get this once, on the
  next run. If the database has not been extended yet, the job says to run `setup\Initialize-SIDataSql.ps1` again and
  keeps loading as before.
- **Services per collection (#255) -- and THE service-membership resolver.** After the views' data, the job decides
  which CMDB service(s) each asset of the collection belongs to and pre-computes the risk per service
  (`sidata.ServiceRisk`) and per service and asset (`sidata.ServiceAsset`); the membership itself is kept in
  `sidata.ServiceMember`. "Which service(s) does an asset belong to" is answered in ONE place, so any CMDB can plug in:
  - **The contract.** `Get-SIDataServiceSources` (`engine/_shared/data-sql/SI-DataSql.ps1`) returns an ordered list of
    membership sources. Each source is a name (1-32 of letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`; stamped on every membership it
    contributes) and ONE read-only `SELECT` (no `;`, no write or DDL verb, `@CollectionId` its only parameter) that
    returns `AssetKey` (the `sidata` CI key), `ServiceKey` (the service's stable id, e.g. its CMDB number) and
    `ServiceName` (may be NULL) for that collection; it may read `sidata.*` and `cfg.*`. A source that breaks the
    contract is refused when it is registered and again when the statement is built.
  - **Many-to-many.** An asset may belong to several services (one row per service). The same (service, asset) from
    two sources is kept once, stamped with the earlier source. Only assets with findings in the collection count.
    Assets with no membership form the no-service row (`ServiceKey` = empty).
  - **Today's source** (`risk-analysis`): the CMDB service each Risk Analysis row carries -- `cmdbId`, else `cmdbName`
    -- which the asset profiling's Reconcile stage stamps from the CMDB provider's service records (a profile rule's
    `set.cmdbId`, or an identity match to a CMDB CI). The data job copies them into `sidata.Finding.CmdbId / CmdbName`
    in the same ranges as the views' columns.
  - **Plugging in a CMDB** (an SI-homed CMDB, an external CSV in the CMDB.csv format, ServiceNow): call
    `Register-SIDataServiceSource -Name <n> -Sql <select>` before the sync derives; `-Replace` makes the registered
    sources the whole list (an authoritative CMDB). A membership change applies to a collection the next time it is
    derived: set its `sidata.Collection.ServicesDerivedAt` to NULL and the next sync recomputes it (otherwise a
    collection keeps the membership it was derived with).
  - **The CMDB in the Pro database** (section 6c) is plugged in this way: when it is configured -- an external CMDB is
    chosen, or SecurityInsight's own CMDB holds a service -- the job makes it the ONLY source (`cmdb-si`, `cmdb-csv`
    or `cmdb-servicenow`, reading the authoritative CMDB's current memberships); otherwise `risk-analysis` stays the
    source. Every change to the CMDB (a link, an import, a source switch) marks the newest collection to be derived
    again; older collections keep the services they had.
  If the database does not have the service tables yet, the job says once to run `setup\Initialize-SIDataSql.ps1`
  again and derives everything else as before.
- **Retention.** Collections older than the retention setting (default 90 days) are removed in batches. The
  vulnerability state, the identity ledger and the settings are never purged.
- **The newest complete collection and the one before it.** Each Risk Analysis run stores around a million finding
  rows, so the finding rows of older collections are not kept for 90 days. Per kind (Risk Analysis and Risk Analysis
  Summary) the data sync keeps the newest COMPLETE collection -- what every view shows -- and the complete one before it,
  which the comparison between runs reads; also kept are a collection whose rows a kept collection's not-complete report
  shows (its last complete result), and every collection still loading that is newer than the newest complete one (a run
  in progress; one run at a time per install). The finding rows, recommendations and prepared issue rows of every older
  collection are removed, and so are those of a collection a stopped or failed run left loading, once a newer one of the
  same kind is complete -- with what that run staged. While no collection of a kind is complete, nothing of it is
  removed. The collection itself stays, marked, with its aggregates: the day totals behind the trends, the department
  and service totals and the per-report results keep their history until the 90 days above; a marked collection is no
  longer listed, never loaded again and never recomputed from no rows. Removing an old collection never changes the
  current one, its findings' lifecycle or the close-loop. The database itself refuses to mark the newest complete
  collection (and a run still loading after it); every removal is in batches on the tables' clustered keys and removes
  rows only of a marked collection, so a removal that stopped part way is finished by the next run. One line in the run
  log names what was kept and the rows removed per table, and the audit trail records each removal. A failure is said and
  tried again on the next run; it never fails the data sync.
- **How full the database is.** Every data sync reads how much of the database's maximum size its data uses (the same
  reading the daily heartbeat carries). Above 70 % the run says so in its log and on its run record, in plain words, so
  the database never fills up unnoticed -- when it is full, nothing new can be stored.
- **Setup.** `setup\Initialize-SIDataSql.ps1` creates the schema (additive); the job's identity needs read and
  write on the database.

### 5a. Correlation evidence -- why SecurityInsight says these records are ONE asset

One CI per real asset, across Entra, Active Directory, Defender, Azure, the Exposure Graph and a CMDB, is what
SecurityInsight adds over a single-source discovery. It is shown with its evidence, so it can be checked.

- **Recorded, never re-decided.** The correlation engine already publishes, per identifier, whether it is the key that
  joined two records and how the group was joined (a durable id = deterministic, an Exposure Graph node = graph-inferred).
  The data sync carries that verdict into the Pro database with every load; nothing here joins or splits anything, and
  nothing is read from or written to a source system -- only what the profiles and the correlation map already published.
- **Evidence per CI** (`sidata.AssetEvidence`): one row per source record and key -- the source system that reported it
  (the record's own `EntityIds` source, else the system that issues that key type), the rule that put the record into the
  CI and its confidence: a durable id two records share = **exact**; a shared Exposure Graph node = **strong**; a key on a
  record that joined by another key inherits that record's confidence; a lone record is exact; a CI known only from a
  finding (no source record matched) is **weak**. Defender's and the Exposure Graph's own last-seen times travel with
  their keys. The CMDB / ServiceNow reconcile verdict on the record is evidence too (pinned exact, by an id or a rule
  strong, by name weak), but is never a discovery source and never part of the CI's confidence.
- **Id history** (`sidata.AssetIdHistory`), found by the database from what moved between two loads, on durable keys only:
  **alias** (a record's SI id moved while its durable id stayed -- the MGMT1 shape), **rekey** (the CI's key changed),
  **merge** (a CI's durable ids now belong to another CI that already existed). The identifier ledger's older rows count
  too, so history from before the evidence existed shows from the first load.
- **Conflicts shown, not hidden** (`sidata.AssetConflict`): name (first DNS label; an id standing in for a name is no
  name), OS, domain and CMDB CI where the CI's records disagree; and **possible duplicates** -- two endpoint / VM CIs with
  the same host name and no shared durable id -- named on both, never merged.
- **The correlation-quality report** reads `sidata.AssetCorrelation`, pre-computed per collection and CI: records, source
  systems, weakest confidence, how they were joined, conflicts, id changes, possible duplicate, CMDB state. Matched /
  SecurityInsight-only come from the CMDB matches on the profiles; **CMDB-only is not measured** (SecurityInsight does not
  read the CMDB's own CI list) and is shown as such, never as 0.
- **Never fails a load.** A database without the tables is told once; an evidence write that fails is said loudly and the
  collection still loads -- its `CorrelatedAt` stays empty and the pages say so.
- **Pages.** The asset page's Evidence section (every source record in plain words: "Seen by Defender as device
  fd73f1d4… (on the same source record)"), the id history and the disagreements; Assets & services > Correlation quality
  (sources per asset 1 / 2 / 3+, single-source per source, weak, conflicts, id changes, possible duplicates, CMDB match
  rate, a trend over runs, every figure a drill-down into the shared grid with Excel / CSV export).
- **Reading the report (#315).** Four groups, each ONE plain question with what is good and bad, and "What to do" where something
  can be done. A figure links to `#assets`: the list sits straight under the figures (above the trend), headed with what the
  assets ARE ("4 assets seen only by the Exposure Graph"), the clicked box highlighted, Clear filter / Back to the overview,
  "None" when empty. **Confidence colours** come from one mapping (`CorrelationGroups` / `Tone`) used by the boxes, the grid's
  Confidence chip and the CI evidence badges: green High confidence (exact, 3+ systems, in the CMDB), teal Good (strong, 2
  systems), amber Check (weak, 1 system, single-source, possible duplicates, not in the CMDB), red Act (conflict), blue Info
  (id change / merge, CMDB copy too old); a zero is muted grey. Colour is never the only signal: every box carries the word.

### 5b. Closing vulnerabilities -- absence is not remediation

A vulnerability is closed as fixed only when it has been missing for several complete runs in a row (`SI_VulnSync_CloseAfterRuns`, default 2), each on an asset that was actually seen in that run with its own vulnerability data. An asset missing from a run is unknown: its findings stay open, and the run says "asset not seen this run, held". Partial runs, halted runs and the same data read twice count nothing. A finding that is seen again starts its count over; a closed one that returns is reopened. An asset that is positively retired or excluded closes with that reason. The plan and the run log state why each item closed or was held. One consequence: when a device's very last vulnerability is fixed, nothing is left to show the device was seen, so that finding stays open until a later run proves it.

### 6. Pro web app

The Pro web app runs in the customer's own container environment and signs users in with Entra ID. Who may do what
is the role framework in 6a (Reader, Delegated, Admin, SuperAdmin -- the same four roles as PIM Manager -- plus a
kiosk Wallboard sign-in).

- **Findings** replaces the Excel file: pick a collection, filter and pivot on the server, most important first,
  drill down to one finding, export CSV. Dashboards, trends and the wall board read only the daily aggregates; the
  findings pages read one collection's indexed rows.
- **Summary** (*Risks > Summary*, `/Summary`, #583) -- the RiskAnalysis_Summary workbook in the browser, management
  friendly: one row per recommendation x tier x severity x risk factors x CMDB group, exactly the workbook's rows. One
  section per tier, Tier 0 first (rows without a tier last, "No tier"); each section opens with a headline -- how many
  Critical and High recommendations it holds and on how many assets, of how many in the tier -- and lists the most
  critical risk first (rating Critical, High, Moderate, Low, then the highest risk score). A row shows the
  recommendation with its domain / category / subcategory, the severity, the rating as a coloured badge, the risk and
  weighted scores, the risk factors in plain words ("Consequence: high machine risk, internet exposed · Likelihood:
  exploit available, RCE"), the CMDB group, the impacted asset count and the first five impacted assets, each a link to
  its CI page (an asset not matched to a CI links to the CI list searched for its name); "+ N more" opens the row with
  every asset and every column. Filters on tier, rating, severity, domain, category, subcategory, CMDB group and
  report, a search over recommendations, ids, CMDB groups and asset names / ids; without a tier filter each tier shows
  its first rows (10 to 500) with "Show all N of Tier X", with one it pages. *Export to Excel* is the workbook's sheet:
  its 33 columns in its order (SecurityDomain ... ComplianceTags), every row the filters keep, in the page's order. It
  reads the newest complete Risk Analysis **Summary** collection, which the data sync copies (section 5); an account
  limited to departments does not see it (the rows span every department). The former Risks item -- one row per
  finding key x tier x severity x CMDB group, with the action bar -- is the tab *Assets & services > Assets (CIs) >
  Findings per finding key* (`/Cis/Summary`).
- **Collection views.** Fifteen views of one collection at a time (the newest by default; the picker opens any
  older one), spread over the *Risks*, *Assets & services*, *Security recommendations* and *Changes & trends*
  menus, for Admins and Viewers:
  1. **Raw rows** -- every row, as the Risk Analysis workbook has them.
  2. **Correlated CIs** -- one row per CI, with how many linked objects the correlation joined into it (one server
     seen in Defender XDR, as an Azure VM and in Active Directory is one CI with three) and which systems see it.
  3. **CI view** -- everything known about one CI: what it is, its linked objects and identifiers, what each source
     system reports, its history across collections, its items in the vulnerability close-loop, its Defender for
     Cloud recommendations and its findings.
  4. **Vulnerabilities** -- one row per CVE, most critical first, with CVSS, known exploit, the assets and tiers it
     hits and the close-loop items open for it.
  5. **Risk score** -- how the scores spread, and every CI's total, highest and average score.
  6. **Weighted risk score** -- three tabs. **By service** (the default): the CMDB business services of the
     collection, the ones your CMDB rates most critical first (Critical / High / Medium / Low, or 1-5), then the most
     weighted risk; per service its criticality (a coloured chip; "not set" when the CMDB has none), assets, findings,
     risk total, weighted total, highest weighted finding and top asset. Sort by weighted risk alone instead, or turn
     the dimension around (asset -> the services it is in, its most critical service first). A service expands in place
     to its assets and opens them; an asset opens its findings. The assets no CMDB service claims are a group of their
     own, linked to the correlation page's "not in the CMDB". The criticality is the CMDB's own (the authoritative
     source's services, looked up by service number and by a migrated service's original id); without a CMDB the page
     says to import one and orders by weighted risk. **Pivot**: drag fields (service, service criticality, service
     owner, department, asset kind, asset, tier, domain, report, severity, CVE / issue) to Rows, Columns or Filters and
     measures (findings, assets, risk total, weighted total, highest, average) to Values -- or use the buttons on each
     field, which work from the keyboard. The table is answered in SQL from that fixed list only (no free SQL; filter
     values travel as parameters), with row, column and grand totals; sort on any heading, export to Excel or CSV, and
     save it as a named view (yours; an Admin can share one with every reader) with its own link. A finding on an asset
     in two services counts under each. **Score distribution**: how the weighted scores spread, and every CI's weighted
     total, highest and average. An account limited to departments sees its own CIs on the first tab and its own
     findings in the pivot.
  7. **Risk rating** -- findings grouped Critical / High / Moderate / Low (the customer's thresholds, shipped 50 / 30 / 15; set on Admin > Settings > Risk rating, #696).
  8. **MITRE ATT&CK** -- findings by tactic and technique. 9. **Compliance** -- findings by compliance tag.
  10. **CVSS** -- findings by CVSS band.
  11. **Excluded / exempted** -- the exemptions in force when the collection was taken (and those that were not),
      and the exclusion rules. Excluded findings are left out before a collection is written, so the view shows
      the rules, not hidden rows; Admins follow the link to *Operations > Deviations* for who and why.
  12. **Lifecycle** -- findings added and closed since the collection before, and what the close-loop opened,
      closed and reopened until the next collection.
  13. **What changed** -- two collections side by side: findings and CIs new, gone or changed.
  14. **Connector changes** -- every connector run and every item created, updated or closed until the next
      collection.
  15. **Services** -- the CMDB business services of the collection, the one carrying the most weighted risk first:
      per service its weighted risk in total and per asset, its assets, its findings by severity (critical / very
      high, high, medium incl. medium-high, low) and by tier, and its highest-risk asset. A "(no service)" row holds
      every asset no service claims, so nothing hides. A service opens its assets (highest weighted risk first), an
      asset opens the CI view with its findings. An asset may belong to several services; it is then counted under
      each, so the services' totals add up to more than the collection's -- the *Also in another service* column
      and the drill-down's *Services it is in* say where. The view reads the per-collection service tables the data
      job pre-computes (never the finding rows), and its cache key carries when they were computed, so a re-derived
      membership is never served stale.

  Every view has the same grid: sort on any column, a filter per column (several values at once), a search over
  every text column, rows selected to show only them or to export them, paging on the server, and *Export to
  Excel* / CSV of the whole filtered view. The whole state is in the address, so a link opens the same view.
  The views read the Pro database only -- never Log Analytics -- through fixed, read-only, parameterised
  statements with a time limit, use the counts pre-computed by the data job, and keep answers in memory per
  collection (a complete collection never changes; close-loop and connector data are kept for minutes).
- **Choose the columns, export all of them (the CI pages, #588).** *All CIs* and *At risk* carry the same **Columns**
  chooser: tick the columns to show, in the order they are listed; *Save for me* keeps them as your own, an Admin can
  save them as the tenant default; reset goes back to the tenant default, then the standard columns. Each page keeps
  its own layout (All CIs `cis`, At risk `collection-assets`, in `cfg.ColumnLayout`). *Export to Excel* writes the
  columns you chose. **Export all columns** writes, for the same rows (the page's filter, its search, the selected
  rows; at most 50,000):
  1. **CIs (all fields)** -- one row per CI: on At risk first every column of the view, shown or not; then EVERY field
     of the CI's own document (`si_ci_id`, `si_asset_name`, then the rest by name) -- whatever columns the page shows.
     A list or an object is written as compact JSON text.
  2. **Full details** -- every property each source reported about the CI, when full details are collected
     (`SI_AssetProperties = full`): one row per CI, source, source record and item (the newest copy), with the CI's key
     and name, the source, the record, the item and when it was collected, then one column per property named
     `source.property` (`mde.osBuild`, `arm.location`), sorted by name. An object at the top is opened one level
     (`arm.properties.provisioningState`); anything deeper, and every list, is compact JSON text. When full details are
     off, not collected yet or not in the database, the sheet says which in one row. More than Excel's 16,384 columns or
     1,048,576 rows: the rest is left out and the Export sheet says how much.
  3. **Export** -- the page, the filters, the rows per sheet and anything left out (as every export).
  Numbers are numbers and times are dates, so Excel shows them in your own regional format. The download is recorded in
  the audit trail (`data.export.download`). **How a CI finds its full details:** they are stored per collection CI key --
  the correlation's id for the CI, which is the CI's id, or for a record the correlation did not join, the source's own
  id (an MDE device id, an Exposure Graph node id, `az:` + an Azure resource id). So All CIs reads a CI's details under
  its id, the ids of its linked objects and its records (`sidata.CiLink`, `sidata.CiRecord`); At risk reads them under
  the row's own key. Read in batches of 500 CIs, twice per sheet (the columns first, then the rows), so a large export
  never holds every document in memory.
- **Tier board** shows every asset by tier, who decided the tier and why -- as tiles over ONE table, with a
  drawer per row. Nothing is dragged.
  - **Tiles.** One tile per tier (Tier 0-3, and *No tier* for the assets nothing gave a tier) with its count. Inside
    a tile, chips count who decided the tier (an SI rule, your tag, a manual override, the default, the CMDB) and
    the kind of asset (devices, identities, cloud resources, public IPs). A tile and a chip are links that toggle a
    filter of the table below -- several can be on at once, and the address carries them, so a filtered board can
    be linked or bookmarked and is remembered like any view's sort and filters. Assets with nothing recorded about
    who decided are counted as *not recorded*, never as a chip. The counts are two grouped reads over narrow, indexed
    columns of the CI table (never a CI's document), read once until new data is stored.
  - **The table** is the CI grid itself (the same code as the CIs page, under its own view): search, the view bar,
    the column chooser with every column a CI carries, each person's own layout, and the all-rows and all-columns
    exports. It opens with the name, the CI id, class, asset type, tier, who decided it, the tier explanation, owner,
    department, environment, risk score, open findings and last seen.
  - **The drawer.** Clicking a row opens its details beside the table without a page load: the tier in one
    sentence, and every claim on the tier -- what matched, which rule or source made it, and whether it decided,
    the deciding claim first -- read for that one CI by its key. Someone who may change sees two forms there,
    *Pin to a tier* and *Exclude the asset*, and on each claim that a rule made its own buttons: *Turn off*, *Move to
    tier* and -- on a rule that is moved -- *Put back*. The buttons name the rule by the key the claim carries, so no
    rule key is typed or picked. A claim no rule made has no button and says why in a word (*set by your tag*, *manual
    pin*, *rule pack*); a claim of a CI that was last built before claims carried their rule's key says *known after
    the next run*. Each one stages a change: the button stays where it is, the answer is a short message, and the row,
    the tile, the drawer and the claim say *staged* until the change is committed on *Review & commit* (or discarded
    there). The role and scope check, the audit entry and what a commit writes are those of every staged change.
  - **Without script** the board still works: tiles and chips are plain links, the table is the normal grid, and
    each row has a *Details* link that shows the same content on the page (`/Tiers?ci=<CI id>#panel`), where the
    forms post and return with the same message.
  - Links from other pages keep working: an *Unclassified* count opens the board filtered to *No tier*, and an
    asset opens its details (by its asset key, which is mostly the CI id; otherwise the CI is found through its
    linked objects). An asset that no CI stands for yet -- for example a subscription that only an Unclassified
    finding names -- is not a row of the table, but its link still opens what is known about it, with the same
    *Pin to a tier* form.
  - There are no lanes, no cards and no lines ("wires") between assets and sources: the asset-map view borrowed
    from PIM was removed (#314), and the lanes with drag-and-drop were replaced by the tiles and the drawer.
- **Vulnerabilities over time** and **Trends** come from the close-loop's events and the daily aggregates.
- **Trend cards.** Trends split by asset tier, severity, security domain or nothing shows one card per
  group instead of a multi-line chart: the newest day's value large, its change against the day before and against
  7 days earlier (▲ / ▼, the number and the percentage; fewer findings or a lower score is green, more is red, no
  change is grey), and a small line of the period drawn on the card's **own** scale, so a tier with 45 findings is
  as readable as one with 8,205. Point at or tab to the line to read a day and its value (arrow keys step through the
  days); click a card to open that group's findings. The cards use the Tier board's tier colours and sit two per row
  on a phone, five in a row on a desktop. A report split keeps the line chart, since it can hold dozens of reports.
  One component draws them (`Pages/Shared/_TrendCards.cshtml` over `TrendCardMath`, the hover in
  `wwwroot/js/app/sparkline.js`: inline SVG, no chart library).
- **Risk score measures.** A risk score belongs to one finding. Wherever the app summarises scores -- Trends, Risk
  score, Domains, Top risks, the wall board, the chat -- it shows the **average risk score per finding** (how serious
  a typical finding is), the **highest risk score** (the single worst finding) and how many findings are **Very High
  or High**. Adding every finding's score together is not shown: that total grows with the number of findings and
  cannot tell a better day from a worse one. Risk scores are shown as whole numbers.
- **Severity order.** Very High, High, Medium-High, Medium, Low, Informational -- in every list, filter, chart,
  view and export, never alphabetical. Clicking a Severity column sorts most severe first, again for least severe
  first.
- **Numbers in your regional format.** Counts and scores follow the browser's language and region: 12.205 and 2.293
  in Denmark, 12,205 and 2,293 in the USA (Danish, English, German, Swedish and Norwegian formats; US English
  otherwise). Dates stay in ISO form. CSV exports stay machine-readable (no thousands separator, "." decimal) and
  Excel exports hold real numbers.
- **Times in your own time zone.** Every time on a page -- the collection picker, grid columns, histories, audit
  rows, job runs, tooltips, the wall board -- is shown in the browser's time zone (daylight saving included) as
  `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm`, never UTC. Times are stored in UTC; the server writes each one as
  `<time datetime="...Z">` (or marks an element whose text it built, such as a drop-down option or a tooltip,
  `data-utc`), and one browser script (`local-time.js`) shows it in the viewer's zone -- also for rows a page
  adds later. Audit and evidence views add a small zone label (CEST) with the UTC value in the tooltip. The
  audit trail's from / to days are read in the viewer's zone. Without script a page shows the UTC time, marked
  UTC. Exports, mails and generated reports keep their own formats.
- **Tier-0 exposure** lists every Tier-0 asset with findings, with its rank among all the estate's assets and
  whether it is among the 100 riskiest.
- **Jobs** (run, enable/disable, logs) and **Connector status** use the app's managed identity.
- **Nothing is written directly.** Tier changes, documents and settings are staged and written on
  *Review & commit*, each in one transaction with an audit row; nothing is deleted (an exemption is ended).
  Exemptions follow their own flow -- request, then an approver's decision, which writes them (section 4d).
- **Links.** Mails link to the page; optional magic links (off by default) are signed, short-lived, single use
  and open one page read-only.
- **Access.** Two supported ways to reach it: from the internet behind Entra sign-in (the guided install's default;
  add Conditional Access) or from your network only (internal ingress; `Deploy-SIManagement.ps1`'s own default). See
  *Architecture and security*, A3.
- The same read layer serves the MCP tools for chat: `findings_query`, `trend_analytics`, `vuln_lifecycle` and
  `filter_values`.

#### The menu: one navigation model (#310)

The menu has ONE source: `pro-management/src/SI.Management.Web/Navigation/NavModel.cs`. `NavModel.Items` is the list of
groups and items -- *Overview*, *Assets & services*, *Security recommendations*, *Remediations*, *Changes & trends*,
*Operations*, *Configuration*, *Help* -- each item `{Section, Page, Label, Need, Tabs}` (the Razor page, the label, who sees it); the
layout renders it, filtered per role (`NavAccess.Shown`). A text that names a place in the menu never spells the path:
a page writes `<nav-ref page="/Admin/Departments/Index" />` (rendered as *Configuration > Departments (setup)*, a link
for someone who sees that item, plain text otherwise; `then="..."` adds a tab on that page), and a service message
uses `NavModel.PathOf("/Admin/Departments/Index")`. Renaming or moving an item therefore changes every text with it.
Text outside the web app (engine log lines, setup, the guard / audit / settings catalogs) writes the path by hand, and a
test checks each one against the model. Only pages that stand on their own are in the menu: a DETAIL page (one CI, one
finding, one department, one task) is reached by clicking it; `/Collection/Asset` opened without a CI goes to
*Correlated assets (CIs)*.

**Tabs instead of near-duplicate items (#388).** Pages that showed the same data under different names are ONE menu
item with tabs: `NavItem.Tabs` lists them (`NavTab {Page, Label, Need}`), the item opens the first, and the layout draws
the tab strip (`nav.tabs.page-tabs[data-nav-tabs]`) on every page of it, filtered per role, the page's own tab marked
`aria-current="page"`, and the menu marks the item. Each tab keeps its own page and URL, so an old link or bookmark
still opens it, now under its item. `<nav-ref>` / `PathOf` name a tab other than the first as *Item > Tab*
(*Changes & trends > Vulnerabilities over time > Per collection*). A retired page answers with a redirect to the page
and view that replaced it. The menu since 2026-10-19 (#636):

| Group | Item | Tabs (former menu items) |
|---|---|---|
| Overview | Executive overview | Topics (the Overview landing page: headline tiles + topic buttons) · Risk trend (was *Risk score*) · Domains · Tier-0 exposure |
| Overview | Executive report | Key figures (the blocks, top to bottom; Export PDF) · Risk Analysis (was *Executive reports > Risk Analysis*) · Management summary |
| Overview | Top risks | Top 50 risky assets · Top 10 asset drilldown (the live *Riskiest assets now* redirects to Top 50 risky assets) |
| Overview | Wall board · Ask about your estate | -- |
| Assets & services | Assets (CIs) | All CIs · At risk (with findings) · Findings per CI · Findings per finding key · Records per source · Not onboarded in Defender (#858) · Manual overrides |
| Assets & services | Correlation quality · Tier board | -- |
| Assets & services | Risk scores | Per asset (was *Risks > Risk score*) · Weighted, per service (was *Risks > Weighted risk score*) |
| Assets & services | CMDB | CMDB · Services · Service map · Not seen anymore |
| Security recommendations | Summary | -- one row per recommendation with its affected assets (the stored groupings of the Detailed findings); named views |
| Security recommendations | Detailed | -- one recommendation on one asset (was *Risks > Findings* and *Raw rows*); named views |
| Security recommendations | Exemptions | Exemptions · Excluded / exempted |
| Remediations | Top 10 assets to fix · Top 10 fixes by reach · All remediations | -- |
| Changes & trends | Trends · What changed · Vulnerabilities over time | -- / Opened and closed · Per collection |
| Operations | Tasks · Departments · Review & commit · Jobs · ... · Connectors · Audit trail · Commits (undo) · Deviations | as before |
| Configuration | Settings · Backups · Environment report · Reports & outputs · Risk index · Risk factors · ... · Templates | as before |
| Help | Help + glossary · Documentation | -- |

**The menu restructure (#636, owner 2026-10-13, approved; decisions 2026-10-19).** SecurityInsight holds ASSETS and
SECURITY RECOMMENDATIONS; risk (rating, score) is a dimension to filter and sort by, not a place -- so the menu *Risks* is
gone. Every old address still opens what replaced it: `Navigation/RetiredPages.cs` redirects a BROWSER NAVIGATION (the
request says `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate`: a bookmark, a mail link, a typed address) with the collection, the filters and the
search carried; a handler of the old page (an export still open somewhere) and a programmatic read keep answering there.

| Old address | Opens |
|---|---|
| `/Findings` (`tier`, `sev`, `dom`, `rep`, `kind`, `q`) | Detailed, with the same filters (`f.Tier`, `f.Severity`, `f.SecurityDomain`, `f.ReportName`, `f.AssetKind`, `q`) |
| `/Summary` | Security recommendations > Summary |
| `/Collection/RiskRating` · `/Collection/Mitre` · `/Collection/Compliance` · `/Collection/Cvss` | Detailed, view *Critical and High* · *MITRE* · *Compliance* · *CVSS* |
| `/Collection/Vulnerabilities` | Summary, view *Vulnerabilities (CVE)* |
| `/Collection/TopFindings` | Summary, view *Critical and High* (the most weighted risk first) |
| `/Management/RiskAnalysis` · `/Management/Summary` | unchanged addresses, now tabs of *Executive report* |

**Named views** (`Navigation/NamedViews.cs`): saved layouts SI ships for Summary and Detailed, a picker at the top of the
page -- All · Critical and High · On Tier 0 · Vulnerabilities (CVE) · Known exploited · MITRE · Compliance · CVSS. A view is
its filters and sort in the URL (`?view=mitre&...`), so the link shares it; MITRE, Compliance, CVSS and the rating show the
collection's counts per value under the picker, each narrowing the table (what the retired pages showed above their rows).
An Admin hides a shipped view with the setting `SI_Pro_HiddenViews` (view ids; `summary:` / `detailed:` for one page);
a person's and the Admin-published layouts stay in the toolbar's Layout list. Detailed filters on Domain > Category >
Subcategory, rating, severity, tier and department (typed columns of `sidata.Finding`; `IX_Finding_Category`).

**The tight frame.** A page that opts in (`CollectionPageModel.CompactFrame`: Summary, Detailed, the Remediations pages)
shows the title, the view picker, then the toolbar's one filter line and the table; its explanation sits behind *About this
page*. A test measures the order and the text above the table (`MenuRestructureTests`).

**Remediations** (`engine/pro-data/_shared/SI-DataRemediation.ps1`): one remediation = the same fix applied to many assets.
The data sync gives every finding a key, the first rule that has a value (each part trimmed, lower-cased, spaces removed,
cut at 400): `update:<si_fix_recommended_update_id>` · `update:<si_fix_recommended_update>` · `config:<configuration id>`
(not a CVE) · `software:<vendor>/<product>` (a CVE without a named update) · `cve:<CVE>` · `title:<title>`. The kind is
`si_remediation_type` when a source names it (patch | configuration | upgrade | policy | manual), else from the rule
(update -> patch, config -> configuration, software -> upgrade, cve -> patch, title -> manual). Stored per collection,
read-only towards every source: `sidata.Finding.RemediationKey` (`IX_Finding_Remediation`; Detailed filters a fix's
findings on it: `?fix=`), `sidata.Remediation` (kind, the fix, what to do, effort, owner, department, assets reached,
findings closed, risk removed = the weighted risk of its open findings, best tier, status) and `sidata.RemediationAsset`
(the 100 most important assets -- tier first, then the most open weighted risk -- and their fixes). `Collection.RemediationAt`
says when; until then the pages say the remediations are being prepared. Reporting only: buttons and agents come later in
the same place.

**The key figures' windows are settings (#859, owner 2026-10-21: "do we have static values in the code ?").** Every window a
figure counts over is a setting of the install with today's value as its default -- `SI_KeyFigures_RecentDays` (30: opened /
fixed in the last N days), `SI_KeyFigures_MeanTimeToFixDays` (90), `SI_KeyFigures_StaleAdminDays` (90), `SI_KeyFigures_CveAgeBands`
('30,60,90') -- read by ONE reader (`Get-SIKeyFigureWindowSettings`), passed to the statement as parameters (the data sync and the
update's refigure step alike) and recorded with the figures (meta `window` rows), so a label always says the window THAT
collection was worked out with. A literal day count in a figure / view statement fails `SIv3-NoStaticWindows` unless it is
allow-listed with its reason (read bounds, retention, cadence arithmetic, display spans).

**The accepted lifecycle is for patches (#860, owner 2026-10-21: "grace 0 for non-patch").** A finding gets the accepted-lifecycle
grace (`SI_ProtectionScore_GraceDays_*`) only when it is a PATCH -- it names its fix: a fix release date, a recommended update
(name or id) or a source's patch cycle In monthly cycle / Catch-up (`Test-SIProtectionPatchFinding`; the Pro SQL the same).
Every other finding -- configuration, identity, Azure, attack paths -- has its own grace per asset type
(`SI_ProtectionScore_OtherGraceDays_*`, default 0: a risk from day one). The age is the first known of the fix's release, the
source's first-seen and SI's own first detection ("first seen by SecurityInsight on <date>"); a finding with no date is "a risk
with no first-seen date", counted and shown on its own. The key figures resolve a finding's CI also from `objectid=<guid>`
(the CI linking the Entra object, else the record carrying it as AadObjectId), `az:<ARM id>` and an ARM id inside a composite
key; the marker `meta/grace_by_kind` makes the update figure existing collections again.

**Rows per page (#857).** Every paged grid offers 50 / 100 / 250 / 500 in the shared toolbar beside "Showing 1–50 of N"
(`GridSql.PageChoices`; `GridSql.PageSize` validates the "size" parameter -- anything else is 50): plain links that keep the
view's sort / filters / search and start at page 1, remembered with the view's other choices ("size" is view state). One place
to choose it: the filter forms carry the size as a hidden field. Paging stays in SQL, so a 500-row page reads 500 rows.

**Key figures** (`engine/pro-data/_shared/SI-DataKeyFigures.ps1`, `sidata.KeyFigure`): ONE source for the Executive
overview (to explore: headline tiles, topic buttons, small tables with pivots) and the Executive report (to read: the blocks
1 Patching, 2 Exposure, 3 Coverage, 4 Identity, 5 Cloud, 6 What to do first, 7 Trend, each with "change since the last
report" = the same row of the collection before; its PDF; the management mail carries the chosen blocks, default all). One
row per collection + block + figure + two dimensions, written by the data sync from the stored findings, the CIs and the
finding lifecycle -- never computed per page load. A figure SI cannot answer is stored "not available" with its reason
(e.g. no fix due dates, no MFA state), never as 0. The Risk Analysis run's own 0-100 KPI is kept with the collection too
(figure `ra_kpi`), but it is not shown as a key figure: the management number is the protection score. *Missing patches & findings*: CVEs only or every security finding, per OS family
(`si_os_platform` until `si_os_family` is stored) x device type (Server / Client = workstation / Other), per component
(`si_component`), per affected software and per recommended update ("fixes by reach", with how far behind: current, 1 month,
2+ months, from the update's month), split by the PATCH CYCLE -- `si_patch_cycle` when a source gives it, else: no
recommended update = *no single update*; an update released (the 2nd Tuesday of its month) at most
`SI_PatchCycle_CatchUpDays` (30) before the collection = *in the monthly cycle*, older = *catch-up*. The topic and the
report block are laid out as the owner's mail: the total and the three groups as tiles, then a section per group with a
suggested action worked out from the data.

**#906 -- the patch cycle never hides findings.** Risk Analysis classifies each finding's `si_patch_cycle`
(`Get-SIPatchCycleFacts`, `engine/data-model/SI-Classification.ps1`, rows `patch-cycle-*`): the fix's release date (an
explicit date, the KB's date from the Security Update Guide, else the month the update's name says), and WITHOUT one dated
update the finding's first detection -- SI's (`si_first_detected`) else the SOURCE's first-seen, `si_source_first_seen`
(the field `RA-SourceFirstSeen.ps1` writes from Defender's software vulnerabilities export, before scoring). The facts read
other names only before #906, so every browser / third-party CVE (no recommended update) fell to Unknown -- the internal
install showed 12,709 CVE findings on 13 workstations as Unknown and the page said "Clients: 0 findings on 0 devices". A
finding that names NO recommended update (no update name, no update id; a generic fix text is no update) and has no date
is *No fix available* = group 3, *no single update* -- the rule the SQL twin (`Get-SIKeyFigurePatchesSql`) and
`SI-PatchCycle.ps1` already had. *Unknown* is left only for an update whose month cannot be read (a KB number alone, an
update name without a month). Wherever the three groups are shown -- the Executive tiles and sections, the Executive report,
the management mail (`MgmtSummaryComposer.KeyFiguresHtml` reads the same blocks) and the Risk Analysis mail
(`ConvertTo-SIPatchCycleMailHtml`) -- the Unknown findings are a 4th group, *Not classified (unknown cycle)*, with clients
and servers, whenever there are any (the headline total is then "all four together"). **From the next run:** a stored
collection keeps the cycle it was classified with (no history is rewritten); the first Risk Analysis run after the update
classifies with the new rule, and older collections still show their Unknown findings in the 4th group. The protection
score's accepted-lifecycle view follows (a no-update CVE now aged by first-seen is a patch finding with the device grace).

**The protection score** (#636, owner 2026-10-19: "a new number which defines our ability to protect our assets. that is a
% from 0-100. a higher number is good"). The share of the in-scope ACTIVE CIs -- devices, identities (groups left out),
cloud resources, public IPs -- in GOOD STANDING: no open, non-exempted finding of a counted severity
(`SI_ProtectionScore_Severities`, default Very High / Critical / High), each CI weighted by its tier
(`SI_ProtectionScore_TierWeights`, default 8 / 4 / 2 / 1; unclassified = Tier 3). Two views, both always shown: *technical*
-- every such finding counts (a patch released yesterday lowers it); *within accepted lifecycle* -- a finding younger than
its asset type's grace (`SI_ProtectionScore_GraceDays_Device | _Identity | _CloudResource | _PublicIp`, default 30 days)
does not count. A finding's AGE is the first that is known: the fix's release (`si_fix_release_date`, else the 2nd Tuesday
of the recommended update's month), the source's own first-seen (`SourceFirstDetected`), SI's first detection (the finding
lifecycle, `sidata.CiFindingState`); with none it always counts, and how many had no date is stored (`agebasis`). Stored per
collection in `sidata.KeyFigure` (block `protection`: per asset type x tier, and the headline twins `protection_technical`
/ `protection_lifecycle` that the change-since and the 90-day trend read). Shown side by side with a toggle (default
*within accepted lifecycle*; a CISO switches to *technical*) on the Executive overview (tiles + the *Protection score*
topic), the Executive report (its first block), the management mail and the wall board.
**#827 (owner 2026-10-20) -- the words, the bands and the switch.** The two views are named *Protection Score, Actual Risks*
(the technical view; URL code `technical`) and *Protection Score, within Accepted Lifecycle* (`lifecycle`), "(higher is
better)" kept. Every value carries its BAND -- `data-model/protection-score-bands.locked.json`, ONE file (Very Good 90+, Good
75+, Moderate 50+, At Risk below; ranges to confirm with the owner): the engine reads it (`Get-SIProtectionBand`, the Risk
Analysis mail), the web app embeds an exact copy (`ProtectionBands`), and the value reads "96,5 % · Good" in its band's
colour (a score, not a risk: a good band may be green). The SEVERITY scale is a separate, ordered warm-to-neutral one with
NO green (`app.css` `--rs-*`, Low = slate; `exec.css` refers to it): every severity is a risk. The view switch keeps both
tiles in place and drives the wall board's domain x severity table: the data sync stores the findings of each view per
collection (block `protection`, figures `findings_technical` = every open finding, `findings_lifecycle` = on an active
in-scope CI and past its grace, Dim1 the Risk Analysis domain, Dim2 the severity bucket); a run without them shows the kept
Risk Analysis table for Actual Risks and "not computed for this run" for the lifecycle view.
ONE ENGINE FUNCTION, BOTH EDITIONS (owner 2026-10-19: "replace it with the Protection score everywhere ... retire the old
KPI ... same core functionality"): `engine/_shared/SI-ProtectionScore.ps1` (`New-` / `Add-` / `Complete-SIProtectionTally`,
the settings reader `Get-SIProtectionScoreSettings`). Risk Analysis runs it in the Detailed run over its findings and the run's
CI index (CI class, asset type, tier, stale = inactive), after the shared-cache override, and keeps the answer on the KPI
(`$global:RA_KPI.Protection`), in the kept view (`Kpi.Protection`) and in the shared cache (a Summary run shows the Detailed
run's score, else says it comes with the Detailed run). Pro writes the same rules as SQL per collection
(`Get-SIKeyFigureProtectionSql`); a real-SQL test holds the two to the same rows. The summaryoff grouping
(`SI-SummaryGroupings.ps1`) groups FINDINGS by fields; the protection score needs the asset inventory (assets without findings
count as good), so it does not fit and is not reused. The old 0-100 KPI is RETIRED from every output: the Risk Analysis mail
(its headline and "Risk by domain"), the Risk Analysis page (hero and domain tiles), the management summary (KPI section,
plain summary, domain lines) and the wall board (score card, scale, marker); `GlobalScore` stays only inside the engine's
summary / detailed cache agreement and in views kept before.
THE SOURCE'S OWN FIRST-SEEN (`si_source_first_seen`, `engine/risk-analysis/_shared/RA-SourceFirstSeen.ps1`, checked against
Microsoft's documentation 2026-10-19): Defender for Endpoint vulnerabilities -- the software vulnerabilities export
(`GET /api/machines/SoftwareVulnerabilitiesExport`, Vulnerability.Read.All, GZIP files of JSON lines; `FirstSeenTimestamp`
"first time this product CVE was seen on the device"), read once per run, the earliest per device + CVE, put on the
`Device_Missing_CVEs_*` rows (advanced hunting's `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` has no such column; `SI_RA_SourceFirstSeen`,
default on); Defender for Cloud `firstEvaluationDate`; Shodan -- the first banner SI collected for the IP (`si_banner_first_seen`;
Shodan has no first-seen per service). NO SUCH DATE: secure configurations (the export's `Timestamp` is the LAST sighting),
the identity posture checks (Entra ID Protection's `riskDetection.detectedDateTime` belongs to risk detections, which no SI
report lists as findings), Defender for Identity investigation priority (a score), exposure graph paths, the active-compromise
report (it reads the CI's flag, not the alerts' `firstActivityDateTime`). The Pro column `SourceFirstDetected` takes
`si_source_first_seen` first, then `si_source_first_detected`. The CI build is not touched (no CI content-hash change).
SCHEMA BEFORE CODE: every new column and table of #636 is guarded and additive in `sql/si-data-schema.sql`; the updater applies
the release's schema (`Invoke-SIProSchemaApply`, `container/updater/_shared/SI-UpdaterDatabase.ps1`, gated by
`Test-SISchemaIsAdditive`) BEFORE it rolls the web app and the jobs (#352, `SIv3-UpdaterSchema`).
**One "change since".** `Pages/Shared/ChangeSince.cs` + `_ChangeSince.cshtml`: the change is judged on the value AS SHOWN
(a difference that rounds to 0 is "no change", neutral), green or red by the measure's direction -- lower is better for
counts and the average risk score per finding, higher for the protection score (shown in percentage points). Owner
2026-10-19: *risk score* / *weighted risk score* are the per-finding priority numbers (no limit, higher = more risk; an
asset's totals are the *asset risk score* / *weighted asset risk score*), the per-finding average is the *average risk
score per finding (lower is better)*, and the 0-100 management number is the *protection score* -- never called "Risk
score". The Risk Analysis run's own 0-100 figure is the *Risk Analysis KPI*.
*New vs fixed* (`/Management/Vulnerabilities`) showed the close-loop's new / fixed / reopened per week -- the same
numbers as *Vulnerabilities over time* per week -- and now redirects there (`?weeks=4/12/26/52` ->
`/Management/Closure?days=30/90/180/365&grain=week`). *Per collection* (`/Collection/Lifecycle`) shows only what the
close-loop did between one collection and the next; the finding / CI counts it used to repeat link to *What changed*.

**One source for the risk score over time.** *Executive overview > Risk score* and *Trends* showed the same score from
two places (the Log Analytics daily summary and the Pro database). The Risk score page now reads the Pro database's
daily aggregate -- the same query as Trends, split by asset tier and added together (the average re-computed from the
parts; Tier-0 assets with findings = the Tier 0 group's distinct assets) -- and says so on the page. Trends split by
"Nothing (total)" shows exactly its numbers. *Executive overview > Domains* does the same: the Pro database's daily
aggregate split by security domain, so Trends split by "Security domain" shows identical numbers.
### The CIs page is fast at any size -- columns, late document fields, cached filter values, sizing (Pro web app, #584)

Owner 2026-10-11: *"why is the performance so bad"*, *"takes 10 sec to open a view"* (the CI inventory, `/Cis`). Measured
on internal (8,799 CIs, 85 MB of CI documents in `sidata.Ci.DocJson`, SQL S2, web app 0.5 CPU / 1 GiB): the grid read the
16 fields of the default layout that are not columns of `sidata.Ci` out of every CI's document (`JSON_VALUE` per row:
~27 s of database time, 724,000 LOB reads, for one page) and the filter values read the asset subtype out of every
document (~4 s). The other CI and collection pages measured 0.1-0.2 s (`/Cis/Summary`, `/Cis/Findings`, `/Collection/Assets`,
`/Findings`): they read columns only.

- **Columns.** The default layout's scalar document fields are columns of `sidata.Ci` (`CiColumns.Promoted`, mirrored by
  `$SIDataCiDocFields` in `engine/pro-data/_shared/SI-DataCi.ps1`; a test holds the two lists equal): AssetSubtype, OsName,
  OsPlatform, OsVersion, OnboardingStatus, Owner, Department, Hostname, IpAddress, AzureResourceType, IdentityType, Purpose
  (NVARCHAR(400)), AccountEnabled, MfaRegistered (BIT), plus `DocFieldsHash` -- the content hash the columns were filled
  from. Added in place by `sql/si-data-schema.sql` (guarded, nullable), with `IX_Ci_Page` (weighted risk score DESC, CI id,
  covering every grid column, never the document) and `IX_Ci_Type` (asset type, subtype).
- **The fill.** The data sync, after the finding totals, fills the columns of every CI whose content hash moved
  (`Get-SIDataCiDocFieldsSql`: one `OPENJSON ... WITH` parse per CI, batches of 2,000, set-based; ~1.7 s for all 8,799 CIs
  on internal, then only what changed). A database without the columns is skipped; a failure is a warning, never a failed
  sync. The CI build is not touched.
- **Three read modes** (`CiFieldMode`, from `CiViews.DataStateAsync`: one narrow `SELECT` over the covering index):
  *Document* -- the columns do not exist yet (the schema update has not run): the document, as before; *Fallback* -- some
  CIs' columns are not current (a CI build ran after the last fill): per row, the column where `DocFieldsHash` = its content
  hash, else the document; *Columns* -- the columns alone. So an existing install shows correct values at every moment, and
  is fast from its first data sync after the update.
- **Late document fields** (`GridLate`, `GridColumn.LateSql`): a field still read from the document (the list fields
  Components and Linked objects, any field a person adds to their layout, and every promoted field before the fill) is
  computed for the page's rows only -- the page is chosen (filter, sort, count, offset) over a narrow source, then joined
  back by CI id. Only a field the request filters, sorts or searches on is read for every row. Measured on internal, the
  same page: ~27 s -> ~0.3 s (Document mode, before any column exists).
- **Filter values cached** per data version in the web app (`CiViews.CiFacetsAsync(state)`: newest collection time, CI
  count, unfilled count): a page load reads them again only when a CI build or a fill changed the data.
- **Sizing.** The web app (ca-si-management) is 2 CPU / 4 GiB at install (`Deploy-SIManagement.ps1 -Cpu 2.0 -Memory 4Gi`;
  owner 2026-10-18: *"reduce web app to 2cpus 4 gb ram"* -- 7 days of telemetry: at most 0.1 CPU / 0.5 GiB used of 4 / 8 GiB;
  the MCP server keeps 0.5 / 1 GiB via `-McpCpu / -McpMemory`), and every update SETS an existing web app's own container to it
  (`Invoke-SIContainerUpdate.ps1` step 8d, `SI-JobSizing.ps1 Invoke-SIWebAppSize`: one read-modify-write PATCH of the whole
  template, revision suffix dropped, waits for the new revision so the web app roll that follows is not refused, reads the size
  back): a smaller one is raised, the product's earlier 4 / 8 GiB (3.75 / 7.5 behind the sign-in front) is lowered, any other
  larger size is the customer's and kept; `SI_Bootstrap_WebAppCpu` / `SI_Bootstrap_WebAppMemory` (Pro database first, then the
  config) win both ways. The sign-in front sidecar (0.25 / 0.5 GiB) is never resized: the app is 2.25 CPU / 4.5 GiB.
  The Pro database is S3 (above); `SI_Bootstrap_SqlServiceObjective` (Pro database first) sets it both ways, never below S1; the identity ledger stays S1 whatever is set (#756).
### What a view shows by default is prepared in SQL (Pro, #592)

A column of a data view's SHIPPED layout -- the CI id, the identifier values, the linked objects, the CI context, the
finding context -- is a typed column the data sync fills. A page reads its 50 rows' values from those columns by key; the
JSON documents (the CI document, the finding's whole row) are read only for a column a person ADDS on top of the default,
and then only for the rows of the page.

- **One list** (`pro-management/src/SI.Management.Core/ProData/DataModel/view-stored-columns.json`): the web app embeds it
  (`ViewStoredColumns`), the data sync reads the same file (`engine/pro-data/_shared/SI-DataViewContext.ps1`). An entry is a
  layout key, its column, its type and whether the column is indexed. Adding a field is one entry plus its guarded column in
  `sql/si-data-schema.sql`; tests name a line that is missing.
- **The CI** (`sidata.Ci`): next to its own columns and the CI grid's, the fields of the list (owner object id, subscription
  id + name, resource group + id, management group path + id, tenant, app, service principal, group; list fields as their
  JSON text) and the identifier values and linked object ids as '; '-joined text. `CtxHash` is the content hash the columns
  were filled from and `CtxSet` the identity of the list they were filled for (a hash of the list): the data sync fills a
  CI whose content moved, or -- after a field was added -- every CI once, in batches, without a CI build. The identifier
  columns are rewritten only where their values moved. The web app reads a CI's columns only when its markers are current;
  a CI built since the last data sync is read from its document, by key, so every moment is correct.
- **One finding** (`sidata.Finding`): affected software / product / vendor / version, description, the recommended update
  and its id, remediation, more details, published, exploit words, category, subcategory, impact and the CMDB group are
  columns, filled per collection from the finding's row -- parsed once per finding, the first of the column's names that has
  a value (the same rule the row read uses), in id ranges sized from their measured time.
- **One row per CVE / issue** (`sidata.IssueContext`, one row per collection and key): the distinct values of each context
  column over EVERY finding of the key (most risky finding's first), the software as "product version (vendor)" items, the
  first affected asset names and the exact number of affected assets -- built set-based from the finding columns and
  written with the collection's stamp (`sidata.Collection.ContextAt`) in one transaction. A page reads its keys' rows by the
  primary key. A finding belongs to the key it carries as its CVE or as its configuration id; where the findings of a key
  are still read (below), each half seeks its own index and the two are united -- never one OR across two columns.
- **A collection without the stamp** (stored before this release, until the data sync reached it) is read the way it was:
  the finding's row by its clustered key, a sample of a key's findings through the two indexes. The data sync prepares every
  complete collection that has no stamp, newest first, within a time budget per run; what is left follows on the next runs
  and is said in the log. Nothing in this step can fail the data sync.
- **The chooser's lists** (which fields, identifier types, source properties and finding fields exist) are cached per
  data-sync state -- the newest collection, the newest CI build, the newest full details and records -- and read again only
  when one of them moved; the state itself is asked at most twice a minute.
- **Indexes.** Each prepared read is a key seek: the CI by its primary key, the finding by the clustered (collection,
  finding) key, the issue row by its primary key, an asset key's own identifiers by their unique index. The views' own
  statements gained covering indexes where they read the wide rows that carry a JSON document (findings per CI, records per
  source, the asset a finding row joins).
- **Typed columns.** An entry's type says how the value is stored: a text (cut at its length), a number (`INT` / `FLOAT`), a
  yes / no (`BIT`), a date (`DATETIME2(3)`, UTC), a list or object as its JSON text, or values '; '-joined. A number, a
  yes / no and a date are stored as such -- a filter or a sort compares values, never text -- and a value that is not one
  stays empty rather than guessed. The CI grid reads a typed column for a catalog field of the same kind; a field whose
  catalog type differs from the list's is read from the CI document instead, and a test names it.
- **The context of the sources.** The list carries what the sources add about a CI: who answers for it (owner, manager,
  primary user, support and assignment group, the service and CMDB owner -- each as id AND name), where it lives
  (subscription, management group, tenant, environment, location), how it is protected (MFA strength, whether Conditional
  Access enforces MFA, encryption, compliance, backup, pending updates, the Defender plan), how it is used (the last
  sign-ins, alerts and admin logons) and what it is attached to. And about a finding: the exploit probability (EPSS), the
  CVE tags, the mitigation status, the end-of-support status and date, the fix owner, due date and grace period, the
  evidence, the secure score control and gain, the attack paths, the certificate expiry. On the per-issue row a text is
  the distinct values over the key's findings, a number the HIGHEST and a date the EARLIEST -- what a person prioritises on.
- **Nothing a source says is cut.** The description, the remediation and the evidence of a finding are whole-text columns;
  the shorter columns that existed before stay (the schema only adds) and are no longer what the views read.
- **A collection is prepared for one list** (`sidata.Collection.ContextSet`, as `CtxSet` for a CI): the identity of the
  finding part of the list. A field added to the list reaches the collections already stored -- the data sync prepares
  each once more, newest first -- and until then the web app reads such a collection from its finding rows, so an added
  field is never shown empty where the data has it.

### Open alerts per device, and "Autopilot enrolled" from Intune

**Open alerts.** Advanced hunting says which alerts named a device in the last 30 days, but not whether an alert is still
open. The security alerts of Microsoft Graph do. Once per run the endpoint collection reads the alerts whose status is
*new* or *in progress* for the whole tenant -- one paged read, read only, with the permission `SecurityAlert.Read.All` --
and summarises each page per device as it arrives, by the Defender device id in the alert's device evidence. There is
never a request per device and no cap on the alerts read. A device then carries: how many open alerts name it, the
highest severity among them, and the newest one's title, id and time -- next to the 30-day fields, which stay.

*Unknown is not zero.* Only a read that reached its last page lets a device no alert names say **0**. A read that is
refused (the permission is not granted yet), fails or stops early writes nothing: the fields stay unknown. A refusal is
