said once in the run log with the permission to grant; a failure once with its reason. If the source does not accept the
status filter, the same read is made without it and each alert's status is checked as it is summarised. The later parts
of the same run reuse the one answer.

**Autopilot enrolled.** Only the beta version of Microsoft Graph says whether an Intune device is Autopilot enrolled, so
the Intune device read is made on beta. A beta version can change without notice, so the read has a fall-back: when beta
refuses, fails, stops before its last page or answers rows that are not devices, the whole read is made again on the
stable version. Every Intune field is then there exactly as before, "Autopilot enrolled" stays unknown (never "no"), and
that is said once in the run log. Nothing read from beta is kept beside the stable answer -- no device twice. Where beta
names a property differently, both names are mapped.

The open alert count, the highest severity and the Autopilot flag are prepared, typed columns, so the device list
shows, sorts and filters them without reading the CI document.

### The default layout of a view, by what its rows are (Pro)

A view opens with the context that lets a person prioritise without opening each row; a person or an Admin may choose
otherwise (the chooser), and every column below is a prepared column either way.

- **A view that mixes classes** (the findings, the CIs at risk, All CIs unfiltered): the cross-class context -- owner and
  owner id, department, environment, OS, IP, host name, subscription id and name, resource group, management group, the
  support group id and name, the CMDB item, last seen. What only one class carries is one click away in the chooser; a
  mixed view never opens with dozens of mostly-empty columns.
- **A list of ONE class** (All CIs filtered to a class) adds what that class carries: devices -- the primary user,
  encrypted, Autopilot enrolled, the last management check-in, device value, the open alerts and their highest severity,
  alerts in 30 days, on a public network, the last admin logon; Azure resources -- subscription name, environment,
  management group, backup protected, pending critical updates, the Defender plan tier; public IPs -- what it is
  attached to, an expired certificate, the earliest certificate expiry.
- **Identities open with a layout per KIND**, because a user and a service principal carry different things. The kind is
  the asset type the CI carries (the asset type filter of All CIs): *User* and *Guest* are users, *Service principal* and
  *Managed identity* are service principals. Filtered to identities and ONE kind: **users** -- sign-in name, MFA strength,
  whether Conditional Access enforces MFA, risk level, the role paths, the level inside Tier 0 in words (where set), the
  manager (sign-in name and id), the last interactive sign-in; **service principals** -- the owners (sign-in names and
  ids), the days until a credential expires and what to do about it, the resource the identity is attached to (name and
  id), the last app sign-in. Identities with both kinds in the list, or with no asset type chosen, are a mixed list: the
  cross-class context only, never half-empty columns. Only the shipped layout follows the filter -- a layout a person or
  an Admin saved is shown as saved.
- **A finding** opens with the affected software, the description and the evidence, the fix and remediation with the fix
  owner and due date, the exploit details with EPSS, the CVE tags and the mitigation status, the end-of-support status
  and date, then its CI's cross-class context. One row per CVE shows the same with the highest EPSS and the earliest dates.
- **Every reference is a pair**: an id is never shown without its name or a name without its id -- subscription,
  management group, tenant, resource group, support group, assignment group, owner, primary user, manager, attached
  resource, backup vault, CMDB item, service. A half the layout lacks is added next to the half it has.
- **Filters on the context.** A listed column with a short closed vocabulary (environment, MFA strength, risk level, device
  value, Defender plan tier) is a filter above the CI list. Its choices are read from the column's own index and kept per
  data version; the filter works whatever columns the layout shows (its column is carried by the statement, hidden).

### A view's page is read once per data version (Pro)

The collection views keep what they read per collection (a complete collection never changes). The views over the CURRENT
data had no such key and ran their whole statement on every page load: All CIs, the findings per CI, the findings per
finding key, the records per source, the correlation figures and their trend over the collections, the pivot of the
findings browser and the tier-0 ranking. They are kept per **data version**:

- **The version** is one row of narrow reads (`Core/ProData/DataVersion.cs`): the mark the data sync sets when it has
  stored its data (`sidata.ViewState`, a new value at the end of every run that wrote), the newest collection and when the
  newest views' data was computed, the CIs (their newest collection time, how many, how many without their prepared
  columns), the newest collection time and number of the findings per CI and of the records, and the CI build's state.
  Index ends and counts of narrow indexes -- never a document. It is asked at most every few seconds.
- **A result is kept until the version moves -- never by time alone.** While the data stands still a page is not read
  again; the first load after new data reads again. The key is the statement and every parameter value (sort, page,
  filters, search, selection, the layout's columns) and the request's exempted-findings scope. A version that cannot be
  told (or a failure to tell it) reads live. The cache is bounded; reaching the bound drops the entries, never a row.
- **An export is always read live** -- every matching row, never kept.
- **Not kept on purpose:** lists whose rows the web app itself changes (the exemption requests and decisions, the CMDB
  services, an asset an Admin retires early) -- a decision must show at once, and the data version does not move with it.
- **The remaining reads became seeks:** the vulnerability items have an index that leads on the asset and state (the
  assets no longer seen, the task lists, one CI's vulnerabilities) and one on the finding key (when a top finding was
  first seen); a department's findings have an index that carries every column their grid shows; the management
  drill-down reads a finding's category from its prepared column (from the finding rows only on a database without the
  column, or while the newest collection is not prepared yet).

### The page timing log (Pro web app)

A page that is slow says so in the web app's log, so a slow moment can be explained afterwards. A request that takes
longer than one second (`PageTiming:SlowMs`, in milliseconds; the Container App's environment `PageTiming__SlowMs`;
below zero switches it off) writes ONE line at Information level through the log category `SecurityInsight.PageTiming`:

`slow page: GET /Cis/Index -> 200 in 7412 ms; database: 14 calls, 6980 ms; slowest 4120 ms: SELECT c.CiId, ...`

- **What it counts:** every call the request made to the Pro database -- the web app has one seam to it, and that seam
  adds each call's time (opening the connection included) to the request it belongs to. Work outside a request (a
  schedule's pass) is not counted.
- **What it never carries:** the address (the page's route is written, so an id is `{id}`), the query string, the
  user, or a value of a statement -- the slowest statement is shown as its first 80 characters with comments, quoted
  texts and numbers removed.
- **Not timed:** static files and the health probe. A request that fails is timed like any other.

### The CI views always read their stored columns (Pro)

The CI views filter and sort on stored, indexed columns of each CI (the CI list's columns and the view context). A CI
whose columns are behind its document makes the views read that CI from the document instead -- correct, but without
the indexes. That used to be the case from the end of every CI build until the next data sync, because only the data
sync filled the columns.

- **The CI build fills them as its last data write**, inside the build's lock and before it records that it finished:
  the same two set-based, batched statements the data sync runs, which pick exactly the CIs whose content changed since
  their columns were filled. A build that changed nothing writes nothing.
- **The data sync keeps running them** (they are idempotent): after a build it finds nothing to do; it still covers a
  changed list of view columns and an install whose build ran on an older release.
- **Never a reason for a build to fail, and never an alert:** a failure is one informational line in the build's log
  with its reason -- a warning of the CI build is an alert, and nothing is wrong with the build or its CIs -- and the
  data sync fills the columns as before (and warns itself if it cannot). A database that does not have the columns yet is left alone, and the free edition -- which has no data sync
  -- does not load the step at all.
- **Two small reads are kept in the web app:** which CI tables and columns exist (five minutes, like the other schema
  reads) and the CIs' state (fifteen seconds, like the data version). Every CI view asked both on every request.

### A device without a name, the devices not onboarded, and one page of assumptions (#856 / #858)

- **A CI without a name** (#856): a device Defender only DISCOVERED on the network has no name in Defender either -- only
  its addresses. The views show it by its best identifier: its IP address, else its MAC address, else its primary source
  link's id (last its CI id), MARKED as a fallback (italic, CSS class `ci-noname`, "(no name)", a tooltip that says why).
  It is a DISPLAY value only (`CiDisplayName`, `SI.Management.Core/ProData/CiDisplayName.cs`): `si_asset_name` stays empty,
  the CSV / Excel exports keep the name empty, and nothing sends it to ServiceNow as a name. The CI grid carries it as a
  hidden LATE column (`NameFallback`: read for the page's rows only, never chosen, filtered, sorted or exported); the CI
  page heads with it from the document.
- **The IpAddress column** is the best of the device's OWN addresses where the CI has no public IP: the data sync's fill
  (`Get-SIDataCiDocFieldsSql`, also run as the CI build's last write) takes `si_ip_address` (the public IP of a public IP
  CI), else the best of `si_ip_addresses` (an IPv4 address first, then IPv6, loopback last), else its one text; the web app
  reads the same rule from the document where the column is not current (`CiDisplayName.IpFromDocumentSql`). ONCE per
  database, the devices filled before get theirs (set-based, only rows that get a value, marked `sidata.ViewState`
  `ci-ip-fill`). The CI document is not changed -- `si_ip_address` keeps its meaning (the public IP) for Risk Analysis
  -- so the CI build version is not bumped.
- **Active devices not onboarded in Defender** (#858, `/Cis/NotOnboarded`, Assets (CIs) tab; the executive coverage
  figure "Devices not onboarded" links it). THE INCLUSION RULE (decided by the owner): a device Defender only discovered is
  an asset and counts -- a real device that is not protected -- but only while it is ACTIVE (the lifecycle's seen window);
  a not seen or retired one never counts; a customer excludes one by tag (asset tagging, `si_is_excluded`). The view
  (`NotOnboardedViews`): the active device CIs whose onboarding state is set and not `onboarded`, and the Azure machines
  without a Defender for Endpoint device (Defender for Cloud: no state, no MDE device id), split by status -- can be
  onboarded (actionable), Azure machine without the agent (actionable), unsupported, insufficient info, other -- with the
  name (fallback above), IP, MAC, OS, first / last seen and the source; the excluded ones are counted apart, never listed.
  Read from the CI columns (the document only for the page's own fields and the exclusion tag), paged 50 / 100 / 250 /
  500, the newest seen first. A not-onboarded device has no Defender vulnerability data: its 0 missing patches is not
  measured -- the page says so.
- **Assumptions** (#858, Configuration > Risk rating & lifecycle > Assumptions, Admin): every assumption in plain words with
  the value IN FORCE and a link to where it is set -- what counts as an asset (the CI classes, the discovered-device rule
  and its three automatic exclusion switches, the disabled-account and first-party / inactive settings), the seen window
  and every grace period, the views that open on active assets, how a tier is decided (override, SI rule, tag, default),
  what "fixed" means (remediated only), the risk rating thresholds (Low = less than Moderate), the accepted lifecycle and
  the days to fix, and what is not measured. Built from the SAME readers the pages use (`ICiLifecycleRulesReader`,
  `LifecycleModel.LineOf` for a setting's value in force, `RiskRatingThresholds.InForce`, the asset tagging gates) -- no
  number is written in the page; a test holds every value shown to its reader.

### Pages stay fast and whole while a data sync runs (Pro)

A data sync stores a lot in steps: a collection's rows, its views' aggregates, the prepared context, departments, the
counted aggregates, the findings per CI. Three things made the pages slow or incomplete while it ran; each has its own
rule now.

- **A collection is shown by the collection views when its view data is written.** A collection is `Complete` when its
  rows are loaded -- minutes before its aggregates and prepared context exist, and a page that opened it then had to
  work its columns out row by row. The data sync now marks a collection ready for the views
  (`sidata.Collection.ViewsReadyAt`) after the views' aggregates, the prepared context, the departments and the counted
  aggregates, and the collection views list on that mark. Every other reader -- mails, reports, the finding lifecycle,
  data quality, the load plan -- keeps reading `Complete`, exactly as before. The mark is set for every complete
  collection that does not have it, on every run: a run that died before that step leaves its collection out of the
  views (the previous one stays the newest shown), and the next run finishes and marks it. A step of the view data that
  fails says so and does not keep a collection hidden. On a database that does not have the mark yet, and while no
  collection carries it, the list is read as before; when the mark is added, the collections already complete stay
  shown.
- **The findings per CI are replaced in one step.** They were emptied by the first chunk of a new collection and
  refilled chunk by chunk, so "Findings per CI" showed a partial list for a minute or two. The chunks now go to a
  staging table (`sidata.CiFindingStage`), and one transaction replaces the stored set from it: a reader sees the whole
  previous set until it commits and the whole new set after, and a failure inside it leaves the previous set as it was.
  The number of staged rows is checked against what the run wrote first -- a set that is not the run's own is never
  swapped in. A rename or a partition switch would need rights to change the schema, which the data sync's identity
  does not have; this keeps the table, its indexes and its rights as they are. Since #639 a database without the
  staging table keeps its stored findings and the run says so as FAILED (a collection read in pages is never emptied
  and refilled in steps); the updater adds the table.
  **Only what changed is written (#834).** The whole-table delete and insert logged every row and index entry twice a
  day though most findings are the same as the day before (measured on a small database: the delete alone 236 s). The
  replace now keeps a stored row identical in every column to a staged one (a SHA-256 of all its columns, NULL kept
  apart from empty, matched by its place among identical rows), removes the other stored rows and inserts the staged
  rows without an identical stored one, in staged order -- the same stored set as before, its count checked against the
  staged count inside the transaction (a mismatch rolls back and keeps the previous set). An unchanged finding keeps its
  row.
- **The data sync's heavy parts on a small database (#834).** Measured on a small Pro database (one sync 99.6 min, 21.1
  the day before):
  - *Old collections are marked right after the loads* (`Invoke-SIDataCollectionRetention -MarkOnly`): the same plan and
    guards as the removal -- per grain the newest complete collection and the one before it are kept, the published run's
    collection and a result waiting for the data sync are never marked -- so no later step derives, prepares or groups a
    collection the same sync removes (one collection in three on that day: the third one was the collection the cleanup
    removed at the end). No row is removed by a mark; a marked collection is never shown again.
  - *Their rows are removed while no run is running.* Started by the pipeline (a running step of a running pipeline run),
    the sync only marks; the pipeline runner's wake-ups remove the rows once the run has ended (the stopped-run cleanup:
    the same retention, a marked collection with rows left is finished, inside each wake-up's time budget) -- on a
    database the sync no longer loads (measured: 26.3 min, most of it the pacing waiting on the database the sync itself
    had saturated). By hand or on its own schedule the sync removes them at its end, as before.
    **#892: also while a run is going.** At the largest install a run is nearly always going, so the marked rows were never
    removed (2026-10-23: 3.75 M finding rows, ~75 GB, in collections marked days before). Every wake-up now removes the rows
    of collections the DATA SYNC marked (superseded / abandoned) BEFORE the running pipeline run started -- nothing in that
    run can be writing them. A 'stopped run' mark #882 makes while a run goes can hit a collection the data sync is still
    loading from Log Analytics, so those rows wait for a wake-up with no run going, as before (review B1). In key ranges on
    the clustered key: each range works out its end first, then removes exactly that range; it starts at the collection's
    first row; it is never larger than SQL Server's lock escalation allows, counting one lock in every index of the table
    (4,000 / indexes), so a range never becomes a table lock that holds a run's writes; the mark (and the condition above) is
    checked again inside the DELETE. Paced by the database's load, inside what is left of the wake-up's budget; the next
    wake-up goes on. Never a collection that is not complete and started at or after the owner floor, never the published
    one -- refused inside the DELETE, under the publisher's own app lock (shared; the publisher takes it exclusive), and the
    mark statement reads the published pointer in the same transaction under the same lock, so a mark or a range never
    interleaves with a publish -- never a kept one (it is not marked). A refused range is said as refused, not removed.
    Without a floor, a run start or a time budget nothing is removed.
  - *The security owners' categories* are read from the Risk Analysis row's Category stored on the finding when its
    views' columns are derived (`sidata.Finding.RaCategory`, the same expression the pairs read, NULL for a row that is
    not JSON) through a narrow index, instead of one `SELECT DISTINCT` over every finding's JSON (239 s per collection on
    that database). A collection derived before the column existed reads the JSON as before.
  - *The prepared context* ran over three collections that day because a field had been added (every kept collection is
    prepared once more for a new field set): a one-off; a normal day prepares the one new collection.
- **The pages the web app has are served until the run ends.** The web app keeps what its views read per data version
  (above), and every step of a run moved one of the version's figures -- so the kept pages were dropped and read again
  about seven times per run, while the database was busiest. The data sync now says that it is running: one row
  (`sidata.ViewState`, name `sync`, with its start time), written before its first write and taken away in the same
  transaction as its end mark -- or by the run itself when it fails. While that row is there, the figures a data sync
  moves (the collections, the CIs' prepared columns, the findings per CI) are held at what they were when the run was
  first seen, so the version does not move; it moves **once**, at the end mark.
  - *A run that died* leaves the row behind: a row older than **60 minutes** is ignored, and the pages follow the
    figures again. (A run that really takes longer than that is treated as before this rule from then on.)
  - *What a data sync does not write still shows at once*, also while it runs: the CIs and records (the CI build, which
    also carries a person's tier decision) and the CI build's state move the version as before. What a person changes
    in the web app itself -- an exemption, a CMDB service, an asset retired early -- is not kept by this cache at all.
  - A page that is not kept yet (a new filter) is read from the database as it is at that moment.
- **Every page says so.** While a data sync is running, every signed-in page carries one calm line under the menu:
  *"Data is being refreshed (started 10:37) -- the pages show the previous data until it is done."* The time is shown
  in the viewer's own time zone, like every other time on a page. It reads the same row as the rule above (one small
  read, kept for 30 seconds), shows nothing when no run is running or the row is older than 60 minutes, and a failure
  to read it shows no line -- it never fails a page.

### The data sync holds one page, never a tenant-sized set; a short read replaces nothing (#639)

At a large install (~105,000 records, 33,000-69,000 finding rows, 8 GiB per job) the data sync held whole sets several
times over and timed out storing them. The rule now: **what is held is one page; what is stored replaces the old only when
it is whole.**

- **The findings per CI** (`SI-DataCi.ps1`, `Invoke-SIDataCiSync`). With the copy to Log Analytics off (the default, #829)
  they are made from the database in one set-based statement; what follows is the read when the copy is on. One small count query pins the newest `SI_Finding_CL`
  collection: its time (as text -- every page matches it, so a newer collection arriving meanwhile cannot mix in), its row
  count and its measured size. Its rows are read a page at a time by a hash of their own key (`_pk` = the row's
  `_ItemId`, CI and finding key), exactly as the findings load reads a collection (`Read-SIDataPages`: the page count
  from the measured size; a page too large to answer or to hold is read again in two halves, alone). Each page becomes its
  items, is staged in SQL in chunks -- the findings into `sidata.CiFindingStage`, the lifecycle input into
  `sidata.CiFindingLifecycleStage` -- and is let go before the next page is read. **Only when the rows read equal the
  count** does one transaction replace the stored findings (the swap, which also checks the staged count) and the
  lifecycle run. A short read replaces nothing, advances nothing, empties what it staged and is a FAILED issue naming
  both numbers -- the stored findings and the lifecycle stay exactly as they were (working rule 4: a finding missing from
  a cut answer is unknown, never absent). The data sync hands the raw Log Analytics reader to the page reader under its own
  name (`-LaQuery`): its `$readOrSkip` reads a variable named `$Query`, which inside the page reader would be the page
  reader's own parameter.
- **The finding lifecycle** reads its input from `sidata.CiFindingLifecycleStage` (Kind `f` = a finding, Kind `a` = a key
  the recommendation equivalence changed) -- the same statement with its source swapped (`Get-SIDataFindingStateSql
  -FromStage`), never the whole collection as one JSON string in one parameter. Which owners' absent findings freeze is
  computed in SQL against the staged input (`Get-SIDataCiStagedFrozenOwnersSql`). A database without that table stores the
  findings and skips the lifecycle for that run (a WARNING: nothing is closed). The staging table is emptied after the
  lifecycle ran; the next run's first chunk empties it too.
- **Data out** (`SI-DataOut.ps1`). Every output reads ITS grain itself, a page at a time (`Read-SIDataOutItemPages`: the
  CIs and records by their key, the open findings by `CiFindingId`, the closed lifecycle rows by `(OwnerKey,
  FindingKey)`). **Page by page, end to end (2026-10-21, any size):** the writer PULLS the next page only when its
  destination asks for it (`New-SIDataOutItemCursor` / `Get-SIDataOutNextPage`); each page is filtered, mapped, hashed,
  compared with what was sent for THOSE keys (`cfg.DataOutItem` read by the page's keys), handed to the destination and
  recorded (state upserted and change entries written in bounded chunks) before the next page is read. An Excel output is
  streamed into its sheet (the streamed sheet writer of the workbook step) and continues on `<sheet> (2)`, ... past Excel's
  1,048,575 rows -- never cut; another output's sheet in the same file stays. A ServiceNow output checks the connection,
  table and columns once per run, then checks and sends each page (a value that would be cut holds the rest; what was sent
  is recorded, what was held goes on the next run). The keys an output has seen are staged in the data database
  (`sidata.DataOutKeyStage`); the items no longer sent are found by paging what was sent before against them, and are
  logged / removed only when the destination took the run. The findings summary is staged too
  (`sidata.DataOutSummaryStage`) and its groups are built set-based. Nothing is cached across outputs.
- **Every Excel output is optional** (owner 2026-10-21): off by default in Pro (the findings workbooks, the records
  workbook and the CI workbook -- every row is in the web app); the Community edition keeps its CI workbook on. Switched on
  (`SI_DataOut_Outputs`) it writes as above at any size.
- **The Log Analytics reader** (`SI-AzRest.ps1`, `Invoke-SILaQuery`). The lean read is the default on pwsh 7: the answer
  arrives as bytes -- read once into an array of the length the service sent -- and its rows are read from those bytes;
  the answer is never also held as text or as a second copy of its tables. `.Tables` is one schema entry (the primary
  table's name and columns, no rows; `.Columns` the same) -- what the Risk Analysis reader takes its column types from.
  **Read as it arrives (#730, on in every engine since #836).** Risk Analysis' reads (`SI_LaStreamRows`, set by
  `Invoke-LogAnalyticsKqlQuery` for its call) and every lookup / compact-row read (`SI_LaCompactRows`: Risk Analysis'
  lookups, the vulnerability close-loop's snapshot) are read from the response STREAM (`engine\_shared\SI-LaStreamRead.ps1`,
  a System.Text.Json reader compiled once per process): each row becomes its row object as soon as its bytes are in, and
  the answer is never held whole -- the same rows, columns, order, text values, schema and error as the lean read. Every
  other read is the lean read, unchanged. Nothing of the reader lives only in a script scope: a function reads `$script:`
  of its CALLER's script, and in a container the entry point loads `SI-AzRest.ps1` once while each engine runs as its own
  script -- so the C# source is a function (`Get-SILaStreamReaderSource`), the compiled type is found by name, and the
  process-wide state is global (`$global:SI_LaStreamReaderOff` = the reason streaming is off, `$global:SI_LaStreamLast` =
  the last read's bytes / largest buffer / rows). **The older read stays the fallback, never silent:** when the reader cannot
  be built, every read is the lean read and ONE plain line on the run log says so and why (once per process); when a stream
  read fails on an answer (`Read-SILaQueryStreamSafe` answers a marker instead of an error), the same query is read again
  the lean way (data first) and a line says so -- a reader fault turns streaming off for the rest of the process (a fault
  never doubles every read), a network fault does not. A refused answer (4xx) is never handed to the stream reader.
- **The Risk Analysis Summary collections.** `Get-SIDataLoadPlan` answers its plan as ONE list; the Summary step wrapped
  it in `@(...)`, so with several collections the plan was one item, no item had an Action, and no Summary collection
  was ever loaded (the large install: "4 ... 0 to load, 0 already loaded, 0 not complete", `sidata.SummaryLoad` empty).
  The plan is assigned and enumerated now; every collection listed must be accounted for (to load, already loaded, not
  complete) -- one that is none of them is a FAILED run. A database that holds no complete Summary collection lists every
  Summary collection inside the retention window once (the backfill of what was never loaded; a new install the same).

### A caught failure never ends a run green (#639, working rule 4)

Every failure a step catches and goes on from is a **run issue** (`SI-RunOutcome.ps1`: `Add-SIRunIssue`,
`Get-SIRunIssueOutcome`) with one plain line naming what is missing:

| Level | When | Run record |
|---|---|---|
| WARNING | the data is still delivered whole elsewhere (the stored set stays the last whole one, the source still holds it, or only a convenience was not done) | `success-partial` + the line |
| FAILED | data is short or missing where it should be | `error` + the line; the job fails where that is its only record |

Nothing downstream closes or resolves anything on a short result: the lifecycle and the close-loop do not close on it,
and the collection a partial Risk Analysis run produced is marked partial. Per step:

| Step | Spot | Level | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data sync | findings per CI not stored (failure, short read, no staging table) | FAILED | the newest collection's findings per CI are missing; the stored set is kept, nothing closes |
| Data sync | finding lifecycle not updated (no answer, a failure, no staging table) | WARNING | the findings are stored; nothing was closed |
| Data sync | CI list columns / CI context columns not filled; disabled or out-of-scope owners unreadable | WARNING | the views read each CI's document; unknown never closes |
| Data sync | Summary collection not loaded; Summary plan misses listed collections | FAILED | those rows are not in the database |
| Data sync | a data-out output failed or not whole | FAILED | the customer's file / hand-off is missing or short |
| Data sync | exec view not carried | WARNING | whole in Risk Analysis's blob; the Overview keeps the last one |
| Data sync | data quality not measured | WARNING | nothing is missing from the data |
| Data sync | full asset metadata not stored | WARNING | its snapshots stay in Log Analytics; the next run stores them |
| Data sync | a collection's correlation evidence not written | WARNING | the collection loads; its pages say "not computed" |
| CI build | a batch did not reach SI_CI_CL | FAILED | Risk Analysis reads its CI context there; the correlation job fails |
| CI build | the CI workbook not written; CIs not retired | WARNING | every CI is whole in the database and the web app |
| Risk Analysis | SI_CI_CL unreadable -> empty CI index | WARNING | findings scored without CI context: in the log and on the END record (`success-partial`) |
| Risk Analysis | the CIs could not be built in the run (Community) -> the stored ones | by design | a fallback to the last complete build, said as a warning in the log |
| CMDB (ServiceNow) | an engine profile unreadable | FAILED | its assets would be missing from the hand-off: nothing is sent, the run is recorded failed |
| CMDB (ServiceNow) | SI_AssetProperties_CL unreadable | WARNING | every asset handed over with the narrow attribute set; recorded `partial` |
| SQL CMDB | hand-off rows not written | FAILED | ServiceNow must not import a short staging view |
| SQL CMDB | a kind / the map unreadable for the hand-off; the hand-off connectors did not run | WARNING | the previous rows / the last whole batch stay |
| Vulnerabilities | CI key history or asset aliases unreadable | WARNING + nothing closed this run | a record under a previous key could look absent |
| Vulnerabilities | reports' tier scope or retired assets unreadable | WARNING | only fewer closes (out of scope / AssetRetired) |
| Collection | Log Analytics post failed after the records reached the database | WARNING (unchanged, by design) | the records are whole in the database (the CI build's source); Risk Analysis marks itself partial on it |
| Correlation map | ledger unavailable -> provisional ids | by design (unchanged) | labelled in SI_IdSource; a connector never creates CIs from them |

### Every column on every data view -- the chooser, the context, the exports (Pro web app, #589)

Every page that lists assets, CIs, findings, vulnerabilities, records, CMDB items, exemptions, tasks or a management
drill-down lets the person decide the columns, opens with the context that makes a row readable on its own, and exports
exactly the columns chosen. One mechanism, every view plugs into it:

- **The columns a view offers** (`Columns/DataViewLayout`): its own columns, and -- by what its rows are tied to -- the
  extra columns of `Core/ProData/DataColumns.cs`: for rows that are CIs or tied to one (a CI id or the collection's asset
  key) the CI id (`ci.id`), every CI document field (`ci.f.<field>`), one column per identifier type with its VALUES
  (`ci.i.MdeDeviceId`, `AzureResourceId`, `AadDeviceId`, `ExposureGraphNodeId`, the SI asset id, any other type the data
  has), the linked objects (`ci.links`: every linked object id) and every property each source reported
  (`ci.s.<source>.<property>`, one nested level, deeper values as compact JSON -- the Full details level); for rows that are
  findings the finding context (`fc.*`: affected software, vendor, versions, description, the fix = the recommended update and
  its id, remediation, more details, published / modified, exploit, category, subcategory, impact, CMDB id + name +
  criticality -- each read from the first of its field names the row carries, the si_ names first) and every finding field
  (`fi.<field>`); for one row per CVE or per issue the same context over a sample of its findings, the software as a
  distinct list, and the affected assets ("names, + N more").
- **Read late, for the rows shown.** The page (or the export) is chosen first -- filtered, sorted, counted, paged -- then
  its rows' extra values are read by their keys: the CI and its document, the identifiers and links, the newest objects of
  the wanted sources (index seeks on the shown keys; never the documents of every CI), a finding's row by its clustered key,
  a CVE's sample through the CVE index. The values are cut out in the web app, so 5 or 50 extra columns cost the same reads.
  A SQL grid keeps its statement and its cache whatever a person chose (`GridLayout`): the layout decides only what shows.
- **One chooser** (`Pages/Shared/_ColumnChooser.cshtml`): the columns shown now, in order, then everything else per group
  (This view, CI, Identifiers, Linked objects, one group per source, Finding context, Finding fields) with a search box, so a
  list of hundreds stays usable. It saves through one page (`/Columns`): a person's own layout, or (an Admin) the tenant
  default, per view (cfg.ColumnLayout), up to 1,000 columns. A stored key the view no longer knows is dropped when read.
- **Each person's own fine-tuning, per view** -- kept in the Pro database by sign-in name, so it follows the person to any
  browser. The chooser partial also renders a *view bar* above every data view's table, and the same `/Columns` page takes
  every save; one read per view and page (a marker row and key seeks in one batch) brings the columns, the last sort and
  filters, the widths and the named layouts.
  - *The last sort, filters and search* (`Columns/ViewState`): the state is the view's own address parameters (sort, dir,
    q, size, `f.<column>`, the named filters of the CI grids), stored as a JSON object in cfg.ViewState. The page's script
    reports it after a change the person makes on the page; the server puts it into the request only when the address names
    no sort, filter or search. An address that names one always wins and opening it stores nothing -- links, bookmarks,
    drill-downs and exports behave as before. The page number and the selected rows are never stored. *Clear* in the view
    bar (or any link of the page back to the bare view) forgets it. A table that is sorted in the browser has its sort,
    search and filter row remembered and restored by the script instead.
  - *Move a column on the table header*: small move-left / move-right buttons in each column header (keyboard reachable,
    labelled for screen readers) and drag-and-drop of a header, saved at once through the same save as the chooser. A grid
    the server sorts is rearranged in place; a table sorted in the browser is loaded again in the saved order.
  - *Column widths*: drag a header's right edge (or focus it and use the arrow keys); double-click sets the column back to
    automatic. Stored as `{"column key": pixels}` in cfg.ViewState and applied by the script (the content security policy
    allows no inline style).
  - *Named layouts* (cfg.ViewLayout): the columns in their order, the sort and filters and the widths under a name, chosen
    from the *Layout* box of the view bar. Choosing one makes it the person's set-up; "(changed)" shows when they changed
    something since, and *Save the changes* writes it back. A layout can be renamed and deleted (whoever used it keeps the
    columns they see). An Admin can publish a layout for everyone; a published layout is changed only by an Admin, checked
    in the same batch that writes. *Reset to the tenant default* still returns to the tenant's columns.
  - Without script the Columns panel still chooses, orders and saves, the Layout box still switches and Clear still clears;
    the header controls and the remembering of sort and filters are added by the script. Every save is in the audit trail.
  - *What the audit trail records of a view.* Layouts: saving or resetting the columns of a view (a person's own and the
    tenant default) and creating, changing, renaming, deleting and publishing a named layout. Not recorded: a person's own
    last sort, filters and column widths, and CHOOSING a named layout -- switching changes nothing but what that person
    sees, the layout itself is unchanged. The action names of the unrecorded steps stay on the closed action list, marked
    as no longer recorded, because rows written by an earlier version may carry them.
  - Both tables are additive: a database that does not have them yet shows every view as before.
- **Shipped layouts** (`Columns/DataViewDefaults`): the view's own columns first, in the order they always had, then the
  context its rows carry -- for a finding the software, description, fix and remediation and its CI; for a CI its id,
  identifier values, linked objects, owner, department, OS, IP, subscription, CMDB and last seen; one row per CVE names its
  software in the title's place. Every reference is shown as id AND name (subscription, management group, resource group,
  tenant, app, service principal, owner, group, CMDB item, CI): when one half is shown, the other is added -- empty until the
  data carries it.
- **Exports** (the words in `Columns/ExportLabels`): *Export all rows (CSV)* and *Export all rows to Excel* -- every row
  matching the filters (every page), exactly the columns chosen; *Export selected rows to Excel / (CSV)* -- the ticked rows,
  the same columns; *Export all columns* -- every own column and every extra column on offer, and for CI rows the CI
  document's every field and the Full details sheet. Where a row stands for several findings (a CVE, a CI, a service) the
  action bar also offers *Export the findings of the selected rows*.
- **Page tables** that are not SQL grids (CMDB, exemptions, tasks, the management drill-downs, findings, the Summary) use the
  data table (`Columns/DataTable`, `Pages/Shared/_DataTable.cshtml`) with one export handler (`DataViewPageModel`,
  `?handler=TableExport`).
- **The list of pages** (`Columns/DataViews`): every page of the menu is a data view, a decided redesign, or keeps fixed
  columns with its reason (configuration, dashboards, operations, editors). The shared grid takes preset filters and a
  row-click hook that opens a side drawer without a page reload (`data-row-drawer`, `js/app/row-drawer.js`) -- the tier
  board's redesign builds on both.

### 6a. Access and roles (Pro web app)

The web app has the same four roles as PIM Manager, so both products work alike.

| Role | What it can do |
|---|---|
| **Reader** | Every view, every export and the chat. No changes. |
| **Delegated** | What an Admin can change -- exemptions, overrides, tier moves and reviews -- but only inside the **scopes** assigned to it. Read-only everywhere else; the Admin pages (settings, connectors, templates, jobs) stay closed. |
| **Admin** | Everything in the installation, except roles and the installation's own lifecycle. |
| **SuperAdmin** | Everything an Admin can do, plus assigning roles and scopes (*Configuration > Access (roles + scopes)*), the licence, product updates and template releases, and support access. |
| *Wallboard* | The kiosk sign-in of a big screen: the wall board and nothing else. |

**Two layers.** The app roles on the Entra app registration decide who can sign in at all: *SecurityInsight
SuperAdmin*, *SecurityInsight Admin*, *SecurityInsight Reader* and *SecurityInsight Wallboard* (Reader is the role that
earlier releases called Viewer; existing assignments keep working). On top of that, a SuperAdmin maps Entra **users and
groups** (by object id, shown with their name) to a role on *Configuration > Access (roles + scopes)*. The **effective role** is the higher of the
two: an Admin app role is never lowered by a mapping, and a Reader can be raised to Delegated or Admin without touching
Entra. A mapping only ever raises someone who can already sign in. Every change on the Access page is written at once
with the SuperAdmin's name and a reason in the change history, and applies at the person's next page load.

**Groups.** The sign-in token carries the security groups a person is in, so a mapped group applies to its members.
Someone in more groups than a token can list gets only their own mappings, unless the web app's identity may read group
membership from Microsoft Graph (the setting `Access:GraphLookup`, with the application permissions GroupMember.Read.All
and User.ReadBasic.All granted to the web app's identity by an administrator; setup does not grant them).

**The first SuperAdmin** is whoever holds the SuperAdmin app role. Setup assigns it to the person who runs it, and the
administrators named in the install get Admin. From there, a SuperAdmin assigns everyone else. A SuperAdmin who holds
the role only through the Access page cannot lower their own access there; another SuperAdmin can.

**Scopes.** A Delegated assignment names what the person is responsible for, as pairs of *scope type* and *value*:
security domains (Endpoint, Identity, Azure, PublicIP, CrossEngine and any other domain in your data, or every domain),
optionally narrowed to asset kinds and tiers. A change is inside the scope when it is inside every part the scope names:
"Identity, Tier 2 and 3" allows an exemption on an Identity finding of a Tier 2 asset, not on a Tier 0 one. A change
that spans more than the scope is refused -- an exemption of one issue on *every* asset spans every tier, a shared tier
rule spans every domain, and moving an asset from Tier 2 to Tier 1 needs both tiers. Several assignments (a person's
own and their groups') add up. A security-domain scope does not hide anything: the person sees every view and changes
only inside the scope. A scope type can also restrict what its holder **sees**: the data queries then carry a filter
built from the scopes, so such a person sees only their own assets and findings (this is how department scopes will
work; no scope type restricts visibility today).

**Checked on the server, every time.** Every page and every action is checked against the role and the scope by the
server; hiding a button is never the check. A refused action answers *Not allowed* (HTTP 403) with the reason, and
nothing is written. A bulk action -- several findings selected, or all matching a filter -- is allowed only when every
selected row is inside the scope; otherwise the whole action is refused and says how many rows are outside. Staged
changes are checked again on *Review & commit*: if a scope was taken away in between, the change shows why it can no
longer be committed, and nothing is written. One decision service answers every one of these questions, so the
exemption flow's owners and approvers per security domain are Delegated (or Admin) assignments -- not a second
permission system.

**How someone signed in** is part of every decision: an Entra sign-in, a magic link, or a magic link confirmed with a
one-time code. A role can require a strong sign-in (Entra, or a magic link with a code) for an action such as
approving; none of today's roles does.

**For developers -- the one check.** `IAccessScope` (web app, `Auth/Access.cs`): `Can(user, action, target)`,
`CanAll(user, action, targets)` for bulk, and `Visibility(user)` for the data-query filter. Actions: View, Exempt,
Override, TierMove, Review, Comment, Recommend, Approve, Administer, ManageAccess, Licence, Lifecycle, SupportAccess. A
target is a value per scope type (`new ScopeTarget(domain, assetKind, tier)`, `.With("department", value)`). Roles are
data (`RoleDefinitions`: rank, actions, scope-bound, actions that need a strong sign-in) and scope types are data
(`ScopeTypes`: anchor, restricts visibility, the finding column it filters), so a new role or scope type is one more
row, not a change for the callers. An exemption approver for a domain is `Can(user, AccessAction.Approve, new
ScopeTarget(domain, null, null))`. The mapping is the table `cfg.AccessAssignment` in the Pro database (every change in
`cfg.ChangeLog`, Name `access/<object id>`).

**The header** shows the effective role -- *Reader*, *Delegated (Identity, Azure)*, *Admin* or *SuperAdmin* -- and the
*No access* page tells each person their role and what the page they opened needs.

### 6b. Chat (Pro) -- on every view, answering about what is on screen

Ask questions about your estate in plain language, either on the **Chat** page or from any Security posture or
Management view (Findings, Tier board, Vulnerabilities over time, Trends, Risk score, Domains, Top risks,
Tier-0 exposure, Template conformance, Template releases). **Ask about this page** opens the chat beside the
page, and it already knows what you are looking at: the view, the collection, the filters in the address bar and the
selected asset or finding. So *"top 3 here"*, *"explain this"* or *"why is this Tier 0?"* are answered about what is
on screen. The wall board is a big-screen page and has no chat.

- **Read-only, curated.** The chat can only call SecurityInsight's fixed, read-only tools -- the same ones the MCP
  server offers. Every answer lists the tool calls and the query behind each. It cannot change anything.
- **Same access.** Reader, Delegated, Admin and SuperAdmin can ask; the Wallboard account cannot. Only an Admin's chat can read the settings
  history.
- **The page's context is data, not text from the page.** It is sent as a small structured record (view, collection,
  filters, selection) and checked again on the server; nothing from the page's HTML reaches the model.
- **It uses SecurityInsight's own words.** Severities are *Very High, High, Medium-High, Medium, Low* -- there is no
  "Critical". When a question uses another word, the chat reads it the way SecurityInsight means it ("Critical",
  "crit" or "severe" = Very High, "Tier 0" = tier 0, "devices" = Endpoint) and says so in the answer.
- **"Nothing matched" is never "there is nothing".** "Top vulnerabilities" or "top risks" means the highest risk
  score, not a severity filter. When a filter matches no rows, the chat is told which values exist in that collection
  and looks again before answering, so it never reports an empty estate because of a wrong guess.

### 6c. CMDB -- SecurityInsight's own, or an external one (Pro)

Business services, and which assets belong to them, come from ONE CMDB at a time. You choose which on the *CMDB
source* page:

- **SecurityInsight owns the CMDB (SI-homed).** For customers without a CMDB of their own. Services are added on the
  *CMDB* page, each with a number -- SVC-0001, SVC-0002, ... -- that is never given to another service, a name, and
  the fields the old CMDB.csv carried: owner and owner e-mail, criticality (Critical, High, Medium, Low -- the words
  risk weighting reads), data sensitivity (Restricted, Confidential, Internal, Public), environment, description and
  department. A service is **retired**, never deleted: it keeps its links and its history, stops counting
  everywhere, and cannot be changed again. Every change is in the change history with who, when and why.
- **An external CMDB.** Either a **CSV** in the CMDB.csv format (`cmdbID;cmdbName;DataSensitivity;Criticality;Owner;
  OwnerMail`, plus Environment, Description, Department and any column of your own, which is kept as written) --
  uploaded on the CMDB page or read from a path by the scheduled CMDB import -- or **ServiceNow**, whose business
  services and their members are pulled through the ServiceNow connector. An external CMDB is imported as a whole:
  services that are gone from it are retired here, and with a memberships file (`cmdbID;AssetName` or
  `cmdbID;AssetKey`) or ServiceNow's relations, links that are gone are removed. The file is checked line by line
  first and **nothing is imported when a line is wrong**; the page lists every wrong line. A ServiceNow read that
  does not complete imports nothing either. An asset a link names but SecurityInsight does not know (or whose name
  is not unique) is reported, not stored. In SecurityInsight the external CMDB is **read-only** -- the CMDB page and
  the service map say so, and changes are made in the source.
- **Switching** is explicit. The review says what happens before anything is saved: from the next data sync the
  services of the chosen CMDB are used; the other CMDB's services stay stored with their links and history, unused,
  and switching back makes them authoritative again. Nothing is copied or merged.
- **Your v2.2 CMDB.csv** can be imported once into SecurityInsight's own CMDB -- with the button on the CMDB page or
  the setup step `setup\Import-SICmdbCsv.ps1` (which checks and counts first and imports only with `-Apply`). Each
  service gets a new number and keeps its old cmdbID; the result is counted (added, already there, links added, links
  not imported).

**The service map** links assets to services on a board of lanes: services are columns, assets are cards (name,
kind, tier and weighted risk from the newest collection), loaded page by page and filtered on the server by asset
kind, tier, department (of the services) and "unlinked only". Select cards (their checkbox or Ctrl/Cmd-click) or
tick *all matching the filter*, and drag them onto a service to link them; drag cards from a service back onto the
asset list to unlink them from that service; drag from one service onto another to add them there too. **An asset may
belong to several services**: it then appears in each of their columns, with a badge saying in how many services it
is (their numbers on hover); linking it to one more service never takes it out of another. A drop writes nothing --
it stages one change for all the selected assets on *Review & commit*, like the tier board, which shows what changes
and warns when an asset will belong to more than one service.

**One answer to "which services does this asset belong to".** The data sync plugs the authoritative CMDB into the
service-membership resolver (section 5, *Services per collection*), so the Services view, the weighted risk per
service and departments all read services the same way. Without a configured CMDB the CMDB.csv columns Risk Analysis
carries are used, as before.

**In Pro the runs read this CMDB.** The asset profiles' CMDB columns (`cmdbId`, `cmdbName`, `cmdbCriticality`,
`cmdbDataSensitivity`, and every other CMDB column as `CMDB_<column>`) and the CMDB criticality / data-sensitivity
weighting of Risk Analysis come from the CMDB cache the profiling run refreshes. With a Pro database configured that
cache is filled from the authoritative CMDB's services instead of a file:

- **One switch point.** The CMDB source resolver picks *the CMDB in the Pro database* wherever a Pro database is
  configured (with CMDB enrichment on); it ranks above a CMDB.csv, which is then not read -- one CMDB is ever active,
  never a mix. Without a Pro database nothing changes: the CSV is read as in 2.2 (now also from `SI_CmdbCsvPath` when
  the file is kept outside the SecurityInsight folder -- that location was previously not recognised by the resolver).
- **The same shape.** The services are handed to the cache in exactly the rows the CSV gave: the same columns, the same
  values, every extra column. A service migrated from a v2.2 CMDB.csv keeps answering to its **old cmdbID**, so profile
  rules (`set.cmdbId`) and existing rows keep matching; a service added in SecurityInsight answers to its SVC number,
  an imported CSV or ServiceNow service to its own number. Enrichment and scoring code are unchanged -- a test feeds
  the same CMDB both ways and requires byte-identical cache records, enrichment, Risk Analysis scores and weights.
- **What the import normalises.** The import trims values and writes criticality and data sensitivity in their
  canonical case (`critical` becomes `Critical`). The weighting already matched case-insensitively and trimmed, so the
  weight is the same; a value with stray spaces (` Critical `), which the CSV path did not count as business-critical,
  now is.
- **Never silent.** When the CMDB in the Pro database has no services but a v2.2 CMDB.csv is still on disk, the run
  warns, names the file and says how to import it -- it does not quietly read the file. A database without the CMDB
  tables is a failed refresh, reported as such.
- **In a container** the job reads the database as its managed identity, as the settings layer does; Risk Analysis
  needs nothing of its own -- it reads the CMDB columns the profilers wrote.
- **Not yet:** links made on the service map do not enrich profiles (as in 2.2, a profile gets its CMDB service from a
  profile rule's `set.cmdbId`); they drive the Services view.

### 6d. CMDB connector -- SQL: every asset as a CI in the Pro database (Pro)

The CMDB above is *inbound* (services you own or import). The SQL CMDB connector is *outbound*: the job
`caj-si-asset-cmdb-sql` (`engine/asset-cmdb/Invoke-SICmdbSql.ps1`, 05:55 UTC, after asset correlation and asset
properties) writes every asset SecurityInsight knows into a CI table in the same Pro database, for reporting and Power BI.
It is the SQL twin of the ServiceNow CMDB connector and follows the vulnerability connector's safety model.

**The tables** (`sql/si-cmdbsync-schema.sql`, schema `cmdbsync`, applied by `setup/Initialize-SIDataSql.ps1`):

| Object | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `ConfigurationItem` | one row per CI: key, name, kind, tier, criticality, owner, owner mail, department, services, sources, first / last seen, state (active / retired), absent runs, retired at, last change, last run |
| `ConfigurationItemIdentifier` | the CI's identifiers (MDE device id, Azure resource id, ...); one that disappears is stamped `RemovedAt` |
| `ConfigurationItemService` | the CI's business services; a link that ends is stamped `UnlinkedAt` |
| `ConfigurationItemHistory` | every change: created, updated (per field, old and new value), retired, reactivated -- with the run |
| `SyncRun` | one row per run: outcome (applied / refused / error), the snapshot it read, the counts, and why |
| `vConfigurationItem` | the reporting view: one row per CI, identifiers as `type:value; ...` |

**The key** is the data backend's (`sidata.Asset.AssetKey`): the identity ledger's correlation id when the asset has a
durable one, else the asset id. A CI therefore joins its findings, department and services directly. Members seen by
several sources (an Azure VM that is also an MDE device) are one CI; its kind, name and tier come from the most descriptive
member and the most critical tier.

**Which assets.** Endpoints and Azure resources by default; public IPs when `SI_Pro_CmdbSql_Kinds` lists `publicip`.
Identities are never CIs (the ServiceNow CMDB connector's rule: whether an Entra identity is a CI is unsettled).
An asset is *seen* when its kind's profile published it within `SI_Pro_CmdbSql_SeenWithinDays` (8) -- low tiers are
re-profiled weekly. Department comes from the data backend's responsibility resolution; services, criticality and owner
from the authoritative CMDB (else the services Risk Analysis carried), the owner of the most critical service first, else
the department's business owner.

**The safety model.**
1. *Never from a partial snapshot.* Each kind's newest snapshot must be shown complete: every shard of the profiler run
   that produced it recorded its end with `success`, and it is no older than the seen-window. Otherwise the run is
   refused: no CI changes, and the run record says why. Without the correlation map the run is refused too.
2. *Plan first.* Create, update (only the fields that changed, each one in the history), reactivate, count an absence,
   retire. A plan-only run (`-WhatIf`, `SI_Pro_CmdbSql_DryRun`) writes nothing.
3. *Absence is not removal.* A CI that is no longer seen is counted absent once per new snapshot of its kind and retired
   after `SI_Pro_CmdbSql_RetireAfterRuns` complete runs in a row (default 2). Reading the same snapshot again counts
   nothing; a kind taken out of scope keeps its CIs as they are.
4. *A collapsed estate is refused.* An empty seen set, or a kind that suddenly sees less than half of its active CIs,
   stops the run.
5. *Never delete; one transaction.* The plan is staged and applied in one transaction under an application lock; a run
   that finds another run applied after it read the table writes nothing and plans again next time.

Each run records its run health (engine `asset-cmdb-sql`), a telemetry run report (`si-cmdb-sql`) and an audit event
`cmdb.ci.sync` (a plan is recorded as a plan). The CMDB page shows a read-only *SQL CI table* card: the last run and its
outcome, when the table was last written, active and retired CIs, the last run's counts and the queries behind them.

### 6d2. SQL CMDB hand-off connector -- the CIs your ServiceNow imports (Pro)

A connector of kind **sql** with the **cmdb** direction (*Configuration > Connectors (setup)*) gives your ServiceNow
SecurityInsight's view of every CI in a SQL database of your choosing. ServiceNow imports these tables with a JDBC data
source (MID server) into an import set; your transform/IRE creates and updates CIs. SecurityInsight writes nothing in
ServiceNow, holds no ServiceNow credential and creates no CI -- every rule that changes a CI is yours.

**Settings** (no secrets): `server`, `database` (required); `changeGuardPercent` (default 10) and `keepBatches`
(default 3). The connector's *Mode* is honoured: *whatif* plans and logs, *apply* writes. It is run by the SQL CMDB job
(`caj-si-asset-cmdb-sql`), right after the Pro database's own hand-off, from the same rows -- read once per run -- and
only when that run's asset collection was accepted as complete.

**The tables** (`sql/si-cmdb-handoff-target.sql`, schema `snowstage`, created by the job's first writing run):

| Object | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `Batch` | one row per run: state (*writing*, *complete*, *held*, *failed*), the counts (CIs, new, changed, missing, key-values, relations), the previous batch it was compared with, and why |
| `BatchCi` | one row per CI: the stable SecurityInsight key, its class hint (device, Azure resource, identity) and proposed ServiceNow class, name, FQDN, DNS domain, serial number, MAC address, Azure resource id, Entra device id, Defender device id, Entra object id, tier and why, criticality, data sensitivity, internet exposure, owner, owner mail, department, the evidence the correlation rests on, last seen, the run, the row hash and the delta time |
| `BatchCiKeyValue` | the CI's Azure tags and Defender machine tags; one that vanished stays as *removed* |
| `BatchCiRelation` | the CI's relations from Azure (VM to disk, network interface, user-assigned identity) |
| `vImportCi`, `vImportCiKeyValue`, `vImportCiRelation`, `vProposedCi` | **the import views**: the same columns as the Pro database's hand-off views (one transform map reads either; `vImportCi` ends with `u_data_sensitivity`), followed by `u_owner`, `u_owner_mail`, `u_department`, `u_batch_id` and `u_batch_time` |
| `vImportBatch` | every batch with its state and counts |

**How a batch is written.**
1. *Never a partial collection.* When a kind (endpoints, Azure resources, identities) or the asset correlation results
   could not be read, no batch is written and ServiceNow keeps importing the previous one.
2. *The complete flag last.* The rows go in under the run's batch id; one statement then marks the batch complete, and
   only when it holds exactly the CIs that were sent. The import views show only the **newest complete batch**, so an
   import that runs while SecurityInsight is writing reads the previous batch, whole. A write that fails leaves the batch
   *failed* and the previous one in place.
3. *The mass-change guard.* When more than `changeGuardPercent` of the previous batch's CIs are missing from this one,
   the batch is **held**: it is recorded as *held* and never shown, the guard *cmdb.handoff.mass-change* mails and
   reports it, and ServiceNow keeps the previous batch. New CIs never trip it. Release it once on *Operations > Guards*
   (or `Invoke-SICmdbSql.ps1 -ReleaseHandoffChange <run id>`); otherwise the next run that is back within the limit is
   handed over by itself.
4. *Plan only writes nothing* -- not the tables, not a batch row.
5. *Delta.* `u_changed_at` is carried from the previous batch while a CI's row hash (its content, including owner and
   department) is unchanged, so an import filtered on `u_changed_at` later than the last import sends only what changed.
6. After a batch is complete, the rows of older batches are removed; the newest `keepBatches` complete batches stay.

Each connector run is recorded in the connector's run history (*Connectors > the connector > Last runs*: new, changed and
missing CIs as planned open / update / close; a held batch as *halted*).

**Permissions.** The job identity needs, in the hand-off database, `db_datareader` and `db_datawriter`, plus
`db_ddladmin` for the first run that creates the tables (or apply `sql/si-cmdb-handoff-target.sql` once yourself). The
account your MID server connects with needs `db_datareader` only. On Azure SQL with Entra-only authentication, create the
job identity as a contained user (`CREATE USER [<identity>] WITH SID = <client id as hex>, TYPE = E;`, the statement the
container setup prints for the Pro database).

**The ServiceNow side** (your ServiceNow team; documentation only -- SecurityInsight changes nothing there):
1. **Data source** -- *System Import Sets > Data Sources*: type *JDBC*, format *SQL Server*, *Use MID Server*, the
   hand-off database, query *Specific SQL* `SELECT * FROM snowstage.vImportCi` (one data source each for `vImportCi`,
   `vImportCiKeyValue` and `vImportCiRelation`).
2. **Import set table** -- let the first *Test load* create it (for example `u_si_ci_import`); every column is a `u_`
   column of the view.
3. **Transform map** (or IntegrationHub ETL) -- map `u_name`, `u_fqdn`, `u_serial_number`, `u_mac_address`,
   `u_azure_resource_id` and the other identifiers to the class from `u_proposed_class`, with the discovery source
   *SecurityInsight*, so every row goes through Identification and Reconciliation (IRE).
4. **IRE identification rules** -- keep your own; add `u_si_correlation_id` as the **last** identifier entry (a
   tie-breaker) on the rule's own table, and a reconciliation rule for the attributes SecurityInsight is authoritative
   for (tier, exposure, last seen).
5. **Data sensitivity (optional)** -- `u_data_sensitivity` is the value SecurityInsight weighs risk with: your
   asset-profile rule's override wins over the CMDB record (the CI's own value, else the most sensitive of its services),
   so it can differ from what your CMDB holds. In the transform map, map it to the field your CMDB keeps data sensitivity
   in (for example a `u_data_sensitivity` field on the class), with SecurityInsight as a low-priority source -- or leave
   it unmapped and keep your CMDB's own value. A change to it moves `u_changed_at`, so a delta import carries it.
6. **Schedule** the import after the SecurityInsight CMDB job; for a delta import filter on `u_changed_at`. The proposed
   CIs (`vProposedCi`) are a report for your CMDB team -- SecurityInsight creates no CI.

### 6e. Reports and outputs (Pro) -- the report designer, exclusions, weights and the output scope per destination

*Configuration > Reports & outputs* replaces editing the Risk Analysis YAML and JSON files. Readers see every page
read-only; an Admin changes it; nothing is written on these pages -- every change is staged and written on *Review &
commit* in your name, one change-history row per item, and refused (nothing written) when an item changed since you
staged it. Every page and change is on the audit trail.

- **Report catalog.** Every report, the vendor's and yours, in one server-side grid (search, domain, source, on / off,
  narrowed scope; sort and page on the server): purpose, domain, the tables its query reads, its severity scope
  (Very High, High, Medium-High, Medium, Low) and tier scope (tier 0-3), the templates it is in, whether it is on, and
  where it comes from (*vendor*, *changed* by you, *yours*). One report opens with checkboxes for its severity and tier
  scope, the on / off switch, *Back to the vendor's*, its query and *Test the query*. Bulk on the selected reports:
  untick Low, switch on / off, back to the vendor's. A report's scope decides which of its findings are reported at
  all; a report that is switched off leaves every template.
- **Report templates.** At the top, one row per template -- name, kind (*Built-in*, *Built-in, changed*, *Your own*),
  the job that uses it in plain words (*Summary report job*, *Detailed report job*; the Container Apps job's name only
  as a tooltip) and its number of reports; the selected template's row is highlighted and marked *Selected*, the
  others offer *Open*. On a phone each row becomes a small card. Below, the catalog (searchable, with *Hide reports
  already in the template*) beside *Reports in <template> (n)* and the job that runs it, in order. A report already in
  the template is muted in the catalog and shows *Added ✓* instead of *Add*; adding or removing one flips it at once.
  Drag a report in, drag to reorder, take one out -- or use *Add*, the ↑ / ↓ buttons, a quiet *Remove* (red only on
  hover / focus), Alt + Up / Alt + Down and Delete on a focused report. Create, copy, rename (your own templates; a
  built-in template keeps its name) and retire templates. Which template each job runs comes from the
  *RiskAnalysis_ReportTemplate_Default_Summary* / *_Detailed* settings; a template a job runs cannot be retired.
  The page's sub-tabs (Report catalog ... Management summary) mark the current one as the selected tab.
- **Custom reports.** *New report from a query*: a KQL editor with the report contract beside it -- the columns every
  row must carry (Category, Subcategory, ConfigurationId, SecuritySeverity, CriticalityTierLevel), the optional risk
  factor columns (RiskFactor_Consequence, RiskFactor_Probability, numbers), the scores Risk Analysis sets on every
  row, and CollectionTime and the other run columns, which Risk Analysis stamps. *Test* runs the query **read-only**
  against your workspace with the web app's own read access (at most 50 rows shown, 60 seconds at most) and shows
  the rows and every contract problem. A control command, a reach into another workspace or cluster, external data
  or an external call is refused before anything runs. *Save* stores it as your own report and links it into the
  templates you tick.
- **Output scope.** What each destination receives of what Risk Analysis finds: *Excel + mail* (the workbook, its
  JSON file, the AI summary and the mail), the *vulnerability connectors* (SQL, ServiceNow) and the *CMDB connectors*
  (SQL, ServiceNow). For a findings destination: which report templates and single reports feed it and which
  severities, tiers and domains pass; for a CMDB connector: which tiers and asset kinds. Each destination shows how
  many findings (CVE findings for the vulnerability connectors, assets for CMDB) of the newest collection pass, by the
  same rule the engines use. Nothing ticked = everything, as before.
  - **A scope never closes anything as fixed.** A CMDB connector leaves an asset outside its scope exactly as it is.
    A vulnerability connector does not send a finding outside its scope, and closes an open record of it with the
    reason *Out of scope* -- never *Remediated*, never counted by the close limit -- and reopens the same record when
    the finding comes back into scope. A finding SecurityInsight no longer reports at all is judged by the close-loop's
    own rules, as before.

**Close reasons of the vulnerability connectors.** Every close carries its reason; only *Remediated* is a fix:
*Remediated* (absent for the configured number of complete runs on an asset seen in each), *AssetRetired* (the asset
was retired), *NoLongerMonitored* (the asset is excluded from assessment), *Out of scope* (still reported, or the asset
still seen, but outside what this connector receives: its output scope, or a tier the vulnerability report no longer
covers -- e.g. an asset that went from tier 2 to tier 3), and *Duplicate* (a second record of a finding that already
has one, retired when an asset's id changes -- the older record keeps the history). The close limit measures only the
closes of a run that end a finding (*Remediated*, *AssetRetired*, *NoLongerMonitored*) against every open record;
findings absent for the first time, held, out of scope or duplicate are never counted. A close that Defender
corroborates -- the run is complete, the device is in the newest results, and Defender assessed it after the finding
was last reported -- is not limited either: a patch round that closes many findings at once goes through, and the
limit only stops closes nothing corroborates (a stale device, a missing source, a partial read).

**Releasing held closes once.** When the close limit stops a run, only the closes it counted are held; they are kept
as one set for that run (the counts per asset and per CVE, and the findings). An Admin can release that set ONCE for
7 days -- on Operations > Guards (safety checks) ("Release these closes", also opened by the link in the guard mail), or on a VM with
`Invoke-SIVulnLoop.ps1 -ReleaseHeldCloses <run id>`. The connector's job starts at once (or its next run picks the
release up): it checks that the newest results are complete, closes the released findings that are still absent,
leaves any that came back open, and lets nothing else past the limit. Releasing changes no setting; both the release
and what it closed are on the audit trail. The SQL table stores the reasons
as they are; for ServiceNow and REST connectors the connector setting *closeReasons* maps each reason to the value the
other system takes (e.g. a close code); a reason that is not mapped is written as it is.
  - **Log Analytics always receives every row**; the Excel + mail scope narrows only Risk Analysis's own view.
  - The rule: an empty list = any value; a blank value on a finding passes (as a report's own scope keeps blanks);
    severity compares by its words (Critical = Very High); tier by number or tier label; a finding passes the report
    list when any report it came from is in it (templates are resolved to their reports for each run).
- **Exclusions.** The global excluded asset tags, and per vendor report the excluded CVEs, configuration ids, tags and
  the minimum CVE age, as lists (add, remove, one search over every list) instead of raw JSON. A v2.2 file
  (*RiskAnalysisGlobalExclusions.custom.json*, *&lt;Report&gt;.exclude(.custom).json*) can be imported into the lists.
  Notes in the document are kept; emptying every list removes the document.
- **Weights.** The weighted risk factors per engine (endpoint, identity, azure, publicip) -- for the whole solution or
  for one report (a report's own weights replace the solution's for it): the combine mode, the cap, and per field its
  value = multiplier map and default (whole numbers, 100 = 1.0x), checked by the same rules as the engine. The other
  sections of a v2.2 weights file (the risk-model mappers) are shown read-only: Risk Analysis 3.0 reads only the
  weighted risk factors.

**How it reaches the engines.** Report and template changes are the Risk Analysis catalog items (vendor templates +
your changes) the settings layer already materialises for every run; an item you did not change is the vendor's, byte
for byte, so an unchanged catalog is materialised exactly as before. The output scope is one more configuration item
per destination, materialised into one file for the run (`config\output-scope.json`) with every named template already
resolved to its reports; Risk Analysis applies the *excel* scope to its own view, the vulnerability close-loop to each
SQL / ServiceNow connector's plan, the CMDB connectors to the assets they plan. No item = no file = everything, as
before.

### 7. Connectors (Pro)

SecurityInsight Pro sends its vulnerability findings to the systems you choose: a SQL table, ServiceNow, or any risk or ticketing system with a REST API. Each connector is set up on the **Connectors** page and stored in the Pro database. It has its own mode (*whatif* plans and logs what it would send and sends nothing; *apply* sends) and its own permission to create and to close items. Every close still follows the close-loop's rule (several complete runs without the vulnerability on an asset that was seen), and a large or sudden drop is held for a person to review. A REST connector is described by a mapping -- how to sign in, and how to list, create, update, close and reopen an item -- so connecting a new system needs no code. It remembers the id of every item it creates and only ever changes those; items others created are never touched. Passwords and tokens stay in your Key Vault: a connector stores only their names. Each run is listed per connector on **Connector status**.

### 8. Close-loop daily mail (Pro)

Once a day, by default at 10:45 UTC after the close-loop, SecurityInsight Pro mails a summary of the last 24 hours: what was opened, closed and reopened by severity and asset tier, what is open now, the most severe new and closed items, and the last 7 days when the data backend is set up. A close because the asset was retired or left the scope is not counted as a fix. A quiet day still sends a short "nothing changed" mail, so it is never mistaken for a missing report. It uses the Risk Analysis mail relay and reads only. Turn it on and choose recipients and the time on the web app's e-mail settings page; a new time takes effect when setup runs again.

### 8a. Severity words in the mails, and no time to fix (#705)

A finding's **severity** is printed with the SI words (Very High / High / Medium-High / Medium / Low); a stored or source
*Critical* is printed **Very High**. The **risk rating** keeps Critical / High / Moderate / Low. Changed 2026-10-15:

- **Close-loop daily mail** -- the counters are keyed on the SI words (`ConvertTo-SICloseLoopSeverity`). They were keyed on
  Critical / High / Medium / Low while the close-loop record holds the finding's `SecuritySeverity` ("Very High"), so every
  Very High item fell into *Other* and the top column showed **0**; Medium-High is its own column (it was read as Medium).
- **Governance digest / review** -- Medium-High has its own rank (2, between High and Medium; it fell outside every rank
  and was left out of the digest); a printed severity goes through `Get-SIGovernanceSeverityLabel`. The setting
  `SI_Pro_GovernanceNotify_MinSeverity` keeps its values (Critical / High / Medium / Low); *Medium* now also announces
  Medium-High. **Department report** -- a printed severity goes through `Get-SIDepartmentSeverityLabel`.
- **Risk Analysis mail** -- the table's top column is headed *Very High*; the body names the report *Summary report* /
  *Detailed report* (`Get-RAMailReportName`), never the internal template id; the "AI narrative not included" line links
  the setting's page instead of naming "the launcher".
- **Web app** -- the executive view and the wall board panel head the top column *Very High* (`ExecKpi.SeverityLabel`);
  the service / department grids and the services pages say *Very High*; a CI's findings print `SeverityOrder.Label`.

**No time to fix** (owner: "it makes no value"): the close-loop mail has no time-to-fix tile, *Mean time to fix* section,
per-item column or SQL; *Vulnerabilities over time* has no time-to-fix table, help text or Excel sheet; the assistant's
lifecycle / close-loop tools return none. Overdue and due dates stay everywhere. No data column was renamed or removed.

### 8b. Asset tagging -- its own job, its own identity, report only by default

Asset tagging is the one SecurityInsight engine that writes to your tenant: Defender for Endpoint machine tags, Azure
resource tags and Entra custom security attributes, chosen by the asset-tagging rules. In Pro it runs as its own
container job, `caj-si-asset-tagging`, by default at 05:50 UTC, after the profilers, with its rules from the Pro
templates and your overrides (the same rules the **Templates** page shows).

| | Collection jobs (every other engine) | Asset-tagging job |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | the shared job identity (`uami-securityinsight`) | its **own** user-assigned identity (`uami-securityinsight-tagging`) |
| Permissions | read only -- `Machine.Read.All`, never a write permission (locked) | reads what its rules query, plus exactly three writes: Defender `Machine.ReadWrite.All`, **Tag Contributor** at the tagging scope, Graph `CustomSecAttributeAssignment.ReadWrite.All` |
| Granted by | `Bootstrap-ContainerAppJob.ps1 -GrantIdentityRoles` | `Bootstrap-ContainerAppJob.ps1 -GrantTaggingRoles` (opt-in), or `setup/Grant-SIIdentity.ps1 -Tagging -Apply`; the guided install asks |
| Writes | never | only when the Pro setting `SI_Pro_AssetTagging_Apply` is on |
